This is a consensus not only between China and the US but also between the Democratic and Republican parties in America. The consensus has been even clearer [since the summit]. Such a consensus will go beyond Trump’s current term and likely endure for much longer.

This is grounded not only in the reality that the China-US relationship rests on a foundation of strength but also in the common recognition by both sides that a conflict between the two countries would not merely affect themselves; it would throw the entire world into chaos.

Today, much of the world conflates issues of sovereignty with those of geopolitical space. They are completely different.

Zheng Yongnian

Meanwhile, there is still much that can be done. First, shaping the future of China-US relations hinges on high-level summits. Communication between the heads of state should continue. This will continue even if the Democrats return to power or another Republican takes office. It is impossible for China and the US to absolutely not engage.

Second, both sides should continue to enlarge and strengthen the economic and trade ballast. For China, this is a force to help keep US capital engaged. As long as American interests are deeply embedded in China’s economy and China’s in America’s, there is a foundation to build on. Economic interdependence does not necessarily prevent war but it can encourage everyone to be more rational and continue to expand bilateral trade and investment reciprocally.

Third, it is critical for bureaucracies on both sides to earnestly materialise the consensus rather than undermine it. That involves communication and coordination between the two countries’ respective bureaucratic apparatuses as a whole, not just their diplomatic services.

Fourth, the overall media environment needs to improve. Mutual criticism is fine, but demonising each other is not. We talked about the American press’ unfriendliness towards China. Chinese media should also tone down their rhetoric about the US being finished, degraded or in decline. Both sides should practise empathy. If the Chinese press attacks the US all day while American outlets constantly attack China, it will only worsen public sentiment in both countries.

Will Trump’s high-level reception for Xi’s Washington visit put Beijing in a stronger position for their potential bilateral encounters during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting in November and the G20 gathering in December?

The summit gave both nations greater confidence to face and discuss problems directly, rather than shunning them. As for the high-level reception offered by President Trump to President Xi, this reflected reciprocity. When Trump visited China in May, Beijing also arranged warm hospitality for him.

This is a good trend. Major powers truly should show mutual respect. It is often difficult for a major power and a small nation to get along with each other due to the gap in strength. However, it is actually easier for major powers to deal with each other, as their strengths are matched, allowing for genuine equality.

From the perspective of the different civilisations they each represent, China and the US are also bound to cooperate rather than be in conflict. In the sphere of media discourse, there are overly simplistic interpretations of one another on both sides. We should see the reality of the two countries rather than solely look through the lens of ideology and moral sentiment.

How might the two further bilateral summits this year help manage or shape the China-US relationship, especially given that the US midterm elections will be held before those meetings?

Apec is about economics and trade. It grew during the heyday of globalisation and free trade. One of the largest concerns in the region has been that security issues have come to dominate the agenda, overshadowing economics and trade. When security becomes the overriding focus, it can lead to a self-fulfilling prophecy where everyone actually ends up less secure. It is not that the US no longer wants to trade now, but it is adjusting its approach.

China and the US can do a great deal not only on the bilateral dimension but also on advancing economic development across the entire Asia-Pacific. It is feasible to build on good interactions between the two countries to steer Apec back towards economic cooperation and trade facilitation, which would benefit all sides.

China is well positioned to contribute a lot in this regard, including on energy, agricultural goods and rare earths. We should think about how to use the positive momentum to take the China-US relationship into its next phase, rather than simply maintaining the current situation. After all, standing still can mean stepping back.

After the four summits this year, how can the momentum be sustained into next year? You have emphasised the importance of stable economic and trade ties. Should we be concerned that while the two-month trade truce extension would offer a window of opportunity, the outlook could again become uncertain?

First, we should recognise that Trump’s trade war is not directed exclusively at China. China is just one part of his broader trade war, which has also targeted US allies. If China has the capacity to expand economic and trade ballast, why not do so? We should not struggle for the sake of struggling. Struggle must have a purpose.

In fact, there is plenty of room for cooperation between China and the US. For instance, both countries are confronting the question of how a major power manages its borders. Many of the problems facing the US come from its immediate neighbourhood, including illegal immigration and drugs. China also faces challenges, such as telecoms fraud operations in Myanmar and Cambodia.

China-US ties are not like the US-Soviet relationship. Never before in history have two economies this large been so closely interconnected. The two countries can build consensus not only at greater depth but also across a wider range of areas. And effective policy implementation will lay the foundation for credibility and trust.

Even if there are no formal meetings next year [as there were in May and September], there will still be the annual Apec and G20 gatherings, as well as many other potential occasions. There are many ways for communication. We do not have to worry too much.

Replicating this year’s high frequency of bilateral summits may not be necessary, but head-of-state diplomacy will certainly continue. The key is not to lose the momentum, which is hard won. China and the US could mobilise the positive forces for the bilateral relationship in both countries.

Negative forces undoubtedly exist too, on both sides. For example, we see constant talk of “China is going to defeat America” or “America must defeat China” within the two societies. We need to shape a favourable media and social environment, which is crucial.

Take China’s unilateral opening-up measures in recent years to welcome more American visitors; both sides should do more of what benefits China-US relations, rather than framing the relationship in terms of who defeats whom. Neither side can defeat the other.

When the two sides agreed in May to build “constructive strategic stability”, the White House cited demands for “fairness and reciprocity”. China echoed the two points this time, and both sides added “respect”. What is your take on this development?

China certainly values respect, as the US has long been accustomed to exercising hegemony. I have argued that managing two variables is crucial to handling China-US relations properly.

First, China must manage its own rise. What we consume and do not consume and how much we consume all affect global markets, and even China-US relations. It is not that the world should applaud simply because we have risen. The way China rises matters a great deal.

It is not enough for us to feel that we are rising; other countries must also come to regard China’s rise as a positive development and welcome it. That would constitute a successful and peaceful rise. The Chinese modernisation also emphasises the path of peaceful development.

Second, the relative decline of the US must be managed too. [In a de facto Group of 2] the US has had a considerable psychological adjustment. It is no longer as arrogant or dismissive of others as it once was, and it has come to view China as a much more equal counterpart, as evidenced by speaking of “respect, fairness and reciprocity”.

That is beneficial for China. But the more this is so, the more humble China should be. Nations are like people – feelings and face matter. It is important to be mindful of the US’ psychological position. It would be unwise to show no consideration for that or adopt an attitude of kicking someone when they are down.

Narratives such as “the East is rising and the West is declining” still resurface from time to time in public discourse. Is this view still open to question?

I have said that great powers are not to be defeated. If the US were to fail, it would not be because China had defeated it, but because of problems within itself. And the same holds true for China. China and the US can only coexist. Neither can defeat the other. If one were to defeat the other, the result would be the destruction of the world.

China now should go for smart diplomacy, approaching foreign policy through reason and wisdom rather than simply acting on instinct.

Great powers must shoulder their responsibilities. Managing the two variables discussed [in the previous answer] is one example of doing so. A country does not become a great power by defeating another. No one would like such a great power, and it will end up defeating itself.

At this summit, both presidents recalled that China and the US were allies during the World War II. Shortly after the meeting, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi spoke with Trump and exchanged views primarily on issues related to China, including security. Meanwhile, new stand-offs have emerged between China and the Philippines in the South China Sea.

With Beijing and Washington agreeing to build constructive strategic stability, how should China manage its relations with US allies in the region, particularly Japan and the Philippines? These countries are also actively strengthening security ties between themselves. Could that in turn affect China-US relations?

[The de facto G2] has implications for many so-called middle powers. Countries such as France, Germany, Canada and the United Kingdom, which have fewer geopolitical disputes with Beijing, are not choosing sides between Beijing and Washington in managing their relations with the two powers.

Meanwhile, Japan appears to be trying to play the role of an “Israel in East Asia”. It likely feels that the US is now paying less attention to protecting it, so the country seeks to take security into its own hands and, based on that, keep Washington tied to its side. But there are limits to this approach.

As long as China and the US have enough trust between them, Japan and the Philippines will have little role to play. As a relationship between major powers, China-US relations constitute a structure within which Japan and the Philippines can only make some autonomous choices. No matter what [Japan and the Philippines] do, they cannot themselves become a structure.

On Taiwan and the South China Sea, there is still considerable room to explore in future exchanges between Beijing and Washington. For Beijing, Taiwan and the South China Sea are matters of sovereignty. For the US and Japan, these are issues of geopolitical space. Today, much of the world conflates issues of sovereignty with those of geopolitical space. They are completely different.

On the basis of mutual respect and reciprocity, we can talk with the American side over how to ensure US interests in the western Pacific. Addressing the Taiwan question and South China Sea issues does not mean Beijing wants to exclude Washington from the region. Likewise, we can also talk with the US about how to assure China’s interests in the eastern Pacific, including in Latin America. These are reciprocal matters the two sides can discuss. That rests on the deeply intertwined nature of China-US relations, and the two countries not carving so-called spheres of influence.

Once the Taiwan question is resolved, we could welcome US warships and aircraft carriers making port calls at the island openly, just as we once welcomed American military vessels to dock in Hong Kong. The two sides should work together to manage the Pacific and the world as a whole instead of trying to exclude each other.

Will the dynamics of Sino-US relations and Beijing’s posture vis-a-vis Washington during this summit affect how middle powers, including Japan and the EU, approach their relations with China?

They have already begun to change. We should go back to the realistic dimension when looking at international relations.

Since the dawn of the modern era, an idea originating from Europe holds that all states are equal. This is an ideal, not a reality. As countries differ in size and strength, we cannot assume that they are fully equal at the starting point. But we can strive for equality. Every nation has its own positioning in international relations. If a country does what it ought not to do, or fails to do what it should, that is not helpful to its own national interests and is not sustainable.

Under the de facto G2 context, both China and the US are repositioning themselves. Other countries will also be doing the same. This is a structural issue that could shape international relations for decades. The boundaries of the China-US relationship may gradually become the boundaries of international relations as a whole. The bounds set by the two countries for the bilateral ties could also define red lines that other states should not cross.

Neither side’s release mentioned Taiwan. Trump said he and Xi “didn’t talk about it too much” at the summit. Should there be concern that the question has been shelved? How might Beijing and Washington approach Taiwan in future exchanges?

The fact that Taiwan was not mentioned in the documents does not mean the two sides did not consider or discuss it but only indicated they had not yet reached a broader consensus on it. Indeed, there is a concern that Taiwan could become the focal point of a conflict if it is not handled carefully, potentially undoing progress on all other work.

But as we talked about earlier, Taiwan is not a subject that cannot be discussed. Many specific issues need to be gradually untangled. If the dialogue simply consists of China accusing the US of being “a force from outside the region” while Washington levels the similar charge against Beijing, it goes nowhere and the two sides could drift towards conflict.

But adopting a more mutually inclusive mindset can make a difference. The US is still a significant actor in the western Pacific. Similarly, China’s influence in Latin America is growing. Every issue has its origins and its solutions. There are always solutions other than war. We should not underestimate human wisdom.

China made no mention of rare earths and critical minerals in its own list of summit outcomes, although the US repeated its concerns in its fact sheet. Does this signal a firm stance by Beijing on the issue, and how might it affect competition in this domain?

The US is looking to reinforce its toolkit, looking for additional means. China is doing the same, like the case of AI start-up Manus. This is reciprocity – and you can only negotiate for reciprocity when you have the strength to back it up. If political trust between China and the US gradually builds and both sides move towards the same direction, I do not think rare earths will be a problem. But if [political trust] deteriorates, more points of friction could emerge.

Rare earths serve as a countermeasure for China but the country’s purpose is rather simple - zhi ge wei wu [a Chinese idiom meaning “true martial virtue lies in stopping warfare”].

If the US weaponises something to pressure us, China has tools of its own to push back. Still, as long as the US remains rational, the Chinese side would not cut off rare earth supplies.

China and the US have agreed to establish an AI dialogue. Given their differing approaches to the technology and divisions within the US on AI slowdown, what concrete outcomes can we expect from AI discussions between the two countries?

First of all, when it comes to AI development, there is little consensus within China or the US, let alone between them. Domestically, the US is currently split into two camps on AI: one believes AI can solve many of our problems, while the other fears it could bring about doomsday. But China and the US do share a consensus on the security risks posed by AI; what remains to be mapped out is the specifics of what they should discuss.

The two countries also follow different models of AI development. Trump supports accelerated development with no regulation. China, at least theoretically, tries to balance development with security.

AI requires multilevel discussion between China and the US. Technology and capital circles essentially dominate the discourse about AI. Trump aligns himself with them, further reinforcing their power. Talk of regulation and slowing down AI development in the US has gone on for a long time but with little real progress. These issues cannot be driven by commercial companies – they can only be tackled by governments.

AI will undoubtedly serve as a major platform for future US-China discussions, much like nuclear weapons did between the US and the Soviet Union. [Former US secretary of state Henry] Kissinger’s final visit to China was also aimed at easing AI negotiations between Beijing and Washington.

Despite their different rhetoric on AI, both sides share the consensus that discussion between them is necessary. When people talk about AI today, they are effectively talking about China-US relations, as its technology and production capacity are highly concentrated in the two countries.

Trump has confirmed his intention to attend the Apec summit, further raising global expectations for the event in November. What impact do you think this could have on the host city, Shenzhen? And how do you view the frequent comparisons between Shenzhen and Hong Kong?

This is certainly a boon for Shenzhen. The entire Pearl River Delta, including Shenzhen and Hong Kong, has an export-oriented economy, for which China-US relations are paramount. Every twist in the relationship would be reflected immediately in Hong Kong and Shenzhen. Hong Kong and Shenzhen can also be key to implementing the consensus reached by the Chinese and US leaders.

If local governments and businesses do more to foster China-US friendship, it benefits not only themselves but the whole country. With the relationship enjoying such good momentum, I expect the Apec summit in Shenzhen to be a great success. It will also mark the first visit to Shenzhen by a sitting US president since the Chinese special economic zone was founded more than four decades ago.

Shenzhen can be proud in showing the world what it has achieved but should also stay humble. Although Shenzhen is a city that buys globally and sells globally, it still has things to learn from Hong Kong when it comes to institutions and mechanisms, and the internationalisation of people.

Apec is a test for Shenzhen. Although much is arranged by the central government, the local side will shape the atmosphere of the summit on the ground. I hope that, through the coming Apec summit, Shenzhen can gradually move closer to Hong Kong, though the city still has a lot to learn.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia is building a new research corridor across Asia to meet China’s rise: scientists
item.description:
When chemical engineer Ahmad Zuhairi Abdullah joined Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM) 22 years ago, Western institutions dominated the field, from global research infrastructure and high-impact publications to the greatest breakthroughs.

Two decades later, the centre of gravity has moved eastward, says Zuhairi, now a professor with the USM school of chemical engineering in Penang.

“[Not much was known] about China at that time when I joined the university. I knew that they had quite a number of good universities and I was aware of their publications because some of them I referred to in my research work,” he said.
item.content:encoded:
When chemical engineer Ahmad Zuhairi Abdullah joined Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM) 22 years ago, Western institutions dominated the field, from global research infrastructure and high-impact publications to the greatest breakthroughs.

Two decades later, the centre of gravity has moved eastward, says Zuhairi, now a professor with the USM school of chemical engineering in Penang.

“[Not much was known] about China at that time when I joined the university. I knew that they had quite a number of good universities and I was aware of their publications because some of them I referred to in my research work,” he said.

“But definitely nothing much was heard in terms of collaboration with Chinese counterparts. Now, you see a lot [of scientists and students] coming here,” for studies, research and fostering collaborations, Zuhairi added.

“Chinese scientists are very advanced in materials science,” he said, pointing to the high volume of publications and contributions to scientific journals.

As China rises as a scientific powerhouse and Malaysia diversifies its research networks to find collaborators closer to home, partnerships in critical domains – from semiconductors to sustainable energy materials – are increasingly shaping regional innovation.

“China is very aggressive and opening its doors to collaborations, which is shifting from probably 10 years back [when] it was quite close to their own things,” Zuhairi said.

He also observed that China was making an effort to include Southeast Asian partners in its research ecosystem, with some provincial funding programmes requiring Chinese scientists to work with researchers from the region.

At the Joint Laboratory of Biomass Chemical Engineering, inaugurated in January, researchers from USM and Huaqiao University in China’s southeastern coastal province of Fujian are working together to turn organic waste and plant material into useful products, as well as developing sustainable energy materials and low-carbon technologies.

According to Zuhairi, one of the common research interests between the two countries lies in combining Malaysia’s abundant agricultural waste with China’s advanced process engineering.

Malaysia’s massive palm oil sector generates vast quantities of biomass, including pressed fibre and kernel shells which contain lignin, a bonding agent in plants that was traditionally treated as a low-value by-product in the pulp and paper industry.

Zuhairi’s research aims to develop specialised catalysts to break down the lignin – the second most abundant biopolymer after cellulose – into smaller molecular fragments.

“Lignin is converted into phenolic substances, [which] will be a feedstock for the conversion into something more valuable,” he said.

These valuable renewable chemicals include adhesives and fuel additives to improve fuel performance and reduce emissions.

While chemical engineering lays the foundation for sustainable materials, advanced hardware and semiconductors are pushing the Malaysia-China corridor into critical hi-tech domains.

At USM’s Institute of Nano Optoelectronics Research and Technology (INOR), director Mohd Zamir Pakhuruddin is leading research into wide-bandgap semiconductors like gallium nitride, solar cells and nanophotonic devices.

The institute has broadened its international research partnerships over the past two years to work with scientists in China, Japan and Saudi Arabia, diversifying beyond its long-standing ties with research institutions in Germany and France.

It has established collaborations with leading Chinese institutions in semiconductor research, such as Chongqing University, Fudan University, Harbin Institute of Technology, Hunan Institute of Technology and Nanjing University.

For Zamir, an associate professor in advanced photovoltaic materials and devices, working across borders is a necessary step towards advancing technology, with the global supply and manufacturing chain for chips an example.

“To be able to realise high-end semiconductor devices, there is no one country that can do that alone. The same goes for the collaboration of the academy as well,” he said.

“We need our partners to be able to complement somewhere across the value chain of the fabrication.”

Malaysia aims to move beyond its back-end chip assembly and testing role towards integrated circuit design, high-end manufacturing and niche equipment, as outlined in its 10-year road map, the National Semiconductor Strategy released in 2024.

“The very goal of the national semiconductor strategy is to enhance the capacity of the nation to be stronger in the front end while leveraging the current strength in the back end,” Zamir said.

When asked about the growing trade friction and technological competition between Washington and Beijing, Zamir said that science and collaborations “should remain open”.

“Malaysia is in the neutral position politically because we do not favour sides. We do not choose sides anyway. The same goes for our academic collaboration. It is more of a diversification of our international partners that we have done in recent years,” he said.

Among INOR’s Chinese collaborators is the Harbin Institute of Technology (HIT), an institution subject to US sanctions and one of the “Seven Sons of National Defence” – universities directly under China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.

In this partnership, the Malaysian and Chinese researchers are co-developing space solar cells with high radiation resilience for low Earth orbit satellite applications.

Asked about how the institute manages its partnership with HIT, Zamir said jointly agreed proposal terms defined the scope of their cooperation.

“In the areas that we agreed to collaborate, I believe these are the areas that are open for collaboration and we should leverage as long as the areas are open for exploration,” he said.

Zamir acknowledged that some fields were restricted but emphasised focusing on open avenues: “For the areas that are open for collaboration, we go by the first principle [that] science should be open and let’s leverage each other’s strengths to win together.”

Over his multiple trips to various Chinese cities in the past two years, Zamir said he observed that Western export controls and sanctions had accelerated China’s push towards domestic self-sufficiency.

“But in science, I think the bright side is it is pushing the capability of the nation to develop your very own technology – from science to technology, to eventually realising technology on the production floor,” he said.

At USM’s school of physics, deputy dean and associate professor Ahmad Fairuz Omar said that global cooperation endured as fundamental scientific inquiry continued to transcend borders.

“Science is very universal,” Fairuz said. “From our engagement with all different parts of the world, including China … everybody is passionate about knowledge.”

In May, the school hosted scientists from the Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics’ College of Physics, who shared insights into using AI in research, nuclear physics and quantum-enabled space exploration technologies.

They also explored potential collaborations in fields such as cosmology and materials fabrication.

Fairuz pointed to his research using optical spectrometers to measure fruit quality metrics like sweetness, pH and firmness across different wavelengths as an area of potential for collaboration with China.

“The final intention is [to] find out several wavelengths that can specifically cater for the measurement of that particular quality of the fruit. That is what we are looking for. But the tricky situation is that fruits are really diversified.”

Looking to build “common understanding on this diversified world”, he said, “we can see that there are many researchers from China also working on visible near-infrared spectroscopy, particularly on agriculture”.

“[With] the growing number of people working in this area, hopefully that will be some sort of meeting point.”

Passionate about science? Dive deeper with the Dark Matters newsletter, a weekly in-depth analysis on China’s rise in science, technology and military that goes beneath the surface. Sign up for free now.

item.title: [SCMP] China has dominated tungsten for decades. Can US cash in Central Asia loosen its grip?
item.description:
The race to loosen China’s grip on tungsten is moving to Kazakhstan, where United States-backed mining projects are attempting to compete in an industry where Chinese investment already has an operating foothold.

Global tungsten prices have surged more than 200 per cent since May 2025, according to commodity and energy information provider Argus Media, adding urgency to efforts to develop alternative supplies. The soaring costs followed Beijing’s export controls on selected tungsten products introduced in February 2025 in a market already facing tight mine supply and increased demand from the defence industry.

The supply squeeze has reached US oilfield equipment makers, which are redesigning one of their most important tools as the global shortage raises the cost of making drill bits.
item.content:encoded:
The race to loosen China’s grip on tungsten is moving to Kazakhstan, where United States-backed mining projects are attempting to compete in an industry where Chinese investment already has an operating foothold.

Global tungsten prices have surged more than 200 per cent since May 2025, according to commodity and energy information provider Argus Media, adding urgency to efforts to develop alternative supplies. The soaring costs followed Beijing’s export controls on selected tungsten products introduced in February 2025 in a market already facing tight mine supply and increased demand from the defence industry.

The supply squeeze has reached US oilfield equipment makers, which are redesigning one of their most important tools as the global shortage raises the cost of making drill bits.

According to Ulterra Drilling Technologies, the cost of manufacturing drill bits had risen by as much as 50 per cent over the past year. The company is responding by shifting production towards steel-bodied models, even as bits containing more tungsten typically last longer when cutting through hard, abrasive rock.

Rival Varel Energy Solutions has made a similar calculation. “Without any stabilisation in tungsten pricing, manufacturers will be forced to transition to steel alternatives,” chief commercial officer Jayme Sperring told Reuters in a report published in May.

China accounted for nearly 80 per cent of mined tungsten globally, producing about 3.7 times the output of the rest of the world combined, according to data from the US Geological Survey. Its dominance extends beyond mining into processing and manufacturing, making it difficult for new producers to compete simply by bringing more of the metal to market.

Prized for its hardness and heat resistance, tungsten is used in industrial tools and some military equipment, including armour-piercing ammunition and missiles, as well as in semiconductors and electronic components supporting AI hardware and data centres.

The US is a major consumer but has recorded no commercial tungsten mine production since 2015. That dependence has made overseas projects increasingly important to Washington’s efforts to secure supplies.

A new front in the race

In April, US mining investment firm Cove Capital acquired a 70 per cent stake in two deposits in Kazakhstan’s Karaganda region: Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty. Their combined estimated development cost is US$1.1 billion, though both remain at the engineering and feasibility study stage, with production targeted for around 2028.

Financing cannot automatically replicate the industrial system China has built over decades

Liu Wenjing, Elistra Advisory

That timetable contrasts with Chinese-backed investments in the country. Hong Kong-listed Jiaxin International Resources already operates the Boguty Mine in Kazakhstan’s Almaty region after the facility began trial production in November 2024 and entered commercial operations in April 2025.

Another proposed tungsten investment, involving Kunxin International Investment and Kazakhstan’s SP Saryarka Tungsten, was among more than 60 agreements signed at Hong Kong’s Belt and Road Summit in September, though few details were disclosed.

This difference in development timelines had given China an immediate advantage in the supply chain, according to Liang Yan, Kremer Chair Professor of Economics at Willamette University. Boguty was already producing, she added, while the US-backed projects still needed to complete studies, secure financing and build their facilities.

Liang argued Kazakhstan could become a “vital producer of tungsten”, citing the Central Asian nation’s more than 2 million tonnes of forecast resources and saying it could eventually supply about 15 per cent of annual global mine output.

“I don’t think US financing can neutralise China’s lead in processing capacity and commercial scale,” said Liang, who is also a non-resident senior fellow at Boston University’s Global Development Policy Centre.

The challenge goes beyond bringing new mines into production. Kazakhstan, Liang suggested, would also need to develop more local refining capacity if it wanted to build a supply chain less dependent on China. Without such capacity, new mines might still have to send concentrate to Chinese processors if alternative facilities faced delays or cost overruns, Liang said.

Liu Wenjing, a member of the Astana International Financial Centre’s Executive Council for the Mining Sector and founder and principal adviser of Elistra Advisory, acknowledged that US financing could significantly lower the barriers to building an alternative tungsten supply chain.

But, she cautioned, “financing cannot automatically replicate the industrial system China has built over decades”.

China’s advantage spanned much of the tungsten supply chain, Liu said. That includes processing mined ore into concentrate and producing ammonium paratungstate (APT), an important intermediate material used to make tungsten products, and making finished products such as cemented carbides.

Geography also matters. Kazakhstan borders China while shipments bound for Europe and North America face longer routes, including across the Caspian Sea. “The US has effectively recognised that investing in overseas mines alone will not solve the problem,” said Liu, who previously served as board secretary of Jiaxin.

That strategy is reflected in Washington’s investments in processing capacity at home, including plans to convert tungsten into APT. In mid-September, Washington announced a US$450 million investment in Elmet Group through redeemable preferred shares.

“This shows that US strategy is moving beyond securing ore towards filling the gap in midstream processing,” Liu said.

The same logic applies to transport, as Northern Katpar is being designed to reach international markets through the Trans-Caspian route. The plans, according to Liu, suggested Western-backed projects were addressing how the metal would reach buyers, not just where it would be mined.

The cost of dependence

This push to develop alternative supply routes has only intensified since China introduced export-licensing requirements in February 2025, the same day new US tariffs on Chinese goods took effect.

While Beijing said the controls were intended to safeguard national security and fulfil its non-proliferation obligations, they were widely interpreted as part of the broader trade and technology rivalry between the two superpowers.

At the same time, China has authorised only 15 companies to export tungsten under its state-trading system for 2026 and 2027. Products covered by the 2025 controls remain subject to separate export licences and end-user checks.

Chinese customs data showed that exports of tungsten products by weight fell 25 per cent year on year in the first eight months of 2026. Exports of sodium tungstate plunged 94.9 per cent, while shipments of ammonium paratungstate, an important intermediate material, dropped 89.3 per cent.

Exports of tungsten-related products from China to the US also fell 21 per cent by volume year on year over the same period. Shipments of unwrought tungsten and tungsten carbide stopped altogether, while exports of tungsten bars fell 42 per cent.

Kazakhstan could move from being a small producer today to a strategically important source of additional tungsten supply outside China

Liu Wenjing, Elistra Advisory

The restrictions, along with tight mine supply and rising demand, have added upwards pressure on prices.

Fastmarkets, a global price-reporting agency specialising in metals and mining, assessed global tungsten concentrate prices at US$2,500–2,800 per metric tonne unit from May 29, up from US$750–850 at the start of 2026 – an increase of about 230 per cent.

The price pressure is reaching manufacturers. MSC Industrial Supply, a major US distributor with nearly US$4 billion in annual sales, told an investor conference in New York last month that tungsten-related input costs had surged by about 500 per cent.

“They have stabilised, but the ripples through the supply chain aren’t over yet,” chief executive Martina McIsaac said during the event, adding that suppliers were continuing to raise prices at different rates depending on their inventories and access.

Higher costs are also prompting Washington to look beyond new mines for additional supply, including recycling. On August 27, it imposed a one-year ban on exports of tungsten scrap to retain material for US processors. According to materials research platform Material Insights, recycled tungsten provided about 25 to 30 per cent of global supply and was particularly important to the US because it lacks domestic mine production.

The scramble goes global

For Kazakhstan, the main question may be how quickly proposed mining and processing projects can be brought into operation. The country still accounts for less than 3 per cent of global tungsten mine output, though Liu said new projects could significantly increase its share.

“If Jiaxin International’s Boguty mine continues to expand, and Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty come into production as planned, Kazakhstan could move from being a small producer today to a strategically important source of additional tungsten supply outside China,” she said.

EarthRarest, a strategic metals research and investment platform, made a similar assessment in a report shared with the South China Morning Post. It estimated that Kazakhstan’s 2.8 per cent share of global mine production represented about one-eighth of production outside China.

“An additional reliable source can matter to buyers diversifying their purchases well before it changes China’s overall lead,” EarthRarest said, adding that the US could help finance mines, processing facilities and transport links, particularly alongside purchase commitments. But it cautioned that it remained unclear whether the projects could produce at competitive costs and deliver reliably.

“The reviewed evidence does not establish that finance alone removes a cost or scale disadvantage,” EarthRarest said.

Kazakh tungsten could potentially reach Western buyers without passing through China if the required mining, processing, transport and customer arrangements all proved workable, according to the report. For the proposed large Kazakh projects, however, “a fully independent route remains a project objective rather than an established operating fact”.

Yet Kazakhstan is not merely choosing between Chinese and American investors. Astana is also seeking to move beyond its traditional role as an exporter of raw materials and develop more of the tungsten supply chain at home.

The Kazakh government’s 2023–2027 geological development strategy called for expanded exploration, digitised geological records, improved mining infrastructure and greater investment in research and skills.

A separate government plan covering rare and rare earth metals through 2028 called for modernising existing facilities, introducing more advanced processing technologies and attracting investment from a wider range of international partners.

Kazakhstan is only part of a broader effort by governments to secure tungsten supplies and capture more value from their mineral resources.

In late August, Britain’s National Wealth Fund announced an investment of up to £71 million in Tungsten West to support the proposed restart of the Hemerdon tungsten and tin mine in Devon. The project is targeting full-scale production in the first quarter of 2027.

Resource-producing countries are also tightening their grip on the metal. Vietnam’s Ministry of Industry and Trade has proposed removing tungsten from the list of minerals permitted for export. It has not specified how long the proposed restriction would last and has stressed that it would not amount to a permanent ban.

Zimbabwe went further in September, suspending exports of antimony and tungsten in all forms, including ores and concentrates, until further notice. The government said the measure was intended to encourage mining companies to refine and process more of their minerals domestically, allowing the African nation to retain more value before export.

item.title: [SCMP] PAS wants urban Malaysia’s vote. Can it win over urban Malays?
item.description:
A string of electoral victories in recent years has inspired the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) to go for more urbanised and developed states in the run-up to Malaysia’s next general election. PAS’ strategy is straightforward: besides leveraging its religious credentials, it also seeks to underscore its ability to govern well. The problem here, however, is that PAS might not have a solid technocratic record to sell to voters.

PAS was established by the ulama (religious scholars) wing of the United Malays National Organisation. As part of an Islamic resurgent wave starting in the 1980s, the ulama leadership began to shape PAS into a movement that represented the “authentic Islam”, as opposed to the more “Westernised” and “secular” Umno.

PAS became synonymous with the image of a party that exclusively focuses on matters of faith and whose solutions to real-world problems can only be found in religious texts. Consequently, the general public perceives PAS’ ulama leadership to be ill-equipped to deal with the complex challenges of modern life.
item.content:encoded:
A string of electoral victories in recent years has inspired the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) to go for more urbanised and developed states in the run-up to Malaysia’s next general election. PAS’ strategy is straightforward: besides leveraging its religious credentials, it also seeks to underscore its ability to govern well. The problem here, however, is that PAS might not have a solid technocratic record to sell to voters.

PAS was established by the ulama (religious scholars) wing of the United Malays National Organisation. As part of an Islamic resurgent wave starting in the 1980s, the ulama leadership began to shape PAS into a movement that represented the “authentic Islam”, as opposed to the more “Westernised” and “secular” Umno.

PAS became synonymous with the image of a party that exclusively focuses on matters of faith and whose solutions to real-world problems can only be found in religious texts. Consequently, the general public perceives PAS’ ulama leadership to be ill-equipped to deal with the complex challenges of modern life.

Currently, PAS controls the state governments of Kedah, Kelantan, Perlis and Terengganu. In the 2022 general election and various state polls the following year, PAS made inroads into states previously controlled by Umno, such as Perak, Pahang and Selangor. These states, however, are more urbanised, economically developed and demographically diverse, and campaigning on a platform of Islamic credibility to govern was not enough to attract Malay voters there. They may be religiously conservative but will not blindly vote based on faith alone.

The results of the Johor and Negeri Sembilan state elections this year show that the more urbanised west coast and southern states pose a challenge for PAS. The only way for PAS to expand its presence is by allying with Malay nationalist parties such as Umno and the newly formed Wawasan.

A nationwide poll in April by the Merdeka Centre showed that 81 per cent of Muslim Malays listed economic concerns as the country’s main challenge. About 53 per cent of Malays feel the country is going in the wrong direction. Most of those making less than 4,000 ringgit per month (US$980), many of whom are Malays, feel the same. PAS is targeting these voters, and it is clear that their top priority is the economy. PAS’ aim is to show them it has a sound and feasible economic agenda and, more importantly, the technocratic chops to carry it out.

At its annual congress, or muktamar, last month, PAS sought to convince the Malaysian public of its ability to govern. The party put forth reformist-like motions, such as the creation of a Royal Commission of Inquiry on the so-called corporate mafia; increasing protection of healthcare workers and ramping up rice production to augment food security. Whether PAS can convince voters of this reformist, welfare-focused vision remains a challenge in the months leading up to the general election.

PAS has some ground to cover from its posturing of the past decade. After purging the “professional” faction in 2015, PAS has since adopted a more ethno-religious stance. It has fused Islamism and Malay nationalism and coalesced around its hardline president, Abdul Hadi Awang. The image turns off many Malays who are pious but do not buy into PAS’ divisive rhetoric. Hence the appeal of technocrats in PAS who are seen as the party’s moderate face.

Since 2018, PAS has been showcasing technocratic leaders such as Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar, the chief minister of Terengganu, and Syahir Sulaiman, MP of Bachok in Kelantan. Ahmad Samsuri holds a PhD in aerospace engineering from the University of Leeds and is a protege of Abdul Hadi. Syahir has a private sector background, having worked with the Sime Darby Group before becoming a full-time politician in 2018.

PAS regularly uses the Samsuri administration in Terengganu as an example of the party’s governing achievements. But PAS might be overstating its case. As an oil-producing state, Terengganu is highly dependent on oil royalties from the federal government, which make up about 80 to 90 per cent of its budget. Such royalties played a big role in the Samsuri administration’s ability to fulfil its populist agenda in its first term from 2018 to 2023. This was primarily due to the unimpeded flow of revenue from the then Perikatan Nasional federal government, of which PAS was part.

The dynamic changed after 2022 when the current Madani federal government took over. These royalty payments are now subjected to onerous conditions set by Putrajaya. This affects the Samsuri administration’s visibility significantly, as the federal government can now claim credit for the payments. The federal government has also opted to develop the state directly by funding myriad projects such as a new hospital in Dungun and a 60 million ringgit (US$14.7 million) poverty eradication programme.

But are the technocrats in PAS actually more religiously moderate compared with the hardline ulamas in the party? Given that PAS seeks to propel an ideologically driven movement, party members must go through a regimented indoctrination process, such as regularly attending usrah (guided study sessions). In short, a PAS technocrat can be as dogmatic as a religious scholar; the only difference is that one wears a suit and a tie while the other wears a robe and a turban. Authority over matters of faith and ideological underpinnings still resides with the ulama council. Economic policies formulated by the party’s technocrats have to get a religious imprimatur from the ulamas.

As Malaysia heads into the 16th general election, PAS needs to make a case for its governing ability to hesitant Malay voters in urban and semi-urban areas. This is especially so when development in PAS strongholds still lags behind Pakatan Harapan-governed areas like Selangor and Penang.

Working with Umno would help PAS leverage the former’s vast experience and proven track record in government. In the 2022 general election and various 2023 state polls, PAS combined forces with Bersatu, allowing it to penetrate Malay-majority areas outside its strongholds. As a result, PAS increased its parliamentary seats from 18 to 43 and made inroads in Perak, Selangor and Pahang.

There is a similar dynamic now with Umno, but a key difference is that Umno is stronger than Bersatu and would not want to play second fiddle to PAS in this partnership. The tussle for dominance will be a key dynamic as the general election looms closer. If PAS decides not to ally itself with Umno, it would face a tough challenge in persuading the sceptical Malay electorate to put their trust in its mixed technocratic record.

Dr Azmil Tayeb is a Visiting Senior Fellow at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. He is an Associate Professor at the School of Social Sciences, Universiti Sains Malaysia. This article was first published on the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg.

item.title: [SCMP] Temu took the world by storm – but has the shopping app lost its thunder?
item.description:
In February 2023, the budget shopping platform Temu announced itself on the world stage in the brashest way possible: becoming one of the youngest ever brands to buy a Super Bowl advertising spot.

“Download the Temu app and shop like a billionaire,” a voice proclaimed in the 30-second commercial, as a woman danced on screen and ordered a series of outlandishly cheap items: from a US$8.99 dress to a US$4.99 wig.

The commercial – which aired twice during the game, costing Temu an estimated US$14 million – was part of a marketing blitz by the platform, as it tried to introduce American consumers to a marketplace built on ultra-low prices, a wide array of products, and a gamified shopping experience.
item.content:encoded:
In February 2023, the budget shopping platform Temu announced itself on the world stage in the brashest way possible: becoming one of the youngest ever brands to buy a Super Bowl advertising spot.

“Download the Temu app and shop like a billionaire,” a voice proclaimed in the 30-second commercial, as a woman danced on screen and ordered a series of outlandishly cheap items: from a US$8.99 dress to a US$4.99 wig.

The commercial – which aired twice during the game, costing Temu an estimated US$14 million – was part of a marketing blitz by the platform, as it tried to introduce American consumers to a marketplace built on ultra-low prices, a wide array of products, and a gamified shopping experience.

That expense paid off: Temu’s downloads jumped 45 per cent on the day of the Super Bowl campaign compared with a day earlier, according to a report by trade outlet ModernRetail, citing Sensor Tower data.

The platform’s breakneck rise continued to gain momentum from there, bringing Chinese-style e-commerce to markets around the world.

However, three years on, Temu’s initial business proposition is being rewritten amid a wave of global regulation, with rising customs barriers eroding some of the advantages that made its cut-to-the-bone prices possible.

At the heart of the change is a simple issue: shipping a dress directly from a warehouse in China to doorsteps in America or Europe is no longer as simple – or cheap – as it was a couple of years ago.

Temu’s ability to offer such ultra-low prices was built on two main factors: its vast, well-oiled Chinese supply chain and a clever distribution strategy that allowed the firm to avoid paying hefty import tariffs.

[PDD] has operated in China for so many years and built a very mature ... and reusable supply chain system

Chen Tao, Analysys International

On the supply side, Temu could draw on parent company PDD Holdings’ years of expertise operating Pinduoduo – one of China’s largest e-commerce platforms, which has built a sprawling supply chain with deep roots in the Chinese manufacturing sector.

PDD “has operated in China for so many years and built a very mature … and reusable supply chain system”, said Chen Tao, an e-commerce analyst at consultancy Analysys International.

Temu had effectively copied Pinduoduo’s business model and rolled it out globally, Chen added.

The model allows Temu to draw on China’s sprawling network of factories, suppliers and cross-border merchants, which is able to produce and ship goods at a scale and cost unmatched anywhere else in the world.

Since China began opening its economy in the late 1970s, specialised clusters for producing particular products have formed across the country, concentrating factories, suppliers, logistics firms and skilled workers into dense, tightly woven ecosystems.

In southern China’s Guangdong province, for example, the city of Dongguan is known for electronics and toys, while Shenzhen is a hub for electronics. Foshan specialises in furniture, and Zhongshan is a major centre for lighting products.

Vast trading and logistics networks have formed alongside these manufacturing clusters, helping factories reach buyers around the world.

Yiwu, a city in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, has developed a gargantuan wholesale market where hundreds of thousands of vendors sell almost any small product imaginable to overseas buyers – from toy cars to Christmas decorations.

The city is home to well over 260,000 cross-border e-commerce businesses, according to non-exhaustive local government data. Temu estimates that about 40 per cent of its merchants are based in the city.

Another critical piece that made the economics work for Temu was the once-permissive trade policy in some of its largest overseas markets including the US, according to Chen.

In the US, the long-standing “de minimis” exemption allowed individual shipments worth less than US$800 to enter the country without the duties normally imposed on larger commercial imports, helping make it economical for Temu to ship low-cost goods directly from Chinese suppliers to American doorsteps.

It had become a major conduit for Chinese cross-border commercial parcels entering the US. About 60 per cent of the more than 1 billion packages that entered the US under the de minimis exemption in fiscal 2023 came from China, according to US Customs and Border Protection data.

Temu paired that trade advantage with its fully managed model, under which Chinese merchants supplied the goods while the platform handled much of the overseas sales process, from pricing and marketing to cross-border logistics.

“For a small merchant, the cost of shipping a small batch is very high,” Chen said. “But with a platform like Temu, many small batches of goods can be consolidated,” significantly reducing logistics costs.

At Temu’s scale, analysts said, orders from different merchants could be gathered in China and transported together across the Pacific, spreading freight costs across huge volumes of parcels while retaining their identities as individual consumer shipments for US customs and qualifying separately for de minimis treatment.

China’s low-cost supply base, Temu’s fully managed model and duty-free treatment of small parcels allowed the platform to sell to consumers an ocean away while keeping inventory in China until they ordered.

However, that formula was attracting scrutiny almost as quickly as Temu was attracting shoppers.

In April 2023, just two months after Temu’s first Super Bowl appearance, research staff at the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, a congressional advisory body, identified the de minimis exemption as one of the regulatory advantages helping Chinese e-commerce platforms expand in the US.

The report said the huge volume of low-value packages made it harder for US authorities to inspect shipments and enforce trade rules, while also pointing to accusations against Temu over product quality and copyright infringement.

The commission said Chinese e-commerce platforms were particularly well positioned to benefit from de minimis because their goods were typically shipped as individual low-value parcels.

Temu did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The formula that once worked like magic began to quickly unravel in the US in May 2025 – four months after Trump was sworn into office – when the Trump administration ended de minimis treatment for low-value shipments from mainland China and Hong Kong. The exemption was later removed for shipments from all countries in August.

The change struck at one of the central advantages of Temu’s original model: goods could still be made cheaply in China, but getting them into the hands of American consumers suddenly became more expensive.

The impact was swift. Temu’s daily US users fell 48 per cent in May compared with March, according to Sensor Tower data cited by Reuters.

Analysts said the policy change threatened to weaken Temu’s low-price proposition by raising the cost of the direct-shipping model that had powered its expansion.

The new taxes would significantly increase the cost of shipping low-priced goods directly to overseas consumers and potentially push up retail prices, Chen said. That posed a particular challenge for Temu because many of its customers were price-sensitive, meaning higher prices risked driving some away, he added.

Zhang Zhouping, executive director at Ben Se Think Tank, a cross-border commerce consultancy, echoed Chen’s view.

“Taxes on small parcels erode the low-price advantage, while tax, logistics and compliance costs pile up,” Zhang said. “If those higher costs are reflected in final prices, price-sensitive consumers could be affected.”

In response, Temu began moving goods closer to American shoppers.

The company had already started recruiting US-based sellers and rolling out what it called a “semi-managed” model in 2024, under which merchants took greater responsibility for moving and stocking their goods overseas.

Under the semi-managed model, merchants take on more responsibility for overseas logistics and warehousing, shifting inventory closer to consumers and reducing reliance on individual parcels shipped directly from China.

The change makes Temu less dependent on the cross-border shipping model vulnerable to changing tariff rules, but introduces more inventory, warehousing and local fulfilment costs into the supply chain.

By early 2025, about 20 per cent of Temu’s US sales were being shipped by local sellers, according to Marketplace Pulse, cited by Reuters. The end of de minimis accelerated that transition.

The pressure is not confined to the US.

The European Union has also tightened rules on low-value e-commerce imports. Since July, goods worth less than €150 (US$177) entering the bloc have been subject to an interim €3 customs duty for each different category of goods contained in a parcel, ending the previous duty-free treatment ahead of a broader overhaul of the EU customs system.

The change has particular implications for Chinese e-commerce platforms, as some 4.6 billion low-value parcels entered the EU in 2024, with 91 per cent coming from China, according to the European Commission.

Other markets have moved in the same direction. Thailand began imposing a 10 per cent customs duty in January on imported goods worth 1,500 baht (US$46) or less, which had previously been exempt from customs duties. South Africa has also tightened tax treatment of low-value e-commerce parcels.

Together, the changes point to a broader erosion of the favourable treatment for low-value parcels that helped Chinese cross-border e-commerce platforms expand internationally, increasing the pressure to rethink a model built heavily around shipping inexpensive goods directly from China to overseas consumers.

PDD has acknowledged the consequences.

At the company’s latest earnings call, Zhao Jiazhen, PDD’s co-chairman and co-chief executive, said cross-border orders in affected markets would face “lower fulfilment efficiency and higher costs”, which would have a “considerable impact” on parts of its business.

For the past decade, we sold the cheapest products in the world … In the next decade, we need our own brands to have bargaining power and pricing power

Wang Xin, Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association

In the longer term, Zhao said Temu would bring in more local merchants and accelerate investment in local warehousing and fulfilment infrastructure to “integrate more deeply into every market we serve”.

That marks a significant pivot for a platform whose original appeal rested partly on reaching overseas consumers without building out the extensive local infrastructure associated with established global e-commerce businesses such as Amazon.

Another response could be geographic diversification, with Chinese platforms accelerating expansion into markets beyond the US and Europe where regulatory conditions differ, Ben Se’s Zhang said.

Analysys International’s Chen said Temu was unlikely to abandon its original model altogether. Instead, he expected it to combine direct shipping where it remained economical with overseas warehouses and locally held inventory elsewhere.

But the transition may ultimately involve more than changing how Temu gets goods to consumers. It could also change what it sells.

If the low-price strategy becomes less effective, Temu could increasingly turn towards branded products carrying higher margins and more moderate prices, Chen said.

PDD has already taken a significant step in that direction.

In March, the group announced Xinpinmu, a strategic project to develop and operate its own brands by combining the supply chain resources accumulated by Pinduoduo in China with Temu’s overseas reach.

The group has injected 15 billion yuan (US$2.2 billion) into the project and plans to invest a total of 100 billion yuan over three years, with the venture developing brands across different product categories and markets for global consumers.

“Temu’s rapid growth over the past three years was a key leap made possible by the strength of China’s supply chain, and has also created a new opportunity to upgrade and reshape the domestic supply chain,” Zhao said when announcing the initiative.

Three years after Temu promised Americans they could “shop like a billionaire”, the factories capable of producing a US$8.99 dress cheaply have not disappeared, nor has the vast Chinese manufacturing ecosystem behind them.

What has changed is the economics of getting that dress from China to consumers thousands of kilometres away, and, increasingly, the kind of goods PDD wants those factories to sell.

Those economics could shift again as Washington and Beijing continue to negotiate the terms of their trading relationship.

During President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington last month, tariffs and other trade issues were high on the agenda as the world’s two largest economies seek to manage a fragile detente.

For Temu and other Chinese cross-border e-commerce companies, the stakes of that meeting are high, as their low-price model is particularly sensitive to tariffs and trade rules that raise the cost of moving goods from Chinese factories to US consumers.

For some in the industry, however, the changing environment is accelerating a broader push to upgrade China’s cross-border e-commerce sector beyond its reliance on low prices.

“For the past decade, we sold the cheapest products in the world,” said Wang Xin, president of the Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association, in an interview with state broadcaster CCTV earlier this year.

“In the next decade, we need our own brands to have bargaining power and pricing power,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Japan’s tame answer to jobseeker sex harassment: name and shame
item.description:
Final-year students invited to recruiters’ apartments for help with their applications. Coffee dates with alumni who promise to explain how the company works. Inappropriate interview questions about boyfriends, marriage plans and sex lives.

For young women in Japan, looking for a job has long entailed submitting themselves to the skewed power dynamics of the recruitment process.

And before Thursday, no official legal safeguards existed to protect these jobseekers from such harassment.
item.content:encoded:
Final-year students invited to recruiters’ apartments for help with their applications. Coffee dates with alumni who promise to explain how the company works. Inappropriate interview questions about boyfriends, marriage plans and sex lives.

For young women in Japan, looking for a job has long entailed submitting themselves to the skewed power dynamics of the recruitment process.

And before Thursday, no official legal safeguards existed to protect these jobseekers from such harassment.

Campaigners and advocates have welcomed the change, but say it lacks teeth and came years too late, even as societal attitudes may have already moved ahead of it.

“It is good that this has happened, but it has taken five years of discussions to get to the point where it has become law,” said Chisato Kitanaka, an associate professor of sociology at Hiroshima University who advises the government on gender issues.

“Government measures against sexual harassment in Japan are very weak, including this kind of harassment.”

Amendments to the Equal Employment Opportunity Act that took effect last week address harassment in its many forms and settings, from misbehaviour in the office to verbal abuse and threats from customers in shops, taxis and elsewhere. One section deals specifically with what the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare terms “job-seeking sexual harassment”.

The ministry’s website lists examples: staff who make sexual jokes or tease applicants such that it causes distress, who pressure them into a sexual relationship, or who repeatedly invite them to one-to-one meals or drinks.

Employers are now legally required to take steps to stop their staff harassing applicants in this way, with corporate compliance enforced through the threat of publicly shaming offending companies and exposing them to the prospect of civil lawsuits and financial damages.

Kitanaka called the changes a “step in the right direction”, but said they did not go far enough.

“There is no formal punishment for companies that let this happen, with the only real sanction the ministry releasing the name of the company publicly,” she said.

She expects large companies and organisations to enforce the rules more stringently than smaller firms, even as part-time workers, freelancers and others in precarious jobs continue to have too few protections.

Sumie Kawakami, a lecturer at Yamanashi Gakuin University and author of a book on gender issues, agreed that reform was long overdue.

“This isn’t something that has only been happening in recent years and is now being addressed,” she said. “It has been going on for decades.”

One in three

A survey of 1,000 recent jobseekers conducted by Japan’s labour ministry in 2023 showed that 31.9 per cent of respondents – nearly one in three – reported being harassed.

Unnecessary physical contact and questions about sexual matters were each cited by over 25 per cent of the harassed respondents, while nearly 29 per cent said they were on the receiving end of sexual jokes and teasing.

One in four of the men and women who had these experiences reported feeling less motivated in their job search and more than one in three said they felt “anger, dissatisfaction or anxiety”.

For two dozen or so, the effect on their mental health was such that they required hospital treatment.

In the past, companies typically tried to hush up such incidents, but a number of court cases over the years have shone a spotlight on the issue.

In 2019, a male construction company employee was charged with indecent assault after allegedly convincing a university student to come to his flat on the pretext of helping her prepare for an interview.

His employer, Obayashi Corp, apologised and promised to “urgently review” its procedures, subsequently setting up a harassment prevention office and conducting “emergency training” for staff involved in recruitment.

Prosecutors ultimately dropped charges against the man without publicly providing a reason. Whether he kept his job is unknown.

That same year, a 24-year-old trading company employee was arrested and charged with sexual assault and theft after a student he met through a networking app accused him of getting her drunk and using a stolen key to molest her in her hotel room. His employer, Sumitomo Corp, issued a statement soon after his arrest, confirming his disciplinary dismissal.

One of the most serious cases involved Kenshiro Maruta, who was sentenced to 25 years in prison in 2023 for drugging and raping at least 10 female students who connected with him through apps designed to match jobseekers with university alumni and career counsellors.

His employer, Recruit Communications, fired Maruta following his arrest and launched an internal investigation, vowing to never allow such an outrage happen again.

“There have been many incidents in the past and gradually the government has changed its policies,” said Kitanaka, the sociologist. “Now, at last, they have changed the law.”

‘Not acceptable today’

Back in the 1980s, when gender studies lecturer Kawakami first joined Japan’s workforce, it was still dominated by men. Women had to work harder than their male counterparts just to be taken seriously or to advance, she said.

“Young women in the past did not feel that they could speak out when this happened to them because they wanted to get a good job and career,” she said of harassment.

Kawakami has watched attitudes shift in recent years, however, especially among the young women at her university preparing to start their careers.

“I think it has changed quite a lot,” she said. “There is far greater awareness among working people and companies about what constitutes unacceptable behaviour, and I believe employers are far less willing to tolerate sexual harassment.”

And while the threat of public naming and shaming a company might seem tame compared to criminal convictions, Kawakami says the threat “is a powerful one”.

“Companies are desperate to find capable and qualified staff nowadays, and negative publicity that would go with a sexual harassment accusation would be hugely damaging,” she said.

“Young women have lots of work options at the moment. Why would they go to a company that fails to act in a situation like this?”

One recent graduate, who declined to be named, told This Week in Asia that outlawing “clearly sexist” comments or actions by recruiters was a good idea, even if she did not believe that women of her generation would put up with such behaviour.

“If one of my friends were asked something inappropriate in an interview or were invited out for drinks, I’m certain that the man would be shouted at and his company would hear about it,” she said. “It’s just not acceptable today.”

item.title: [SCMP] Sinking city, rising rage: Bangkok’s floods fuel fury over government inaction
item.description:
As floodwaters surged from Bangkok’s drains, Fon’s car sank faster than her hopes of escaping the floods unscathed. She had bought it less than a month earlier.

“I woke up at 5am but it was too late,” the 24-year-old said, recalling her decision last weekend to wait until dawn to move her car to a nearby shopping centre. “My car was already submerged. I hadn’t even started making the payments and it’s gone.”

Relentless rain paralysed Thailand’s capital this September, dumping a month’s worth of precipitation on the city in just three days.
item.content:encoded:
As floodwaters surged from Bangkok’s drains, Fon’s car sank faster than her hopes of escaping the floods unscathed. She had bought it less than a month earlier.

“I woke up at 5am but it was too late,” the 24-year-old said, recalling her decision last weekend to wait until dawn to move her car to a nearby shopping centre. “My car was already submerged. I hadn’t even started making the payments and it’s gone.”

Relentless rain paralysed Thailand’s capital this September, dumping a month’s worth of precipitation on the city in just three days.

Bangkok, a city long plagued by a sinking feeling, went fully underwater. Not all of it, but enough of the city’s east and northeast to offer a terrifying teaser of what may lie ahead as this year’s “super” El Nino climate pattern intensifies into 2027.

In the Khlong Chan neighbourhood of Bangkok’s Bang Kapi district, Fon – whose full name is Siraprapha Sangseeluem – was still stranded in her block of flats five days after the deluge.

Her scathing assessment of the authorities’ handling of the floods? “I can say only one thing: the government is totally useless,” she said.

Some of her neighbours have been even less diplomatic. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul was met with a volley of abuse when he arrived to distribute relief to the flats last Sunday.

The reception was similar in several places Anutin visited last week with his cabinet ministers and the media, in a city that largely did not vote for him. His Bhumjaithai Party did not win any of Bangkok’s constituency seats in February’s general election.

Anger has boiled over in recent days at a government that seemed blindsided by a calamity meteorologists had warned was brewing, but which city and central authorities alike played down in the days before it struck.

Anutin’s own campaign boast that his party would make the country “so rich, you won’t know what to do with your money” has come back to haunt him. “I feel so rich”, chanted crowds of angry residents sarcastically as he arrived to distribute food and water.

I know we weren’t good enough, or prepared well enough

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Anutin acknowledged the backlash. “I know we weren’t good enough, or prepared well enough,” he said. “The fact that people scolded me, criticised me … rest assured that I’ve heard you and I’m not ignoring you.”

Critics are unconvinced, however. “If the measurement of the prime minister’s job is to manage the situation, to bring calm, a sense of trust … then he fails miserably,” said political commentator Voranai Vanijaka.

On September 25, as floods swallowed Bangkok’s roads, homes, shops and restaurants, residents struggled to find their bearings. Governor Chadchart Sittipunt, normally hypervigilant, appeared caught off guard by the speed and scale of the rising water. He apologised days later for delayed warnings and a slow start to the relief effort.

Anutin, who is also the interior minister, cut short a diplomatic visit to London to oversee the response. His initial absence was nonetheless felt in Thailand’s highly centralised, hierarchical political system, with key officials seeming reluctant to make snap decisions without him.

On Wednesday, opposition lawmakers blasted the government’s flood response, criticising everything from slow warnings to the sluggish relief effort.

Rain and floods are unpredictable and the lack of comprehensive flood defences of the kind found in Singapore, Shanghai or Amsterdam is the failing of successive Thai governments. But critics still say Anutin was caught flat-footed.

“As a leader, you are the man in charge, and you have to take control of the situation,” Voranai said.

“What he chose to do instead – hit the streets, pass out food, apparently pass out cash, walk through [flood]water with no shoes on – was political marketing. Political marketing is always part of politics … but he can’t forget to be the man in charge.”

Hotter, wetter, deadlier

As the planet heats to unprecedented and dangerous levels, extreme weather events are becoming ever more erratic and destructive, presenting governments everywhere with challenges many are ill prepared to meet.

As of Wednesday, Japan’s capital had logged 35 consecutive days of rain – its longest streak on record – while wildfires continue to rage in Indonesia’s Kalimantan region, sending toxic haze across borders to Singapore and Malaysia.

Thailand’s recent floods have cost at least 40 people their lives, with estimates of the damage running to hundreds of millions of US dollars.

In Bangkok, the floods were the worst in 15 years, filling drains and canals to capacity and affecting roughly one-tenth of the capital. The country’s southern provinces, where the rainy season typically peaks between November and January, are now bracing for a similar onslaught.

Bangkok’s misfortune has been decades in the making. The city’s ever-expanding urban sprawl is slowly sinking into the soft clay beneath it. Concrete has spread upwards and outwards far faster than investment in infrastructure, especially drainage – effectively turning the built-up city centre into a basin with few natural outlets or floodplains.

It floods easily in large storms and in the increasingly common “rain bombs” that dump vast quantities of water on the city in a matter of hours. In 2011, the worst floods in recent memory submerged the north of Bangkok, killing dozens and leaving parts of the capital up to two metres (6½ feet) under water for weeks on end.

This year’s floods, which may not be over yet, were the result of ceaseless rains overwhelming drains and inundating entire neighbourhoods, including affluent ones, with filthy, sludge-filled floodwater.

Drowning in delays

On Tuesday, Anutin’s cabinet approved a 160 billion baht (US$4.8 billion) plan to divert floodwaters away from the capital. It includes a new canal from Chai Nat province that aims to relieve pressure on the Chao Phraya River, which currently carries run-off from northern and central Thailand straight through Bangkok.

But that project is slated to take eight years to complete and critics say more needs to be done about the country’s sclerotic decision-making in the meantime.

Thailand’s hulking bureaucracy meant overlapping agencies were often left duplicating work as they deferred to one another, said Winyu “John” Wongsurawat, an actor turned political commentator and podcaster.

“When a crisis hits, they turn to the prime minister. Only then does the prime minister come in and say, ‘OK, do this.’ The crisis passes, and the water recedes before any real solution is reached,” he said.

“This isn’t limited to Bangkok. We can see it happening all over the country. Bangkok gets more attention because people there are louder, let’s be honest, it’s the capital.”

The central provinces of Ayutthaya and Ang Thong regularly endured weeks or months of flooding, Winyu said, “but just don’t make big news”.

A government that is prioritising growth and foreign investment now faces a conundrum.
