Most of Thailand’s data centres, and the supply chains for printed circuit boards and semiconductors that go with them, are being built in and around Bangkok, central Ayutthaya and the country’s eastern provinces.

All are low-lying and highly flood prone. The 2011 floods hammered the electronics and car industries of Thailand’s central provinces.

How a government with a sky-high ratio of debt to gross domestic product will pay for far-reaching flood resilience, public compensation and clean-up costs that climb each year remains unclear.

Other long-term economic risks are also emerging.

“Repeated calamities from floods in Bangkok and other provinces pose challenges to Thailand’s attractiveness as a foreign investment destination,” said Pavida Pananond, a professor of international business at Thammasat Business School.

Companies pouring billions of US dollars into tech infrastructure “would be at a higher risk given Thailand’s frequent floods”, she said, adding that the latest deluge came just as the nation was trying to attract more foreign investment “in the era of global supply chain shifts”.

item.title: [SCMP] Going ‘car-lite’: why more Singaporeans are quitting driving
item.description:
When the time came to renew his certificate of entitlement (COE), Andrew Tan hit the brakes on coughing up an eye-watering S$112,000 (US$87,400) to keep his car on Singapore’s roads for another 10 years.

Instead, the 49-year-old business consultant decided in May to go without a car for the first time in two decades.

High COE prices, rising running costs and the hassle of parking and congestion are prompting more Singaporeans to reconsider car ownership, as the land-scarce city state expands public transport, cycling infrastructure and other alternatives in a push for a more “car-lite” society.
item.content:encoded:
When the time came to renew his certificate of entitlement (COE), Andrew Tan hit the brakes on coughing up an eye-watering S$112,000 (US$87,400) to keep his car on Singapore’s roads for another 10 years.

Instead, the 49-year-old business consultant decided in May to go without a car for the first time in two decades.

High COE prices, rising running costs and the hassle of parking and congestion are prompting more Singaporeans to reconsider car ownership, as the land-scarce city state expands public transport, cycling infrastructure and other alternatives in a push for a more “car-lite” society.

Quarterly figures released by the government’s Land Transport Authority in July showed there were 516,237 privately owned cars in Singapore, the lowest number since 2019, even as the share of rental, ride-hailing and corporate cars had increased. Privately owned cars still accounted for 79 per cent of all those on the roads, however.

When Tan bought his first car in May 2006, he said the COE cost S$10,000. A decade later it had climbed to S$50,000 and renewing again this summer would have cost more than double that amount.

Other reasons to give up driving included rising road tax, fuel, maintenance and insurance costs, he said, as well as the city state’s congestion-charging system, known as electronic road pricing (ERP).

An automated system that charges drivers a fee for using busy roads during peak hours, ERP dates back to 1998, though there were other paper-based systems in place beforehand.

At the start of last month, ERP charges returned to the Orchard Road shopping district for the first time since the start of the pandemic in 2020.

Singapore has been actively encouraging people to walk, cycle and use more public transport under the Land Transport Authority’s “Move Lite” campaign, first launched in 2022.

In its early days, the campaign mostly focused on the positives of public transport and not owning a car, but the strategy has since moved towards spotlighting the downsides of driving such as being stuck in traffic and wasting time hunting for parking.

Still, its main aim was to promote more sustainable ways of travelling, not deter people from driving, through its use of “relatable, everyday scenarios”, a spokesman for the authority said.

“The campaign seeks to help commuters make informed travel choices while raising awareness of the increasingly convenient and accessible alternatives to driving,” he said, adding that planning and managing Singapore’s transport network meant balancing the needs of different road users while making the best use of limited land.

To achieve this, the spokesman said Singapore was investing in public transport and “active mobility” infrastructure while managing vehicle ownership and road usage to keep transport efficient and sustainable.

“Our objective is not to prioritise one group of commuters over another, but to provide Singaporeans with more mobility options that are safe, reliable and sustainable for different journeys and needs.”

Singapore only has 744.3 sq km (287.4 square miles) of land and roads take up about 12 per cent of it, which is why authorities have been working to make walking, cycling and public transport more accessible and convenient.

The COE system, launched in May 1990, controls how many vehicles are allowed on the roads by requiring motorists to bid for a certificate in online open auctions. Each COE confers the right to own a vehicle for 10 years.

Singapore has maintained a zero-growth policy for private cars and motorcycles since February 2018 and the Land Transport Authority aims to keep this cap in place until January 31, 2028, while allowing for a small expansion of commercial vehicle and bus fleets.

With the cost of living on the rise, Tan said owning a car was a poor coping strategy for uncertain times, especially considering he had to “set aside contingency funds for young children and aged parents as well”.

Rising costs have also prompted other car owners to think twice about renewing their COEs.

Retired engineer Ricky Quek, 63, recently decided to stop driving after 28 years, citing high COE and petrol prices. Renewing his COE would have cost him S$130,000, he said.

“Public transport is reasonably cheap and no hassle compared to owning a car,” Quek said. “Having a car is definitely convenient but drives up the expenses.”

Small annoyances

Mounting expenses are only part of the picture, however. Other factors discouraging driving include efforts to lower speed limits with stricter enforcement and penalties, and extensive road works linked to major construction projects.

Work on a new multilayered expressway known as the North-South Corridor, the multimodal Changi Northern Corridor project near the airport and a new subway called the Cross Island Line is affecting a number of major arterial roads and highways.

Tech entrepreneur Davidson Chua, 27, says he has noticed more of these roadworks recently, especially during the off-peak times when he likes to commute.

“I do often feel a small annoyance when I am expecting less traffic but end up [encountering] lane closures because of road works or pruning,” said the self-proclaimed motoring enthusiast, adding that he typically preferred covered parking spaces though those could be harder to come by.

Chua said he would only drive two or three days some weeks, “because I don’t see a point in driving down to areas like the CBD [central business district]. It costs more time and money.”

His car is now on its second 10-year COE cycle, with the next renewal due in three years’ time.

“I would love to renew,” he said. “But the COE price will definitely play a huge role in the decision-making process.”

Gopinath Menon, a former chief transport engineer at the Land Transport Authority who led the ERP’s roll-out, told This Week in Asia that measures to limit car ownership had been a part of Singapore’s overall transport strategy since the mid-1970s.

“Realising that the small island cannot keep building more roads to tackle traffic congestion, the strategy called for reasonable demand management for private vehicle travel and for public transport to be the main mode of travel,” said Menon, who is now an independent transport engineering consultant.

Higher parking charges were first to be introduced, alongside an analogue predecessor to the ERP known as the Area Licensing Scheme in 1975. The COE bidding framework followed in 1990, with ERP being rolled out later that same decade.

“Higher driving costs have pushed more people to switch from cars to vastly improved public transport and other public modes such as private-hire vehicles and active mobility,” Menon said, referring to walking and cycling. “This is called the push-pull strategy.”

Speed bumps on the road to a “car-lite” concept included “ambition and attitudes towards car ownership”, he said.

But infrastructure can help lead the way. Menon pointed to the increasing number of pedestrianised zones and bus lanes as ways to reclaim road space for non-car traffic.

Some districts and towns are also car-lite by design, with amenities placed close together, public transport prioritised and access to cycle paths and footpaths improved.

Given the high costs of car ownership, Singapore’s government needs to make the case that cars are a luxury, not a necessity, for the vast majority of citizens, according to public policy expert Terence Ho, an adjunct associate professor in practice at the National University of Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy.

“There will naturally be some unhappiness about the high COE and ERP charges, particularly when certain roads are still congested at peak hours despite the charges,” Ho said. “But by and large, the vehicle control measures have been effective.”

The number of private cars, excluding private-hire vehicles, had grown just 1 per cent over the past five years, he said, while the share of resident households owning a car had fallen from as high as 42 per cent in 2012/13 to 36 per cent in 2023.

This was despite the fact that many households included young children or elderly family members, Ho said.

For Derek Wong, 35, a car is a non-negotiable for ferrying around his two young children and ageing parents. He bought a second-hand Honda Freed in December, with a COE that expires in September 2035.

“I just felt we had to bite the bullet and this will probably be our last car since we won’t need it when the children are older,” said Wong, a writer whose children are aged two and seven.

“The benefits of the convenience still outweigh the drawbacks. It is a hefty investment but given the time it saves, we feel it is worth it.”

Whether COE subsidies should be granted to large families or to those with elderly members, young children or people with disabilities has repeatedly been raised in parliament.

In a reply on the government portal AskGov in November, the Transport Ministry said the difficulty lay in deciding which groups should receive preferential treatment. A COE subsidy for families would have to be substantial, it said, and lower-income families unable to own a car would be unlikely to benefit.

“COE revenues go towards funding public transport,” the ministry said, adding that its approach was to provide high-quality public transport, complemented by taxis and private-hire cars.

On the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT), Singapore’s main underground and elevated railway system, reliability hit a record in August, the Land Transport Authority said in a report released last month. The network’s mean kilometres between failures, a measure of the average distance a train travels before a delay of more than five minutes, rose to 2.88 million km (1.79 million miles) from 2.37 million km in July.

About seven in 10 resident households are already within a 10-minute walk from an MRT station and the government aims to raise that proportion to 80 per cent by the 2030s.

Yet the overall decline in private car ownership had as much to do with the cap on total vehicle numbers as improving public transport links, said Walter Theseira, an associate professor of economics at the Singapore University of Social Sciences.

This restriction tended to push car usage towards private-hire models whereby higher utilisation rates made the expensive COE premiums easier to justify, Theseira said.

“The high willingness to pay for COEs suggests that the underlying private demand for cars continues to be strong,” he said.

“The policy objective can’t be to help Singaporeans achieve car ownership ambitions, as it’s a zero-sum game, but … to help Singaporeans stop needing a car.”

Alternative paths

For those ready to ditch the car, Singapore’s expanding cycling network offers a ready alternative. The city state currently has more than 730km (454 miles) of cycling paths and dedicated traffic-free green corridors known as “park connectors”, with work under way to expand the network to about 1,300km by 2030.

Bicycles have been allowed to share pavements with pedestrians since around 2010, according to Menon, with many walkways later widened to ease congestion and improve safety.

Even so, he said cycling was still mainly used for recreation, running errands and so-called first- and last-mile trips to railway stations and bus interchanges. It was unlikely to become the No 1 choice for most commuters given the high quality of public transport, Menon said.

Theseira agreed, pointing to Singapore’s hot climate and the relatively long distance of an average commute as limiting factors – though he saw potential in electric bikes and other motorised devices.

“In many places, very quickly, when people get access to electrified modes of cycling, they usually take that up,” he said, while noting the city state’s current restrictions on such devices, imposed for pedestrian safety, and lack of suitable infrastructure.

Jason Slaughter, an Amsterdam-based content creator who runs the YouTube channel Not Just Bikes, published a video late last month arguing that rules forcing riders to frequently slow down, give way to cars or dismount and push would limit the take-up of cycling in Singapore.

He also critiqued the city state’s cycling infrastructure, highlighting what he called “questionable choices” such as 90-degree turns and lanes that end abruptly, adding he suspected it was “designed by people who never ride a bicycle”.

His video, titled “Cycling Made Difficult (but it’s getting better!)”, had been watched almost half a million times as of Friday.

For Tan, who now relies on public transport and bicycle paths to get around after giving up on car ownership, the trade-offs are worth it.

“I grew up without a car, so I do not have much difficulty adjusting,” he said. “For my Japanese wife, my two young kids and business needs, the adjustments are not as easy. Yet for the amount saved, it’s worth the inconvenience.”

item.title: [SCMP] The myth of brotherhood: Hong Kong’s triads evolve amid new criminal landscape
item.description:
Not long after he entered secondary school, Hong Kong youth Jason* was bullied by an older student with triad links. He was relieved when another senior stepped in to protect him. He helped Jason take revenge on the bully, then recruited him into a syndicate.

Without undergoing any initiation ritual, Jason paid his protector a red packet to become an informal triad member. Later on, he discovered that the two seniors belonged to the same gang but took orders from different bosses.

At first, Jason was just a street-corner kid, pushing people around at a housing estate. But as he drew closer to the triad’s core group, Jason began to realise that brotherhood was a myth and that business was the order of the day. In the underworld, everything was built on money.
item.content:encoded:
Not long after he entered secondary school, Hong Kong youth Jason* was bullied by an older student with triad links. He was relieved when another senior stepped in to protect him. He helped Jason take revenge on the bully, then recruited him into a syndicate.

Without undergoing any initiation ritual, Jason paid his protector a red packet to become an informal triad member. Later on, he discovered that the two seniors belonged to the same gang but took orders from different bosses.

At first, Jason was just a street-corner kid, pushing people around at a housing estate. But as he drew closer to the triad’s core group, Jason began to realise that brotherhood was a myth and that business was the order of the day. In the underworld, everything was built on money.

‘Once I got closer to the boss, I started realising how it worked. He was using the triad to make money. I felt I could actually make a living off this, so I joined the inner circle to give it a shot,’ he said.

Soon Jason was taking job orders from his boss, which were sometimes conveyed through messaging apps. His tasks ranged from property damage to procuring bank accounts for laundering fraudulent funds. Through these assignments, his illusions about brotherhood evaporated.

He saw peers chicken out during vandalism runs and scramble for excuses when the boss ordered them to engage in street fights.

To protect himself, Jason avoided direct involvement in high-risk operations by outsourcing most of his tasks to his peers, taking a cut of several hundred to several thousand dollars each time they completed a job.

“I stayed away as much as I could to avoid getting arrested,” the 26-year-old said.

Shifting focus in illicit activities

The triad Jason joined 14 years ago was Shui Fong, one of four major syndicates still operating in Hong Kong. The others are Wo Shing Wo, Sun Yee On and 14K.

According to experts in the field – including police, a retired anti-triad investigator and a youth organisation – the four triad groups have evolved over the past decade, with rituals simplified and street violence transforming into white-collar crime and cybercrime. Triad groups also often see one another less as rivals than as partners in making money.

“The violent clashes and bloody scenes are gone. Instead, there are less conspicuous crimes, involving underground banking networks, cross-border money laundering and cybercrime. They do not require a physical presence and are much more low-profile,” said Superintendent Joe Au Yeung Tak of police’s organised crime and triad bureau.

According to police, triad-related crimes rose to 2,554 cases in 2022, up 35 per cent from the previous year. Au Yeung said the spike was driven primarily by a sixfold jump in fraud, with 591 such cases accounting for nearly a quarter of all triad crime that year.

Before the surge, the city’s triad-related crimes between 2016 and 2021 hovered at around 1,700 to 1,900 cases annually.

The number of triad-related cases dipped to 1,353 in 2019 amid a wave of social unrest in the city, with police diverting resources to manage widespread violent protests, according to Au Yeung.

As triads shifted into the digital sphere, law enforcement was adapting to keep pace. “As they transformed, we evolved,” he said.

Historically, police relied on high-profile sweeps and mass arrests to deter gangs. Now their strategy has shifted towards intelligence-led operations targeting deception and financial investigations to cut off the triads’ sources of income.

“Our focus has shifted to tracing the illicit funds, specifically the channels they use to launder the money, and figuring out how we can freeze those assets and confiscate them. Hitting them where it hurts financially is the only way to make them truly feel the pain,” Au Yeung said.

Police also cooperated with other jurisdictions and organisations such as banks and telecommunications service providers to combat triad-related deception.

This multipronged approach has yielded positive results. The number of triad-related deception cases decreased steadily to 323, 162 and 129 in 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively. The total number of triad-related crimes was below 2,000 last year.

Besides deception, triads also engaged in money laundering, which often involved the use of cryptocurrency, Au Yeung said. In such cases, his team relied on the expertise of colleagues from the cybersecurity and technology crime bureau.

While low-level triad members still relied on traditional crimes such as vice, gambling, drugs, extortion, illicit cigarettes and illicit fuel for survival, other businesses – selling pirated video discs, controlling red minibus routes and managing nightclubs, for instance – had grown obsolete as society evolved.

Au Yeung said different triads and factions had started cooperating in recent years, creating a “win-win situation” for themselves.

“If the pie is big enough and transnational, it’s really not surprising at all for several triad factions to team up and work on it together,” he said.

In the past, each of the 18 districts in Hong Kong was dominated by a single triad faction, a situation Au Yeung described as “strictly demarcated territoriality”.

However, over the past decade or so, territorial boundaries have become increasingly blurred.

“When everyone shares a common interest, focusing on making money rather than fighting, even different factions can collaborate. Nowadays, having multiple factions coexisting peacefully within the same region is actually not uncommon,” he said.

Tougher laws lay bare the myth of brotherhood

Gregory Lau Tat-keung, a former superintendent who retired from the police force in 2013, is another close observer of the gangs and has written a book about them. He has testified more than 40 times against gangsters in court as a triad expert.

“A lot of people have been misled into thinking that the triads are all about loyalty and brotherhood,” he said.

Despite hailing from a supposedly long tradition of ritualistic oaths, Lau recalled that many of the gangsters he had arrested had lined up to be prosecution witnesses.

“Let me be a tainted witness. I’m ratting out my boss. Otherwise, how can I get my sentence reduced?” he said, describing the detainees’ thinking.

“We shouldn’t believe in loyalty. Actual substantial interests are what matter most, including [having] fewer sentences and getting more money for informants.”

The Prisons Ordinance was amended last year to tighten restrictions on inmate visits, including prohibiting them from receiving outside food. The changes were made after the enactment of the national security law in 2020.

Lau said he believed the amendment was effective in deterring minor offenders from taking the fall for syndicate bosses because they were subject to stricter prison rules while on remand.

“Before, it was relatively easy to convince them to break the law for the mastermind, because they mistakenly believed that as long as they could receive outside food [while on remand], their boss still controlled everything,” he said.

“It wasn’t until they were convicted in court that they realised they were in trouble. They suddenly realised they were subject to strict prison regulations, no outside food, no special perks and fewer visitation rights.”

The stricter rules also made it more difficult for visitors to bring inmates cigarettes, which served as a kind of “underground currency” in prisons, Lau said.

History of political resistance

According to Lau, the triads could be traced back to around 1644 with the formation of the Hung League, a Han underground organisation dedicated to overthrowing the Manchu-led Qing dynasty. Sun Yat-sen, leader of China’s 1911 revolution, was a member of the league.

Over time, some exploited the name of the Hung League, with several developing into secret society factions, known as “huidang”, that turned to illegal activities after the fall of the Qing.

Lau said the history of local triad societies could also be traced back to Cheung Po-tsai, a notorious pirate who was granted an amnesty after giving himself up to authorities in 1810. Some of his followers who refused to do the same turned to banditry, establishing what was considered the earliest prototype of triad societies in the city.

The four main triad groups still active in Hong Kong have different origins.

The 14K triad has historical roots tied to the Kuomintang. According to Lau, its original headquarters was located at 14 Baohua Road in Guangzhou, with the “K” in its name allegedly standing for Kuomintang.

Similarly, Sun Yee On was founded by Kuomintang general Heung Chin. Originating from Chaozhou, “Yee On” was the historical name of the region. The organisation was originally registered with the Hong Kong government as the Yee On Commercial and Industrial Guild. After this registration was revoked, the members formed a new group, prefixing the name with “Sun”, meaning new in Chinese.

Many triad groups in Hong Kong traditionally carried the suffix “Wo”, meaning harmony, including Wo Shing Wo. According to Lau, the naming originated from Chung Wo Tong, a secret society formed by Yau Lit, a close ally of Sun Yat-sen, to support the revolution.

Another prominent group with the Wo suffix was Wo On Lok, commonly known as Shui Fong. It was originally established by workers of the Connaught Aerated Water Co Ltd, with “On Lok” being a Chinese transliteration of the company’s name and “Shui Fong”, meaning “water factory”, used as a shorthand for the aerated water plant.

Traditional rituals succumb to modernity

Lau’s book, From Hung League and Huidang to Modern Triads, published earlier this year, offers a rare glimpse into the triads’ traditional initiation ceremonies.

The rituals – gruelling affairs that could last for hours – centred around a sacred altar draped with command banners and ancestral tablets honouring fallen members.

New recruits were required to recite secret verses before lighting joss sticks and being covered with a sandpaper quilt. They shredded paper lotuses and chopped a chicken’s head to seal a blood oath.

They had to pledge allegiance by reciting 36 oaths and swear to abide by 21 regulations, 10 prohibitions and 10 punishments. Finally, new recruits would present their “protectors” with a red packet containing HK$3.60, a symbolic figure invoking the phrase “three times three never ends, six times six is infinite”.

According to Lau, the knowledge of traditional initiation rites has waned over time, with triads either forgoing rituals to avoid arrest or struggling to maintain them in the face of modern limitations.

“Take chopping off a chicken’s head [as an example]. Where do you even get a chicken’s head nowadays? Ever since the avian flu outbreaks, there are no chicken heads any more. So it turned into chopping an egg,” Lau said.

“And taking a blood oath? What about cross-contamination? We might as well just drink red wine.”

He added that he had seen triad members using a red plastic hosepipe or a red mop handle to symbolise the rank of “red pole” – a senior member responsible for organising fights and enforcing gang rules.

To avoid attention from law enforcement, some triads held ceremonies in the mountains, on barges or in mainland China.

More commonly, initiations were reduced to a mere verbal agreement, a practice known as “hanging the blue lantern”, Lau said.

More like rogue ‘employment agencies’

Michael Leung Siu-kei, a supervisor at the Hong Kong Federation of Youth Groups’ youth crime prevention centre, said triads in the past would recruit youths loitering in public spaces such as football fields, but that practice had faded into history.

Triads nowadays were more like “employment agencies”, with syndicates using Telegram, Signal or even in-game chat rooms to advertise various “well-paying part-time jobs” to lure teenagers to work for them, he said.

“They list how much [they pay] for splashing red paint, how much for distributing illicit cigarettes, how much for criminal damage.”

He added that syndicates paid around HK$500 (US$64) for young people to distribute illicit cigarette leaflets at an entire housing estate overnight and HK$6,000 for a group to commit criminal damage against an office. They offered HK$1,000 to anyone willing to lend a physical bank card and HK$2,000 for an online bank account to launder money.

Once a person accepted a job, it effectively meant they had pledged loyalty to a specific triad boss, although these allegiances were often loose, Leung said.

“In fact, when we ask some youths about their gang ties, they’ll say: ‘I’ve never even met my boss.’ Sometimes they claim to belong to one triad faction, but after a while, we find them working on another job under a different faction.”

Leung said he had to constantly warn youths of the risks and serious consequences of accepting these jobs.

Au Yeung agreed that triads’ tactics for recruiting young people were no longer as blatant as in the past, as police deployed undercover officers to catch recruiters.

“The triads use a much softer entry point these days. ‘Want to make some quick cash?’ ‘Come out and meet some new friends.’ ‘There’s free beer’,” he said.

Police also worked closely with schools to prevent triads from infiltrating campuses and conducted cyber patrols to combat online recruitment, Au Yeung added.

For Jason, earning quick money came at a cost as he became wracked with anxiety about being followed and developed a drug habit.

“You get paranoid. You worry people or enemies might have followed you home and know where you live. Whenever I slept, even the slightest noise woke me up,” he said.

Jason was once arrested by an undercover police officer after divulging that he was a triad member, but was acquitted by the court due to lack of evidence.

At the age of 15, he began taking Ice and got involved in drug trafficking. But as his addiction grew more severe over a year, he started consuming his own supply and ended up owing the triad HK$40,000 for the drugs.

Raised primarily by his grandparents, Jason was surprised when his estranged father stepped in to help clear his debt.

“It felt like he had not given up on me,” he said.

Around that time, the death of his beloved grandfather proved a final wake-up call for Jason, prompting him to quit drugs, cut ties with the triad and return to school.

He now runs his own small delivery team.

Looking back, he said he regretted joining the triad and could see more clearly how the organisation had exploited him.

“At the end of the day, the triads are driven purely by self-interest,” he said. “Your family is always your strongest backing. No matter what happens, they will always support you.”

*Name changed at the interviewee’s request.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong vs Singapore in tackling bad behaviour
item.description:
Singapore is doing something about uncivilised behaviour on public buses. The city state has started enforcing new regulations that carry an immediate fine of up to S$500 (US$390) if you put your feet up on seats, play loud audio on your phone or make a nuisance of yourself in other ways such as eating, drinking and littering.

This aligns with existing rules governing passenger conduct on Singapore’s MRT railway system.

Did you know we have long had similar regulations for Hong Kong’s MTR network under its own by-laws? Probably not, because nobody cares, but they do exist.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore is doing something about uncivilised behaviour on public buses. The city state has started enforcing new regulations that carry an immediate fine of up to S$500 (US$390) if you put your feet up on seats, play loud audio on your phone or make a nuisance of yourself in other ways such as eating, drinking and littering.

This aligns with existing rules governing passenger conduct on Singapore’s MRT railway system.

Did you know we have long had similar regulations for Hong Kong’s MTR network under its own by-laws? Probably not, because nobody cares, but they do exist.

For instance, playing audio loudly on trains is punishable by a fine of up to HK$2,000 (US$250). The same penalty applies for uncouth behaviour such as placing your feet on seats and for ignoring eating or drinking bans.

Not only that, using profanity and language deemed offensive carries a fine of HK$5,000. If the MTR actually enforced this particular by-law, it would collect a revenue bonanza.

Rushing the train doors when they’re already closing, with the warning beeps going off, should earn you a penalty of HK$2,000 as well. It should but it won’t because the difference between Hong Kong and Singapore is that many of these rules are just there for lip service. Nobody bothers to follow or enforce them in one jurisdiction, while they are taken more seriously in the other.

You can resurrect the usual tropes about personal freedoms and repression in this comparison, in which we’re somehow supposed to take comfort in the assumption that at least it feels less controlling here than in Singapore. But if it’s about curtailing the freedom to behave badly in public and shared spaces, then bring on that Singaporean-style repression.

There is the concept of liberty, which is the freedom to act responsibly within an accepted legal and social framework without being a nuisance to others. Then there is licence, which is the entitlement to do whatever you want with zero regard for societal norms and the rights of others around you.

Millions of people in this city can’t be bothered with basic courtesy and social graces. These include holding the door open for someone right behind you, resisting the urge to furiously jab the “close door” button to deny someone entry into a lift even as you’re making eye contact, waiting for people to alight first before storming onto trains and many other daily acts of incivility and social ineptitude.

There is a lot of pent-up rage out there. This is reflected in a whole lot of honking in Hong Kong as rude and impatient drivers blast perceived irritants such as fellow motorists slowing down or getting stuck in front of them, children, cardboard-collecting grannies and even wheelchair users who fail to get out of their way in time.

Also in their way, as well as everyone else’s, are the mobile phone zombies. These people have their noses buried in their electronic pacifier while sauntering along the most crowded streets and walkways in the world with infuriating apathy and total disregard for the natural flow of human traffic.

The cocooned self-indulgence of these sidewalk narcissists and human roadblocks everywhere we go is as exhausting in its nonchalance as it is frustrating in its main-character syndrome. They expect the entire sea of humanity to conveniently part and warp around their immovable bodies like ignorable background noise.

This is not a problem unique to Hong Kong, but there is a difference that makes it all the more egregious here. While most of the world measures population density per square kilometre, Hong Kong’s 7.5 million residents are crammed into just 25 per cent of its total land area – the rest is uninhabitable or designated as protected areas and country parks.

That means when we talk in terms of volumetric hyper-density – how people actually fit into public space – we are in a different league. Vertical urbanism accommodates us, but when we pour out of our anthills to go about our daily business on the ground, the congestion is next-level.

On the streets of Mong Kok, for example, academic studies have shown that the population density can be up to 600,000 people per square kilometre, even though the figure for the wider district is 130,000 people, which is still one for the record books.

On an average footbridge or elevated walkway in Mong Kok, density can be up to 3.5 people per square metre. This is insane, and it is also why people who make it worse should not be dismissed as harmless manifestations of first-world problems. These miscreants with mobile phones are directly and constantly escalating stress levels in an already high-strung society.

Why can’t we have a law against it, just like we have one penalising the misuse of mobile phones while driving?

Should you feel the urge to pause in mid-stride to check your phone while walking elbow-to-elbow with 1,000 fellow humans at any given time, pull over to the side and get your dose of instant gratification without obstructing the rest of us.

If that sounds unrealistic, remember that people said something similar about banning smoking in public spaces some decades ago. Look how we pressed ahead with it and prospered.

Comparisons to Singapore bring to mind what the late Lee Kuan Yew said when he was accused of infringing on personal liberties by micromanaging public behaviour: “I say without the slightest remorse, that we wouldn’t be here, we would not have made economic progress, if we had not intervened on very personal matters – who your neighbour is, how you live, the noise you make, how you spit, or what language you use. We decide what is right. Never mind what people think.”

What a splendid man, unafraid and unapologetic about putting facts before feelings to get things done for the greater good. And what a pleasing thought, imagining what he would have done about the mobile phone menace if he were still around today.

Sure, pearls would be clutched and token noises sounded, but most of us would appreciate the net improvement in the quality of life. I’m not advocating the introduction of caning in Hong Kong, mind you, but perhaps a bit of a spanking is long overdue.

item.title: [SCMP] US sanctions forced Xinjiang cotton to adapt, but survival comes at a cost
item.description:
The fields in Xinjiang’s Awati county – a cotton hub hit by US sanctions – were nearly ready for the October harvest.

Yusup Molamaiti, a 36-year-old technician, recalled what it was like manually planting and harvesting 37 mu (about 2.5 hectares or 6 acres) of scattered plots of land.

“Planting a single mu took up to three hours with two people laying plastic film by hand,” he said. Harvesting would lock his family into year-round labour, yielding just 250-300kg (551-661lbs) per mu.
item.content:encoded:
The fields in Xinjiang’s Awati county – a cotton hub hit by US sanctions – were nearly ready for the October harvest.

Yusup Molamaiti, a 36-year-old technician, recalled what it was like manually planting and harvesting 37 mu (about 2.5 hectares or 6 acres) of scattered plots of land.

“Planting a single mu took up to three hours with two people laying plastic film by hand,” he said. Harvesting would lock his family into year-round labour, yielding just 250-300kg (551-661lbs) per mu.

Today, his 100-household village is a model for Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region’s agricultural overhaul. Region-wide, over 90 per cent of cotton is now harvested by machine, according to China’s cotton association.

Following land consolidation, seeders guided by satellite navigation can plant the entire village in two days, drones spray fields in five hours, and domestic harvesters have pushed mechanisation to nearly 100 per cent, boosting yields to 400kg per mu, according to the village leader’s collective.

For Yusup and his wife, less than five months of work as cooperative technicians yields over 30,000 yuan (US$4,200). Combined with livestock farming, their annual household income now exceeds 90,000 yuan – a 125 per cent increase from before mechanisation.

The cooperative members shared their stories with a delegation of journalists from domestic and foreign media – including the South China Morning Post – during a government-organised media tour in early September.

The tour was part of Beijing’s broader campaign to showcase Xinjiang’s development and to push back against Western allegations of forced labour.

Since the US began placing textile manufacturers on entity lists under the Uygur Forced Labour Prevention Act (UFLPA), Xinjiang’s industrial players have forged a sophisticated survival model, backed by state price supports, rapid mechanisation, technological upgrades, aggressive market diversification and domestic brand substitution.

Yet, on-the-ground sociologists and global trade specialists warn that this resilience comes at a steep hidden cost, including squeezed profit margins, a chilling effect that has triggered a “domestic decoupling” and an unintended spillover into European markets.

Failed legal remedies

Signed into law in 2021, Washington’s UFLPA establishes a “rebuttable presumption” that all goods produced in whole or in part in Xinjiang involve forced labour – a charge Beijing consistently denies – and specifically bars listed companies from exporting to the US unless they can provide “clear and convincing evidence” to the contrary.

Additions to the list in August brought the total number of blacklisted companies to 187 across sectors including gold, pharmaceuticals, aluminium, clothing and food.

From early on, targeted companies tried to fight the restrictions.

A senior manager of a major yarn spinning giant, who preferred to remain anonymous, said that in May 2020, a local subsidiary in Aksu was added to the US Commerce Department’s entity list for alleged human rights abuses, followed by a broader import ban under the UFLPA in June 2022.

“They even included several subsidiaries that had been liquidated five or six years earlier,” he said.

In 2020, the textile maker invited Western clients and third-party social compliance auditors to conduct on-site inspections, where they were shown fully automated lines.

When the press delegation visited the company’s sprawling manufacturing complex in September, both Han and ethnic minority workers were seen moving side by side through the deafening roar of spinning machinery.

Cotton harvested from 5.3 hectares of local fields is fed into automated lines, where raw white fibres are dyed and spun into spools of black, grey and vibrant melange yarns.

According to the manager, foreign clients had acknowledged to him that the automated facilities operated without coercive practices but said their hands were tied by political pressure back home.

“They said: ‘I believe there is no forced labour in your factory, but this is not something we can decide,’” the manager said.

Other efforts proved similarly futile.

Hong Kong-based textile giant Esquel Group – which operated spinning mills in Xinjiang – commissioned independent third-party audits that returned scores above 85 out of 100, finding no evidence of forced labour.

When targeted by US sanctions, Esquel filed a lawsuit against the US Commerce Department in federal court in 2021.

The legal challenge stalled, and by late 2024, the US government added Esquel’s parent group and subsidiaries directly to the UFLPA entity list. Major clients including Nike, Tommy Hilfiger and Patagonia cancelled orders, forcing Esquel to shut factories in Mauritius and Malaysia and shed more than 10,000 global jobs.

Sheng Lu, a professor of fashion and apparel studies at the University of Delaware, noted that hi-tech field mechanisation had done little to ease US customs enforcement because the burden of proof under the rebuttable presumption was extraordinarily high.

“In practice, US fashion brands and retailers regard sourcing cotton from Xinjiang as extremely risky,” Lu said.

“Given plenty of alternative sourcing destinations in countries like Bangladesh and nearshoring opportunities in Mexico and Central America, incentives to challenge the ‘rebuttable presumption’ are extremely low among US fashion companies.”

Pivot and diversification

Faced with an unyielding US legal barrier, textile producers abandoned litigation and launched sweeping operational pivots.

“In 2020, when the sanctions hit, our core leadership established a strict policy: no lay-offs, no pay cuts and no production shutdowns,” the manager of the Aksu spinning giant said.

The company’s solution was a drastic shift towards China’s domestic market and non-Western trade corridors. “Otherwise, how could you keep the workers fed?” he said.

The company redirected 60 to 70 per cent of its capacity to domestic Chinese apparel powerhouses such as Anta Sports. Another 20 to 30 per cent was routed to Southeast Asia, East Asia, Central Asia and Eastern Europe.

Before 2020, overseas markets accounted for 75 per cent of the company’s total business, with the US representing 80 per cent of those export orders. Following its inclusion on the entity list, the company’s US exports dropped to zero, while its Western European share shrivelled to just 3 to 5 per cent.

After years of heavy financial losses, internal balance sheets stabilised in 2024 before returning to profitability last year, the manager said.

Today, the Aksu facility employs more than 5,000 workers and is actively building new production lines to recruit another 1,000 employees. The parent group has set a goal to double its annual revenue to 200 million yuan, according to the manager.

Other industry players have also adopted a “dual-track” sourcing model: using imported cotton sourced from Australia or Brazil in coastal factories to service export orders, while reserving Xinjiang’s cotton for domestic product lines.

This strategy has been reported by Chinese media and confirmed by Lin Fangfei, a professor of sociology at Xinjiang University who has conducted extensive fieldwork across sanctioned supply chains.

National figures back up the domestic absorption.

Data from China’s National Bureau of Statistics shows Xinjiang’s cotton output hit a record 6.17 million tonnes last year, accounting for 92.8 per cent of national production.

Meanwhile, China’s domestic cotton consumption is forecast to hit 8.91 million tonnes this year – up from 7.8 million tonnes in 2024 – with about 1.6 million tonnes of raw cotton imported.

The trajectory of China’s domestic market is critical because local consumers already absorb 50 to 60 per cent of the country’s apparel production, according to Lu.

“This means that China’s domestic market can provide an important buffer for Xinjiang cotton,” Lu said. “But it may not be sufficient to absorb unlimited additional production, particularly if domestic apparel demand weakens.”

The long-term sustainability of this strategy would “depend heavily” on China’s domestic consumption and government policies, such as subsidies, he added.

Since 2014, Xinjiang cotton’s production has been supported by a state target-price subsidy programme that has guaranteed a minimum price of 18,600 yuan per tonne for Xinjiang cotton growers.

When initial US sanctions hit, manufacturers faced existential liquidity crises as banks hesitated to lend.

The government intervened to guarantee bank credit and preserve operating cash flow, preventing large-scale shutdowns. Local authorities have also organised peer-sharing forums for sanctioned firms to exchange mitigation strategies, according to the anonymous manager.

Following an August 2024 resolution by the Xinjiang People’s Congress opposing US sanctions, regional policies now pair state cotton target-price subsidies with legal support and financing for tech upgrades to help targeted firms pivot to new markets.

Meanwhile, the companies have been moving up the value chain by upgrading technology.

Inside the modernised processing plants, contrary to Western narratives of forced labour, the manager said the main challenge was “an acute labour shortage”.

As education levels rise and demographics shift in southern Xinjiang, younger generations increasingly prefer gig-economy jobs, such as food delivery, over factory work.

Rapid industrial automation had also eliminated the demand for low-end manual labour, shifting recruitment entirely towards educated, tech-savvy technicians capable of operating digitised machinery, he said.

Esquel Group has pivoted towards direct-to-consumer retail, expanding its self-owned premium brands.

“Esquel remains focused on our ongoing transformation into a knowledge-based innovation company,” the group wrote in a reply to the SCMP.

It added that the company had also launched the Esquel Innovation and Incubation Village in Urumqi, transforming a former manufacturing facility into an incubation platform for agricultural tech and green technologies.

Chilling effect

While corporate pivots show individual resilience, field researchers stress that looking only at the surviving industrial giants paints an incomplete picture, as the impact varies across different nodes of the supply chain.

According to a forthcoming study in the peer-reviewed International Review of Financial Analysis, the sanctions inadvertently spurred asset growth and production efficiency among “smaller, younger, non-state-owned enterprises with high R&D investment”.

Those companies located in central and western China were able to capitalise on domestic brand substitution, the Chinese researchers found, according to the October study.

Some export-oriented firms in coastal provinces, however, were “dealt a huge blow”, other research shows.

“Even for firms that survived by restructuring, the forced pivot has eaten heavily into their profit margins and introduced extra compliance costs that simply would not exist without sanctions,” Lin said.

She said another major destructive effect of the sanctions was the pervasive culture of fear and the “chilling effect” generated throughout the market.

For years, Chinese officials and businesses have faced a delicate narrative balance. If the media emphasises that targeted industries have adapted, Washington will interpret it as a sign that sanctions were insufficient. But if Beijing reports severe economic fallout, Western policymakers will cite it as proof that their measures are working.

Lin said that during her research, corporate leaders expressed fear that media attention would invite “further US punishment”.

To dodge the risk of secondary sanctions and safeguard their own export revenues, some apparel brands in coastal provinces are quietly severing supply ties with sanctioned Xinjiang mills.

Lin also pointed to an unquantifiable “hidden iceberg” of lost economic activity, where foreign multinationals such as Volkswagen and Tesla have abandoned prospective investments or facilities in Xinjiang.

In the US, however, “strengthening customs enforcement has become a critical part of the Trump administration’s trade policy”, Lu said.

This was especially evident in an executive order signed by US President Donald Trump in June prioritising investigations into forced labour and illegal transshipment through heightened audit frequency, stricter disclosure mandates and rigorous supply-chain documentation requirements, he added.

“The recent US Section 301 investigation is pushing more countries not only to implement their own forced labour laws but also to adopt the US legislative framework and criteria. In other words, the Xinjiang cotton ban is expanding beyond the US to the rest of the world,” he said.

More than 24,300 shipments with a total value of almost US$1 billion have been blocked since the act came into force, according to the US Department of Homeland Security.

US Customs and Border Protection had intensified scrutiny of all major import sources, including potential transshipment routes through Southeast Asia, Lu observed.

But Western fashion companies are not fully decoupling from China.

As of July, China remained the second-largest source of US apparel imports, after Vietnam, and was “increasingly seen as a strategic sourcing destination that offers flexibility, agility, and cost-efficient apparel products, even with relatively higher tariff rates”, Lu said.

In a recent study Lu conducted with the US Fashion Industry Association, respondents indicated that sourcing from China was “somewhat stabilising” this year, and few companies planned to fully decouple from China. Beyond finished garments, China is also regarded as an indispensable supplier of textile raw materials with no easy alternative.

European spillover

According to a May study, researchers from Britain, the European Union and the World Bank found that direct Chinese exports of cotton and cotton products to the US fell by 19 per cent at the intensive margin following the restrictions.

Unlike the US, the EU has not enacted a blanket import embargo against Xinjiang cotton.

However, Jo Van Biesebroeck, co-author of the paper and an economics professor at KU Leuven in Belgium, pointed out that US trade sanctions had triggered unintended spillover effects across Europe.

“We were very surprised that the negative effect on EU imports is as large as we found,” he said.

Their research found that the European retreat from Xinjiang cotton has been driven not by official EU policy, but by voluntary risk avoidance and concerns of “reputational damage” among European importers.

While US customs enforcement heavily targets less processed raw materials and yarns at ports, the drop in European imports is sharpest in finished apparel sold directly to consumers.

He said that because Xinjiang sent very few direct exports to Europe, most European scrutiny fell on downstream manufacturers in other Chinese provinces whose supply chains extended back to the far western region. This indirect link makes traditional factory audits far less convincing to European consumer advocates.

Van Biesebroeck noted that standard compliance audits failed to reassure buyers because European consumer dissatisfaction extended beyond specific forced-labour metrics to broader scepticism towards Beijing’s official narratives.

“I have never seen any real evidence of forced labour, but the overall situation is rather murky,” he said. “It is more the general treatment of the minority population that consumers want to protest.”

Researchers caution against viewing Central Asia or the Middle East as replacements for Western markets, as these regions cannot match the high-margin markets of the US and Europe.

Van Biesebroeck’s work showed that Russia was the only major market that registered a statistically significant increase in Chinese cotton product imports following the US ban.

Over the past five years, Beijing has been building up its own legal shield by enacting the Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law alongside regulations on countering “improper extraterritorial jurisdiction”. But the practical enforcement of these countermeasures remains to be seen.

Lin argued that solution strategies must move beyond micro-level compliance to embrace macro-level institutional support. By building a formal state-corporate community of shared interest, Beijing can prevent cash-flow collapses among Xinjiang manufacturers and avert local unemployment risks.

Beyond borders, China must transition from fighting unilateral sanctions in isolation to forging a broader multilateral coalition against economic coercion, she added.

“Many nations across the Global South have long suffered under the weight of unilateral US sanctions,” she said, adding that by uniting with affected countries and neutral trade partners, China could leverage collective international pressure to gradually rebuild a more balanced global trade order.

item.title: [SCMP] From Hong Kong to Guangdong, exploring the rich tapestry of Cantonese culinary traditions
item.description:
The term “Chinese cuisine” is an almost pointless label, encompassing as it does styles of cooking as diverse as Sichuan, Dongbei and Zhejiang, to name but a few. If thinking about a monolithic Chinese cuisine is inappropriate, does the same hold true for Guangdong’s Cantonese cuisine?

Consider chicken. A classic Hong Kong-style preparation might see white-cut chicken cooked in a simmering aromatic stock so the meat is gently poached and the skin adopts a gelatinous layer.

Further up the Pearl River Delta in Shunde (Shun Tak in Cantonese), the entire bird is deboned without tearing the skin and steamed together with ham and mushrooms.
item.content:encoded:
The term “Chinese cuisine” is an almost pointless label, encompassing as it does styles of cooking as diverse as Sichuan, Dongbei and Zhejiang, to name but a few. If thinking about a monolithic Chinese cuisine is inappropriate, does the same hold true for Guangdong’s Cantonese cuisine?

Consider chicken. A classic Hong Kong-style preparation might see white-cut chicken cooked in a simmering aromatic stock so the meat is gently poached and the skin adopts a gelatinous layer.

Further up the Pearl River Delta in Shunde (Shun Tak in Cantonese), the entire bird is deboned without tearing the skin and steamed together with ham and mushrooms.

From Guangdong’s northern coast, the traditional Chiu Chow or Chaoshan dish of poached saltwater chicken sees the meat steeped in a heavily seasoned salt brine or master stock, cooled and served at room temperature with a pounded garlic vinegar dip.

Hakka culinary heritage, founded in the hills of the province’s interior, takes an entirely different approach, wrapping the chicken tightly in paper and burying it completely in a pot of blazing hot, coarse sea salt.

Four distinct takes, four very different culinary approaches. Yet all of these dishes developed in the historic Guangdong province, an area roughly a third the size of France or Spain. Despite their common origin, should these different culinary traditions all be considered Cantonese?

Yes and no, says Silas Li, chef at Hong Kong Cuisine 1983. “I look at this almost like a family tree,” he says. “Technically, they represent distinct cultural traditions, but practically – and especially here in Hong Kong – they live under the same big roof.”

Historically, geography is a key determinant of a cuisine’s evolution. Li calls it the “true mother of recipe development”.

Shunde, sitting within the fertile Pearl River Delta surrounded by streams and fish ponds, supported a cuisine based on freshwater fish, mud carp, milk-yielding water buffalo, and tender river vegetables. For Li, this is the “cradle of classical Cantonese cooking”, the place where the region’s core standards for knife skills, slow-braising, seafood precision, and controlling the wok were established.

Elsewhere, along Guangdong’s Chaoshan coast, Chiu Chow communities had direct access to the ocean, inspiring a cuisine centred on deep-sea catches, saltwater poaching, and marine preserves, such as home-made fish sauces.

Hakka communities, however, were historically migratory and lived up in landlocked, rugged hills that offered no easy access to the coast or rivers. Consequently, they relied on calorie-dense pork, preserved salted vegetables and heavy salt-baking.

In Hong Kong, however, the different traditions have lived together for so long that the lines have naturally blurred.

“For me, Shun Tak is Cantonese core, while Chiu Chow and Hakka are sibling traditions that make our local food scene so much richer,” says Li, who draws inspiration for modern and classic dishes from all three culinary traditions at his restaurant in Happy Valley.

Chef and restaurateur Du Jianqing from Puning in Chaoshan is behind Shanghai’s two-Michelin-starred Amazing Chinese Cuisine and Selection by Du.

Du says he prefers not to view the question of whether Chiu Chow is part of Cantonese cuisine as a “battle over belonging”. Instead, he casts a wider, more inclusive net, thinking of both traditions as integral parts of the cuisine of Lingnan, a geographical area below the Nanling mountains that encompasses Guangdong, Guangxi, Hainan, Hong Kong, Macau and northern Vietnam, once occupied by the ancient Baiyue people.

“From the perspective of Chinese culinary culture, Lingnan cuisine has always been a rich and open system. Cantonese (Guangfu), Chiu Chow and Hakka cuisines together form the essential components of Lingnan culinary culture,” he says.

Cantonese and Chiu Chow cooking both place great emphasis on seasonality, ingredient quality, natural flavours and a high level of craftsmanship. But for Du, the main defining feature of Chiu Chow cuisine is not a specific classic dish or set of dishes, but an obsessive pursuit of xian, or freshness/umami.

“This freshness is not just about flavour, but an overall respect for seasonality, origin, firepower, knife skills, and the state of the ingredients. People in Chaoshan often talk about ‘eating fresh’ (shi xian), which means savouring the best possible state of today, this season and this exact moment,” he says.

If you just lump everything under ‘Cantonese’, you lose the story, and in fine dining, the story and the heritage are half of what the guest is paying to experience

Silas Li, Hong Kong Cuisine 1983

Chef Huang Jinghui, better known as Chef Fei, was born and raised in Chaoshan. He runs a small empire of celebrated restaurants, all of which specialise in Cantonese and Chiu Chow dishes.

Chef Fei also highlights how porous boundaries between culinary traditions can be. “I see Chiu Chow cuisine and Cantonese cuisine as deeply interconnected culinary traditions, rather than two that need to be clearly separated,” he says.

He points to the considerable overlap in ingredients, techniques and culinary traditions – from delicacies such as abalone, sea cucumber and fish maw to Chiu Chow-style braised dishes, Cantonese barbecue and traditional slow-cooked soups, each with its own expression across the two cuisines.

However, he says that at the same time, Chiu Chow cuisine has its own distinctive regional character and culinary traditions.

“For me, rather than focusing too much on how Chiu Chow cuisine should be categorised, what matters more is the flavour, craftsmanship and traditions it represents, and the richness and diversity it brings to the dining experience,” he says.

While Du and Chef Fei are less fussy about a fluid, inclusive view of Cantonese cooking, Li at Hong Kong Cuisine 1983 argues that maintaining distinct categories remains essential for the dining experience itself.

“If you just lump everything under ‘Cantonese’, you lose the story, and in fine dining, the story and the heritage are half of what the guest is paying to experience,” he says. “If we just call it generic Chinese food, it dilutes the respect these ancient subcultures deserve.”

While he finds diners from the communities whose cuisine he cooks to be his toughest critics, Li notes that the average local guest has become far more sophisticated.

“The modern Hong Kong diner – and even international guests – is way more educated now,” Li says. “They aren’t just looking for a vague ‘Chinese meal’; they want provenance, they ask about techniques, and they appreciate the subtle regional nuances.”

At Yan Garden in Beijing – a restaurant conceptualised by Chef Fei and led day-to-day by executive Chinese chef Peter Chen at the Mandarin Oriental Qianmen – Chen sees this curiosity playing out among broader audiences. He notes that around 10 to 15 per cent of guests are international, while the remainder are local Chinese consumers, with the dining experience itself serving as an educational bridge.

“Dishes such as our traditional marinated specialities, seafood preparations and seasonal Chiu Chow delicacies often spark conversations about the cuisine’s heritage and techniques,” Chen says.

Du observes a similar dynamic at Selection by Du in Shanghai. “Guests from Europe and the Americas tend to view us as ‘Chinese cuisine’, hoping to discover Chinese food through this meal,” he says. “Guests from Southeast Asia, Hong Kong and Macau – owing to the deep Chiu Chow or Nanyang cultural roots in their home regions – more easily recognise the delicate nature and emphasis on original flavours in Chiu Chow cuisine.”

This evolving awareness reflects a broader transformation across Chinese gastronomy. Over the last 10 years, Du notes that diners’ knowledge has expanded rapidly, moving regional cooking into a dynamic new phase.

“More regional cuisines are establishing their own brand identities – Yunnan, Guizhou, Jiangxi, Taizhou, Shunde and Zhejiang cuisines are all receiving increasing attention,” he says. “This does not mean Cantonese cuisine’s influence is waning, but rather that Chinese dining as a whole is becoming richer and more specialised.”

item.title: [SCMP] Tsui Ao-lung’s journey from airport worker to Hong Kong fashion champion
item.description:
Tsui Ao-lung did not walk a conventional path to becoming Hong Kong’s newest fashion-design champion. He has no formal training in garment design and he spent three years away from the industry altogether, earning an income moving cargo at the Hong Kong International Airport and waiting restaurant tables to pay off debts from a T-shirt brand he had co-founded. When he finally returned to the craft last year, it was almost by accident: a stylist had asked him to create stage outfits for a concert, so he taught himself how to design for the stage.

It was a circuitous route that led him, on September 5, to claim the top prize at the Hong Kong Young Fashion Designers’ Contest 2026 (YDC), a highlight of the annual Centrestage showcase, itself a flagship event of the third Hong Kong Fashion Fest, organised by the Hong Kong Trade Development Council. Competing against nine other finalists under the theme “You”, the 29-year-old took home the HK$60,000 cash prize, champion title and an overseas internship opportunity sponsored by knitwear manufacturing firm Fang Brothers Knitting.

His winning collection, “The Tide”, draws its name and mood from “Kuang Chao”, a 1970s Cantopop hit by Hong Kong singer Susanna Kwan Kuk-ying. Tsui used the song as a springboard to dive into the journey of a woman’s life across four seasons, capturing her highs, lows and the experience of existence in four hand-stitched pieces.
item.content:encoded:
Tsui Ao-lung did not walk a conventional path to becoming Hong Kong’s newest fashion-design champion. He has no formal training in garment design and he spent three years away from the industry altogether, earning an income moving cargo at the Hong Kong International Airport and waiting restaurant tables to pay off debts from a T-shirt brand he had co-founded. When he finally returned to the craft last year, it was almost by accident: a stylist had asked him to create stage outfits for a concert, so he taught himself how to design for the stage.

It was a circuitous route that led him, on September 5, to claim the top prize at the Hong Kong Young Fashion Designers’ Contest 2026 (YDC), a highlight of the annual Centrestage showcase, itself a flagship event of the third Hong Kong Fashion Fest, organised by the Hong Kong Trade Development Council. Competing against nine other finalists under the theme “You”, the 29-year-old took home the HK$60,000 cash prize, champion title and an overseas internship opportunity sponsored by knitwear manufacturing firm Fang Brothers Knitting.

His winning collection, “The Tide”, draws its name and mood from “Kuang Chao”, a 1970s Cantopop hit by Hong Kong singer Susanna Kwan Kuk-ying. Tsui used the song as a springboard to dive into the journey of a woman’s life across four seasons, capturing her highs, lows and the experience of existence in four hand-stitched pieces.

However, what the judges and the audience could not have anticipated, when the designer’s creations strutted down the catwalk, is that Tsui had let his exacting nature take the wheel, scrapping and overhauling entire looks in the days before the show, with the final touches to his pieces added right before he had to present them. A real-life Project Runway – Hong Kong edition, that is.

We talk to Tsui about winning the competition, his three years away from design, his ambition to eventually launch his own brand again and how he thinks he can work 18 hours a day without ever feeling tired.

What motivated you to enter YDC this year?

It was to tell stories, to express things I wanted to say. I think YDC is a great opportunity. It has a good platform and a complete system that lets people from all walks of life see your work. I never thought of taking part before, because I wanted to try and rely on myself, to strive on my own. But then, at a certain point, I thought, “Since the opportunity is there, why not give it a shot?”

How did it feel to win the contest?

I felt happy, very happy, but also relieved. So many people were screaming. I worked long shifts leading up to the finale. After that, I slept for hours.

What was your biggest challenge?

I used to do casual wear – simple clothes. YDC was my first time doing fittings, organising so many outfits, shoes and so on – I felt like I couldn’t handle it all. When I finished the four designs, I was very unsatisfied. So, I kept tweaking them, completely redoing some of the looks from scratch, and I ended up remaking the pieces I wasn’t happy with after the fittings, working on them up to the last minute before I had to leave for the show.

What was your workspace like?

I actually went back and forth to Guangzhou to make the clothes. A lot of suppliers are concentrated there, so if I needed materials or components, I could buy them straight away. Because I don’t have my own studio, I worked out of a shared “central sample room” – a space used by several shops. I didn’t have a fixed area on the premises, so whenever a space opened up, I’d drag my dress dummy and tools over there to work. Most of the time, I’d wait until late at night, after everyone else had left and the lights were off, so I could spread all my stuff out and sew in peace, staying until 4am or 5am. It took a lot of patience, and I kept pricking my fingers, but that’s how I got it done. Many friends were helping me. I didn’t ask them to, and I never shared what I was making with anyone. But in the last two weeks, they came to the fittings and helped me. I am so grateful.

How did you arrive at the core theme for your winning collection?

I often refer to music and films to capture a mood or feeling. For “The Tide”, the theme came from a Cantopop song called “Kuang Chao”. I came across it and was inspired to take that mood and expand on it. Since the song is about ups and downs, I thought about leaning into a woman’s perspective to explore the cycles of her life, moving through spring, summer, autumn and winter. I also wanted to connect it to the city – you’ll find elements of Hong Kong hidden in the clothes. Whether it’s a person or a place, there will always be moments of glory, but also moments of decline. It’s just as the lyrics go, “It’s them; it is also you and me”.

What was the most important quality you wanted to showcase?

For me, it’s all about the handiwork and hand-stitched details – they really make up the core of the whole collection. Having that focus on craftsmanship gives the collection a natural, cohesive feel.

What first got you into making clothes?

It was a total accident. After secondary school, a friend – my former business partner – had a group of friends who were really passionate about making clothes and starting brands, so I tagged along to join the fun. Back then, our mindset was purely about having a good time and experimenting together. “You make one for me to wear, I make one for you to wear” – that kind of thing. Slowly, everyone else stopped making clothes and abandoned dressmaking. I’m the only one left.

You spent three years away from designing. What was that period like?

During those three years, I actually prepared a lot; I mapped out plans for the next five seasons. I specifically avoided taking on design work because I’m uncompromising – I didn’t want to enter a system of creating commercial filler to make money. I waited tables and moved goods at the airport to make ends meet. Ironically, even while trying hard to avoid seeing them, I’d still spot people wearing clothes from my previous brand on their way to work. I really want to start a brand again, but I know one thing: you have to be ready before you do it. Once you come out, you have to be confident, professional, strong. You can’t just do it half-heartedly.

Describe your creative process.

First, I think of a story. When we actually start making the clothes, we often look at the fabric first and then build on the basic concept, step by step. I write a narrative, and then build the storyline, block by block, although whether it turns out the way I originally intended is a different matter.

How does Hong Kong shape your designs?

I watch a lot of concerts; they often inspire my work. For example, the second look in my collection, the cheongsam – nobody guessed that the inspiration came from one of Eason Chan Yick-shun’s concerts, where he happened to be wearing a belt styled like a corset. I pull inspiration from plenty of other concert looks, too, though I never copy them directly; I just use them as a starting point.

What kind of designer do you want to be?

I’m open to pretty much anything. My advantage, or maybe my flaw, is that I can see the positives in any style, so I don’t mind doing whatever type. But I’m more drawn to pieces with character. I’ll mostly stick to a story-driven line. I want to tell a story naturally, with relevant clothing elements to package it, while keeping my own touch.

What’s your ideal way of working?

I hope it’s one where I don’t have to rest, because I don’t like being inactive. I did YDC and worked 18-hour days – eating just one late-night meal a day – and had absolutely no problem with it. I didn’t feel tired. I can work straight through the night. It’s not just passion – my body’s simply wired that way. It’s like an engine: once it starts, it runs non-stop. Once I start working, I can’t stop.

item.title: [SCMP] Thailand has had enough of foreign tourists behaving badly
item.description:
At a zoo a short drive south of Bangkok, Charoon Youngprapakorn has spent a lifetime taking the pulse of Thailand’s tourism industry from an unlikely vantage point: the open jaws of crocodiles.

Handlers at his Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm & Zoo have long thrilled onlookers by coaxing tips from the audience and carefully placing the money into the mouths of animals capable of taking off an entire hand.

The crocodiles at this open-air, fan-cooled throwback to 1980s showmanship still take their tips at the end of every show. But these days, the notes are almost all Thai baht, handed over by Thai visitors. The busloads of overseas tour groups have largely disappeared.
item.content:encoded:
At a zoo a short drive south of Bangkok, Charoon Youngprapakorn has spent a lifetime taking the pulse of Thailand’s tourism industry from an unlikely vantage point: the open jaws of crocodiles.

Handlers at his Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm & Zoo have long thrilled onlookers by coaxing tips from the audience and carefully placing the money into the mouths of animals capable of taking off an entire hand.

The crocodiles at this open-air, fan-cooled throwback to 1980s showmanship still take their tips at the end of every show. But these days, the notes are almost all Thai baht, handed over by Thai visitors. The busloads of overseas tour groups have largely disappeared.

Tourism accounts for roughly one-fifth of the Thai economy, from the five-star resorts of Phuket and Koh Samui to the jet-ski operators and massage parlours of Pattaya.

The industry has never been immune to external shocks, however – and Charoon, who is in his seventies, has felt each one register at the ticket office of a business his father founded nearly 90 years ago to sell crocodile leather to tourists.

Sars, bird flu and the global financial crisis of 2007-08 all took their toll on visitor numbers, interspersed with boom years as mass tourism from China, an emerging Russian middle class and increasingly affluent Southeast Asian travellers pushed up attendance.

Then came a three-year closure amid the Covid-19 pandemic and – as with so much else in this world – nothing at Charoon’s zoo has been quite the same since.

“We used to have maybe 100, 200 big tour buses a day,” he told This Week in Asia. “But they stopped and we had to close because of the lockdown.”

By the time the business was able to reopen, tourism trends had changed. “People stopped travelling as big groups and instead they came as FITs,” Charoon said, using the industry acronym for “free, independent tourists”.

The zoo’s ample car park now welcomes only a handful of buses at a time. Across from it, a turreted wall built for elaborate performances once staged for Chinese tour groups stands as a chipped and faded monument to the high-water mark of Thai tourism.

Nearly 40 million people visited Thailand in 2019, the final year before the pandemic’s onset and still a Southeast Asian record.

Last year’s total of 32.9 million fell well short of that peak, despite a 60-day visa-free scheme introduced in 2024 to lure travellers back.

The Tourism Authority of Thailand has now trimmed its 2026 forecast to between 30 million and 34 million international visitors, as this year’s US-Israel war on Iran and Russia’s 4½-year-old war with Ukraine conspire to drive up oil prices and, with them, international airfares to Southeast Asia.

Years of a strong baht, meanwhile, have nudged budget-conscious international travellers towards cheaper alternatives in Vietnam and Malaysia.

Money, geopolitics and changing tastes tell only half the story, however. The rest is down to patience – and Thailand’s is wearing thin.

Misbehaving tourists

Long known as the “land of smiles”, Thailand has for years prided itself on its easy-going approach to hospitality that asks little of guests beyond good manners.

But scroll through Thai social media on any given morning nowadays and the previous night’s transgressions are laid out for all to see: unpaid bills, drunken brawls and arrests for theft or vandalism among them.

Each post gets shared and reshared until the obvious disrespect for a proud local culture starts to sour public opinion on the costs of welcoming millions of strangers every year.

“Thai people are pragmatic. We do like the money [tourism brings],” said Voranai Vanijaka, a prominent political and social commentator. “But at the same time, we are highly nationalistic and we don’t like tourists acting the fool.”

This year alone, tourists have been caught performing sex acts in public, assaulting locals, trespassing on private property and vandalising local landmarks. Recent crackdowns have also revealed dozens of bars and restaurants run by foreigners but masquerading as Thai-owned enterprises.

Other crimes are far more grave. In June, Australian national Simon Peter Carman, 45, was arrested on suspicion of murdering a teenage Thai girl, stuffing her body into a suitcase and disposing of it in the undergrowth near Pattaya.

Authorities have separately uncovered Chinese and Korean cyberscam operators holed up in luxury villas, an Indian national flaunting firearms on social media and a steady stream of British cannabis mules.

All the while, public attitudes against foreigners have been hardening – a sentiment Voranai said had also been fuelled by global nativist trends, nationalism stirred up by the recent border conflict with Cambodia and grievances over foreign nationals buying up land and businesses.

“There is an anti-foreigner, anti-immigrant feeling sweeping the world; it’s not just in Thailand,” he said, describing a “mood and tone” within which every viral episode of misbehaviour now played out, and a “lower tolerance” for such actions.

The steady drumbeat of bad news pushed Thailand to end its 60-day visa-free stays for tourists from September 15. Days later, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters he thought misbehaving foreigners had “gone too far”.

Not for the first time, Thailand has said it will step back from playing the numbers game to focus on attracting fewer, higher-spending tourists instead.

Officials describe 2027 as “the year of transformation”, aiming to attract wealthier travellers willing to stay a week or two at a time.
