A proposed flat fee of 450 baht (US$13.50) on all foreign visitors to fund tourism infrastructure upgrades is also being actively considered.

But this soul-searching over who Thailand wants to welcome, and for how long, comes as hotel bookings during the current low season have disappointed and as travellers appear to be waiting until the last minute to book their stays in the crucial high season that begins in November.

On the upside, Thai tourism authorities are anticipating 200,000 Chinese tourist arrivals during next month’s “golden week” holiday from October 1 to 7, just as a the baht’s recent retreat is offering travellers better value.

Against this uncertain backdrop, Charoon’s crocodile farm has enjoyed something of social media-spurred revival.

In its 1980s heyday, when his father welcomed dignitaries including Singapore’s founding prime minister Lee Kuan Yew, the business made headlines for encounters with reptiles that visitors elsewhere might only see behind glass.

But as the novelty of live-animal shows began to wear off and tastes changed, the zoo’s weekday crowds thinned to a trickle.

Then, in late August, a TikTok video showing a single visitor sitting alone in the stands at one of the zoo’s elephant shows found an audience all of its own, garnering more than 1 million likes and sending a flood of visitors streaming back through gates.

“I was shocked. I didn’t expect that. I never thought one video could communicate to so many people,” Charoon said.

“People are coming in their thousands. I just hope they keep coming.”

Show respect, or go

Thailand is far from alone in pausing to reconsider its relationship with visitors.

In Indonesia’s Bali, a foreign-led running club accused of barring locals from taking part suspended operations this summer; in Sri Lanka, Buddhist monks held a violent protest outside a newly opened Jewish community centre known as a Chabad house last month, questioning its legality; and in Vietnam, authorities have vowed zero tolerance for foreign misconduct after recent drunken rampages and a deadly shooting linked to foreign nationals.

Social media, as ever, amplifies both the insults delivered and how they are received.

One Phuket business owner, who asked not to be named to protect his livelihood, told This Week in Asia that the types of tourists now visiting Thailand were more entitled, demanding unreasonable discounts and firing off insults at the slightest whiff of not getting their own way.

“I don’t think Thais are xenophobic,” he said. “But my mindset has changed, like a lot of people on Phuket. Customers are customers, but if they’re not nice and don’t respect the culture and the people, we are happy to see them go.”

This change in public sentiment appears to have influenced the government’s decision to halve the 60-day visa free-entry. It has also produced unusually blunt warnings from ministers who normally pull their punches when addressing foreign embassies.

In August, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told the Chinese ambassador to “come out and explain” when sensitive issues arise “instead of speaking only to protect Chinese interests” – remarks that followed a viral confrontation between Chinese passengers and Thai officials at Bangkok’s main airport.

His comments also came amid mounting evidence of Chinese nationals illegally owning land and companies in Thailand, in some cases via officials bribed with as little as 500 baht to issue fraudulent birth certificates conferring land-ownership rights.

A small but vocal protest movement against official corruption and the influence of so-called grey money has since emerged, fronted by veteran conservative agitator Sondhi Limthongkul, who has rallied tens of thousands to take to the streets in the past.

Prime Minister Anutin, who himself rode a wave of nationalist sentiment to victory in February’s election, has responded to the backlash by fast-tracking deportations of foreign criminals and opening a wider investigation into “nominee” arrangements that allow foreign business owners to hide behind Thais.

Chinese, French, British, Indian and Russian nationals have all come under scrutiny, but it has been Israeli nationals – many of them military-aged and arriving in the wake of the war in Gaza – who have attracted the most intense attention, accused of building extensive “nominee”-business networks across southern Thai islands and of operating an illegal cemetery in Chachoengsao province.

“This has gone too far,” Anutin told officials on September 17 in response to the outrage.

“If they want to use our existing facilities, we have no problem with that. We have no objection whatsoever,” he said. “But they cannot come here, take our land, and then bury their dead here.”

Anutin’s point man on the “nominee” scandal, Deputy Interior Minister Polapee Suwunchwee, has since said he is investigating several Chabad houses across the country, warning that any found to have been built unlawfully could be torn down.

Following a meeting with Thailand’s foreign minister earlier this month, Israeli Ambassador Alona Fisher-Kamm told local media that bad behaviour was not unique to citizens of her country, adding that Hebrew-language pre-departure awareness campaigns were being introduced outlining Thai laws and cultural norms.

Nationalist commentators with large online followings have seized upon the anti-Israeli rhetoric, some veering into outright antisemitism.

“There is a risk of this getting out of hand,” Voranai said, referring to growing anti-Israeli “paranoia” stoked by hardline conservatives chasing clicks and the political spotlight.

Yet he doubts the swirling public anger will cost Anutin’s government much in the long run.

“There is no risk to the government at all – except for bad press, which they don’t care about,” Voranai said. “Nor should they, they hold all the power and they can just ride it out.”

Meet the neighbours

Amid the blizzard of bad publicity, some are determined to build bridges between foreigners and their Thai hosts.

John Ho, who was born and raised in Hong Kong but swapped a career in hospitality for a new life in Chiang Mai with his Thai wife a decade ago, this month launched CosmoLocal CNX – a government-backed “pop-up village” offering workshops, talks and communal meals to draw the Thai city’s digital-nomad population into closer contact with their Thai neighbours.

“There’s a transitional period where you’re travelling as a tourist, when you may not care that much about the local culture and language,” Ho said.

“But then, if you want to stay longer and set up a base, it naturally comes to a question of: ‘OK, let’s make friends’. It’s better to learn some Thai, and learn some of the laws around business and work.”

His pop-up, which offers discounted tickets for Thai attendees to keep it accessible, trades on Chiang Mai’s slower pace of life, distinctive northern Lanna culture and small-town feel – qualities that have attracted legions of remote workers since the pandemic.

It is a world away from the raucous party scene of Thailand’s southern islands, where many of the recent cultural clashes have occurred.

“We see the tensions,” Ho said. “But the majority of nomads do care – maybe they need more facilitation to meet the locals. This is the first attempt to do that.”

As for the seemingly endless churn of viral confrontations between Thais and foreigners?

“News cycles are news cycles,” Ho said. “I think a lot of it is out of proportion. Everyone in Thailand welcomes foreigners.”

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s Kellett School celebrates 50 years with bold 10-year plan and new Sixth Form Centre
item.description:
Plutarch, the Greek philosopher and writer, once likened the mind to a fire to be kindled rather than a vessel to be filled. Sparking curiosity remains a key goal in education, especially for the teachers at Kellett School, one of the oldest non-profit British international schools in Hong Kong.

This year, the institution marks its 50th anniversary, having grown from two primary classes in Wan Chai into an all-through school that now operates across three campuses on Hong Kong Island and in Kowloon.

Regarded as one of the city’s top international schools, Kellett is pursuing an ambitious road map under principal and CEO Paul Tough, who took the helm in 2024. “Kellett Vision: 2035” is a 10-year, six-pronged strategy with a clear focus: equipping students for an ever-evolving world, centred on pillars such as high-quality education, inclusivity and challenging students to push the boundaries of their potential, learning in and beyond the classroom, celebrating individual and collective well-being and achievements, fostering an environment of acceptance and respect, and making a difference within the wider community and in the world.
item.content:encoded:
Plutarch, the Greek philosopher and writer, once likened the mind to a fire to be kindled rather than a vessel to be filled. Sparking curiosity remains a key goal in education, especially for the teachers at Kellett School, one of the oldest non-profit British international schools in Hong Kong.

This year, the institution marks its 50th anniversary, having grown from two primary classes in Wan Chai into an all-through school that now operates across three campuses on Hong Kong Island and in Kowloon.

Regarded as one of the city’s top international schools, Kellett is pursuing an ambitious road map under principal and CEO Paul Tough, who took the helm in 2024. “Kellett Vision: 2035” is a 10-year, six-pronged strategy with a clear focus: equipping students for an ever-evolving world, centred on pillars such as high-quality education, inclusivity and challenging students to push the boundaries of their potential, learning in and beyond the classroom, celebrating individual and collective well-being and achievements, fostering an environment of acceptance and respect, and making a difference within the wider community and in the world.

With the upgrade of its Pok Fu Lam campus and the opening of the new Sixth Form Centre, designed to bridge the gap between secondary school and university with a mature, independent learning environment, the first year of Kellett’s second half-century is off to a solid start. Along with the Kowloon Bay campus, these three locations form the backbone of Kellett’s educational approach.

Kellett’s Sixth Form Centre is “about much more than additional space”, Tough explains. “It represents the kind of learning environment that we believe young people need as they prepare for university and the world beyond. We wanted a setting that encourages independence, collaboration and intellectual curiosity.”

Beyond the blueprint of bricks and mortar, his plans for Kellett’s next decade are articulated through a commitment to the strategic priorities. “Kellett Vision: 2035” places high-quality teaching and learning at the fore, while championing individual and collective well-being as the bedrock of the school experience.

Central to this evolution is the cultivation of a flourishing community – an ecosystem where academic achievement is bolstered by a “support for all” philosophy, anchored by the creation of dynamic learning environments that place Kellett at the vanguard of education. “Academic excellence remains central to who we are, but young people will also need qualities such as adaptability, creativity, resilience and sound judgment,” says Tough. “Success in life is about much more than examination results.”

Kellett answers this need with the introduction of bespoke, non-examined courses for students in Years 10 and 11 – a crucial period leading up to Britain’s General Certificate of Secondary Education (GCSE) exams. Focusing on life skills and designed to complement traditional academic subjects, these courses, integrating such subjects as entrepreneurship, financial literacy, service, global citizenship and sustainability, will be externally validated to ensure a richer learning experience.

As universities increasingly assess a student’s intellectual rigour and practical adaptability alongside traditional exam results, Kellett closes the distance between classroom theory and real-world application with hands-on learning opportunities.

Activities also take shape as outreach, partnerships or sharing best practices beyond the classroom, leveraging the city’s unique environment for immersive, experiential education. “Some of the best learning happens beyond school walls,” says Tough.

Roll-outs inspired by “Kellett Vision: 2035” have seen students taking part in projects such as providing English-language support in Wah Fu Estate and engaging in sustainability initiatives with a local farm cooperative and cross-border exchanges with schools in the Greater Bay Area, enabling them to contribute to the wider community. More programmes are expected over the next decade.

With input derived from conversations with staff, students, parents, governors, alumni and members of the community, Tough designed the forward-thinking strategy to take the school to new heights over its next 50 years. He sees it as a continuation of Kellett’s story rather than a departure from it.

“My role was really to listen; the vision didn’t arrive fully formed from my office,” he says. “It emerged from hundreds of conversations and a genuine desire to build something that reflects both our heritage and our future ambitions.

“Our students are thriving, our community is strong and demand remains high. At the same time, education is being reshaped by technological change and Hong Kong is positioning itself as a leading international education hub. It felt like exactly the right time to ask ourselves what role Kellett should play in that future.”

Future-proofing the education that Kellett students receive – especially at a time when change is only accelerating – is undoubtedly a priority. Over his career in education, which began in Britain and has taken him to Japan and Hong Kong, Tough has seen many changes in and out of the classroom. But the biggest impact of all has come from technology.

Our job is to help young people make the most of technology while developing the qualities that technology can’t replace

Paul Tough, principal and CEO of Kellett School

“AI will undoubtedly change education, but I actually think it makes the human side of education even more important, because the future will place a premium on qualities such as creativity, communication, collaboration, leadership and ethical judgment. Our job is to help young people make the most of technology while developing the qualities that technology can’t replace,” he says.

Tough has also observed how technology has transformed how students absorb information and learn: “With technology and social media, information is generated in smaller, more rapid chunks; the way that they truncate their learning into smaller chunks enables them to move on very quickly.” While this fast-paced digital consumption has helped students process information efficiently, reading for pleasure has lessened, says Tough. Yet, he praises the younger generation, arguing they should be given more credit: “Students today are full of questions, keen to learn about the world, ready to challenge norms and conventions, and understand why they are there in the first place, which I think is all very healthy.”

Many of us have fond memories of our favourite teachers. On his own education journey, Tough says, he was inspired by three instructors in particular: his parents, a Welsh language teacher and an economics and politics teacher; and his history teacher, who motivated him to specialise in history himself.

In the midst of his studies, Tough realised that teaching would be the next natural step for him. “My first ‘eureka!’ moment was when I was a postgraduate and tasked with teaching some modules as part of an undergraduate course. I had never stood up in front of an audience to share what I knew and help develop their knowledge. So, when I was doing that for the first time, I realised I wanted to be a teacher.”

After a couple of years teaching in Britain, Tough moved to Hong Kong in 1999. Aside from a five-year tenure in Japan, he has been here ever since.

“Arriving in Hong Kong and working at my first international school made me realise that working in that environment was how I wanted to pursue the rest of my career. An environment like Kellett provides opportunities and holistic experiences for children and makes them well-rounded individuals,” says Tough.

His time as a history teacher also instilled in him the conviction that the duties of an educator and a principal extend far beyond school hours. “It’s my duty to help students navigate different periods in their life. I have to ensure that the children have an advocate, a champion and somebody who helps them work through mistakes. It has defined how I lead schools,” he says.

Kellett is unique among international schools in Hong Kong as a parent-governed, independent and non-profit institution, allowing it to take a long-term view and focus entirely on what is best for students, he says.

As evident from “Kellett Vision: 2035”, Tough wants the school to keep pushing boundaries and stay on the cutting edge: “I often challenge myself, our staff and our board with a simple question: ‘Are we being bold enough?’ Kellett is a successful school and success can sometimes make organisations cautious. I don’t think our responsibility is simply to preserve what we have. It’s to build on it. It means being prepared to ask difficult questions, explore new possibilities and think carefully about what our students will need in the future, not just what they need today.”

Buildings matter, facilities matter and strategy matters, but culture matters most

Paul Tough

Most importantly, he has not lost sight of the humans at the heart of Kellett School. “One lesson I’ve learned throughout my career is that schools are ultimately about people. Buildings matter, facilities matter and strategy matters, but culture matters most,” he says. A strong school creates “a sense of belonging while maintaining high expectations”, and, in his experience, “meaningful change happens when people feel involved in shaping it”.

Backed by a strong community and framework, Kellett is well positioned to keep innovating and evolving. No matter what the future holds, the principles that anchored its past will guide its future. As Tough puts it, “Building a great school is about remaining true to the values that have always defined Kellett, while having the confidence and ambition to prepare our students for a very different future.”

item.title: [SCMP] Inside Bangkok’s World Gourmet Festival, where top chefs share the kitchen
item.description:
The 26th World Gourmet Festival returns to Bangkok from September 29 to October 4, bringing together some of the world’s most distinguished chefs. More than a showcase of gastronomic talent, the event serves as a multicultural narrative rooted in food heritage and transnational exchange – and as a crucible where culinary philosophies clash and meld.

Internationally acclaimed chefs like Álvaro Clavijo from Bogotá, Julien Royer from Singapore, and Josiah Citrin from Los Angeles must confront the challenges of merging different epicurean approaches with Thai ingredients, all while maintaining their own culinary identities. In this demanding environment with the world’s top food critics and most ardent foodies present, the stakes are high, and the potential for creative breakthroughs – and culinary disasters – lurks around every corner.

The pressures of collaboration
item.content:encoded:
The 26th World Gourmet Festival returns to Bangkok from September 29 to October 4, bringing together some of the world’s most distinguished chefs. More than a showcase of gastronomic talent, the event serves as a multicultural narrative rooted in food heritage and transnational exchange – and as a crucible where culinary philosophies clash and meld.

Internationally acclaimed chefs like Álvaro Clavijo from Bogotá, Julien Royer from Singapore, and Josiah Citrin from Los Angeles must confront the challenges of merging different epicurean approaches with Thai ingredients, all while maintaining their own culinary identities. In this demanding environment with the world’s top food critics and most ardent foodies present, the stakes are high, and the potential for creative breakthroughs – and culinary disasters – lurks around every corner.

The pressures of collaboration

Beyond now commonplace four-hands dinners and chef residencies, the World Gourmet Festival presents a unique set of challenges. Chefs must traverse language barriers, unfamiliar ingredients, and sky-high expectations from some of the industry’s most trained palates. For many, this tests more than culinary skill; it also challenges adaptability and creativity.

Josiah Citrin, chef-owner of restaurants Mélisse and Citrin in Los Angeles, acknowledges the pressure this event brings. “The expectation is always high, but that’s what makes these events exciting,” he explains. “In the kitchen, food becomes its own language quickly. Once you start cooking together, you find a rhythm, and that’s part of the fun of doing these events around the world.”

This balancing act – maintaining one’s gastronomic identity while embracing the unknown – is central to the festival’s spirit.

Pastry chef Puyachart “Boy” Puttawong of Saneh Jaan in Bangkok frames the goal precisely. “A successful collaborative menu should allow guests to recognise each chef’s individual personality while still experiencing a clear and harmonious connection from the first course to the last.”

Weaving a comprehensive throughline that connects each course, rather than jockeying for attention, helps diners understand the interplay between both cuisines and each chef’s culinary ethos. “Our intention is not to make every dish taste Thai, but to allow Thai culinary knowledge and ingredients to become part of the creative conversation,” Puttawong stresses.

Creating a cohesive dining experience amid such diversity can be daunting. Chefs must develop a menu together that reflects their individual styles while maintaining culinary continuity across courses. “Menu development begins with understanding each chef’s strengths,” remarks chef Pilaipon “Toi” Kamnag of Saneh Jaan. “Compromise doesn’t mean weakening anyone’s culinary identity; it’s about making thoughtful adjustments.”

Clavijo stresses the importance of listening rather than competing for space on the same plate: “I wouldn’t really call it ‘compromise’. If both chefs are trying to prove their identity in every single course, the guest feels that tension. A good partnership requires enough confidence to know when to speak and when to let the other person speak.”

Communicating can be a challenge in itself, with chefs from so many different countries taking part. But for many involved, food serves as a universal tongue, reducing friction.

Thanh Vuong Vo, executive chef of Coco Dining in Ho Chi Minh City, shares his perspective: “In a professional kitchen, communication goes beyond spoken language. You communicate through technique, timing, gestures, tasting and repetition,” he says. “If there is a difference in interpretation, we taste together and use the food itself as the common vernacular.” This fluidity allows chefs to communicate through actions and shared experiences rather than relying solely on verbal exchanges.

Zee Zheng, chef-owner of Fabula in Shanghai, observes, “I believe a chef is simply a messenger of nature. My role is to act as a bridge – connecting dishes while weaving in subtle local touches that add a sense of discovery.

“It’s all about both chefs working together to allow the ingredients to speak for themselves; that is what defines high-level cuisine.” This synergy cultivates an environment where innovation thrives despite the pressures of the event.

Ingredient-led approaches

Despite the challenges, one of the event’s most exciting aspects is the opportunity to experiment with niche Thai ingredients, from produce to proteins. For the chefs involved, these ingredients offer both inspiration and a challenge. Says Vo, “I want to understand the Thai ingredients and techniques first, then see how they can enter my own culinary language naturally.”

His goal is to create something that feels like a genuine conversation between Vietnam and Thailand, rather than simply combining ingredients from both countries. “Understanding their role in Thai cooking allows me to incorporate them into my own cuisine in a meaningful way while keeping the Vietnamese perspective at the heart of my cooking.”

This mindset of exploration is essential for chefs seeking to create dishes that resonate with both their own background and the local culture.

Clavijo’s approach at his restaurant, El Chato, is deeply rooted in Colombia’s ecological variety, and he sees Thailand as a mirror rather than a contrast. “Even though Colombia and Thailand are far apart, there are many similarities in our ingredients as both countries share a tropical climate,” he says. “Rather than forcing Colombian and Thai cuisines together, I prefer to find natural connections and let the products guide us.”

Julien Royer, chef-owner of Odette in Singapore, echoes this sentiment, emphasising the importance of understanding local flavours. “My culinary ideology revolves around the principle that ingredients are a reflection of terroir. My grandmother, Odette, was the one who taught me that respect for seasonality,” he says. For Royer, cooking with Thai ingredients is about respect and balance – finding a natural connection between two cuisines and letting them meet on equal terms.

The costs and benefits of participation

While the festival offers significant exposure and brand building, it also comes with sacrifices. Chefs must balance their responsibilities at home with the demands of such high-profile events. Citrin acknowledges this cost, stating, “Leaving your restaurant means leaving your team, your business, and your family. It has to have a meaningful purpose that extends beyond that one single event.”

Clavijo agrees, explaining that collaboration must go further than mere visibility. “The real value is exchange,” he says. “The lasting benefits of meeting other chefs, discovering new products, and creating ongoing relationships are what make these experiences worthwhile for chefs and attendees alike.”

A celebration of gastronomy

The World Gourmet Festival mirrors the evolving culinary landscape in Bangkok and Asia. As local chefs collaborate with international talents, they bring new perspectives and techniques to the fore. “As Thai chefs, we are proud to be part of the hosting city,” says chef Toi. “Bangkok is no longer simply a destination where international cuisine is presented; it has become an active and influential participant in the global culinary conversation.”

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea wants free ‘AI for All’. Is society ready?
item.description:
In Silicon Valley and beyond, the architects of artificial intelligence are increasingly warning about the risks it poses to humanity.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wants the industry to slow down. A former engineer at his company, who also worked at its rival OpenAI, told reporters after quitting earlier this month that he was “genuinely frightened” unchecked AI development might mean “we could all die in the immediate future”.

Even Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, has warned of the existential threat posed by the technology should it escape human control.
item.content:encoded:
In Silicon Valley and beyond, the architects of artificial intelligence are increasingly warning about the risks it poses to humanity.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wants the industry to slow down. A former engineer at his company, who also worked at its rival OpenAI, told reporters after quitting earlier this month that he was “genuinely frightened” unchecked AI development might mean “we could all die in the immediate future”.

Even Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, has warned of the existential threat posed by the technology should it escape human control.

Concerns about AI run the gamut from autonomous weapons, mass unemployment and machine-driven cyberattacks to deepfake-fuelled misinformation, algorithmic bias and a dangerous overreliance on automation.

South Korea has seen all this – and decided now is the time to hit the accelerator.

Under President Lee Jae Myung’s “AI for All” initiative, the government is preparing to hand every citizen free access to artificial intelligence, integrating it into hospitals, schools, government offices and daily lives in a way few countries have attempted.

“The idea is to substantially lower barriers to access so that the benefits of the technology are distributed evenly rather than enjoyed by only some people,” Seoul’s Ministry of Science and ICT said in a statement to This Week in Asia.

The government, which has a 10 trillion won (US$7.3 billion) AI budget for the current financial year, has allocated an additional 250 billion won for the roll-out through 2027.

A beta version is set to launch later this month, introducing free, unlimited-access general-purpose chatbots and AI agents developed by three consortiums – led by telecoms giants SK Telecom, KT and Kakao – using hundreds of state-of-the-art Nvidia B200 graphics processing units lent to them by the government.

From next year, officials envisage the temporary trial will become a permanent, taxpayer-funded public utility, eventually connecting to government systems to allow citizens to book doctor’s appointments, go house hunting, get tax advice and the like, all through AI intermediaries.

To manage the risks involved, Seoul is relying on its landmark AI Basic Act, which came into force in January, to ensure human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory impact assessments and clear watermarking of synthetic content.

Meanwhile, a state-funded AI Safety Institute has been tasked with serving as a technical watchdog to evaluate the pitfalls and ensure that public AI utilities remain trustworthy, secure and answerable to the citizens who use them.

“Going forward, the government plans to establish an autonomous reliability-assurance system”, the ICT ministry said in its statement, adding this would be based on the seven “AI Ethics Principles” it laid out last month: accountability, human-centredness, privacy protection and fairness among them.

South Korea hopes its “AI for All” push will help it become one of the world’s three leading AI powers, alongside the United States and China, with the government seeing the technology as an antidote to a shrinking workforce and as a way to strengthen its export-driven economy.

But the same society racing to put AI in every pocket is also confronting the consequences of what that means, as workers worry about automation eliminating jobs, police struggle to combat a surge in deepfake crimes and educators watch a generation’s reading scores slide.

Sovereignty is another concern. Of the roughly two-thirds of South Korea’s 51.6 million people who have tried or regularly use AI, 23.45 million are active users of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, 8.45 million of Google’s Gemini and 2.41 million of Anthropic’s Claude, according to government figures.

Yet access to these platforms cannot be guaranteed, as the ministry noted in its statement.

“As we saw recently, foreign AI services can have their availability limited at any time depending on decisions made by foreign governments or companies,” it said, in a possible nod to Washington’s recent attempts to block access to the newest models.

In July, Science and ICT Minister Bae Kyung-hoon unveiled plans for South Korea to develop its own cybersecurity-focused AI model by the end of this year, following the US clampdown.

Brewing with bots

At Unicup Coffee, an independent cafe vying for business against 11 low-cost chain rivals in Busan International Finance Centre, owner Bae Kyung-han, 31, credits AI with helping him beat the competition.

What began a year ago as a cost-saving experiment, with Bae teaching himself how to use generative AI to create promotional posters and menu images, has since taken over nearly every part of the business.

“It’s now running my research, proposal developments, communications and advertisements,” he said, adding that the AI system – his only office-based “colleague” – had also orchestrated a shift in focus towards bulk orders instead of walk-in customers.

Five employees handle customer orders, serving some 13,000 people a month and generating card sales that are, according to Bae, roughly double those of his competitors.

He has also built a second business around the technology, registering as a vendor under one of the government’s chosen AI consortiums to teach novices how to ask better questions of their chatbots.

“The biggest advantage of AI in the workplace is that it reduces the psychological burden of managing people,” Bae said, describing the relief of no longer having to coordinate schedules, repeat instructions or manage employees’ feelings.

“With AI, I can ask questions whenever I need to and revise plans whenever I want to. It’s just more efficient.”

Yet he is still sceptical of the government’s AI strategy, questioning whether domestically developed models – even ones that are provided for free – would actually be able to wean people off premium foreign made tools.

“People who are used to using AI would likely pay for a more expensive US-based model like ChatGPT rather than use a free domestic service,” Bae said.

That is, unless the models were specialised and purpose-built for specific problems, as opposed to another general-purpose chatbot.

“That changes the conversation,” Bae said. “That could do wonders for businesses like mine.”

Elsewhere, at a jobs fair in Seoul’s Yonsei University, technology companies crowded the floor, competing for the attention of soon-to-be graduates before they had even finished their degrees.

Kwon Il-geun, an electronic engineering student hoping to work at semiconductor giants Samsung Electronics or SK Hynix, said AI proficiency had never been more important.

“My skills in using AI tools have nearly doubled in the past year,” he said, comparing the shift to the first industrial revolution or the arrival of the personal computer. “This is just part of the changing times.”

No juniors needed?

Not everyone is sharing in the spoils, however. The number of young South Koreans aged 15 to 29 who were in work dropped by 285,000 between June 2022 and June this year, according to the central bank, which estimated that 94 per cent of that decline was in sectors highly exposed to automation, including publishing, IT services and computer programming.

And the Korea Development Institute, a government-run think tank, projected in July that AI could wipe out roughly 256,000 jobs a year within the next decade.

This has had a knock-on effect on students’ ambitions, with enrolment reportedly falling at academies teaching graphic design and coding, even as institutions preparing young people for stable public-sector careers enjoy booming interest.

At the SKY Entrance Exam Academy in Seoul, enrolment in its military and policy preparation track is up 70 per cent year on year.

Yun Ji-sang, a recent school leaver, is among those preparing to commit himself to five years of officer training and a military career of 15 years minimum.

“Some people think this is a long time to be trapped inside the military, but I just view it as a long time of having a stable job,” he said, noting that it was also one that came with a pension.

The number of young South Koreans in employment fell by 143,000 in August compared to the year before, the Chosun Daily newspaper reported on September 9, marking the 46th straight month of decline for those aged 15 to 29.

Meanwhile, the number of civil servants being recruited nationwide increased this year for the first time in five years, according to the Ministry of Personnel Management.

“I used to want to live as an entrepreneur who would travel abroad frequently and live freely,” Yun said. “But what use is that when we are constantly worrying about making a living?”

Conventional wisdom surrounding which jobs were most at risk from automation had been flipped on its head by the rise of generative AI, said Ko Hak-soo, a law professor at Seoul National University.

“When ChatGPT first emerged three or four years ago, there was widespread concern that jobs involving workers with relatively low levels of education … would be at highest risk,” he said.

“But now, there is a much stronger view that jobs requiring a great deal of human labour may actually be relatively safe while professional occupations, especially entry-level and junior workers in these fields, might gradually disappear.”

New roles were likely to emerge as AI became more integrated into workplaces, Ko said – while warning there was “little understanding of the reality of the shifting labour market”.

Kim Myuhng-joo, executive director of South Korea’s AI Safety Institute, said the disruption was already under way.

“Until just a few years ago, programmers were extremely highly valued, and their salaries were rising rapidly,” he told This Week in Asia. “But AI companies are increasingly using AI for coding … without needing as many junior-level developers.”

Kim further voiced concerns that a new cohort of workers coming of age in the “AI for All” era might never develop the skills needed to operate without the technology.

“In less than 10 years, we could see a new generation entering the workforce that is overly dependent on AI,” he said.

“Companies may expect these new employees to have the capabilities of previous generations, but they … could end up becoming people who are incapable of doing anything without AI.”

AI-fuelled abuse

South Korea’s most visceral fears surrounding AI stem not from the threat of rogue tech, however, but from the recent reality of criminal misuse.

The Nth Room case of 2020 – in which encrypted social media channels were used to produce, sell and distribute sexually exploitative material and blackmail victims – and subsequent scandals led to the country strengthening its deepfake laws in 2024.

Producing such material can now result in seven years behind bars or a 50 million won (US$37,000) fine, while possessing or knowingly viewing it can mean three years in prison or a 30 million won penalty.

Yet police still recorded 1,553 deepfake-related offences last year, accounting for over 35 per cent of all reported cybersex crimes, according to statistics presented at a recent forum hosted by Amnesty International Korea.

In the first half of this year alone, police apprehended 419 suspects for deepfake offences, 17 of whom were physically detained while awaiting trial.

The National Office of Investigation said in a statement that officials were “developing police response technologies at a pace that exceeds the speed at which technology itself is evolving”, including by expanding forensic video expertise and the use of AI-assisted detection tools.

Won Eun-ji is less convinced that technology alone will solve the problem. As director of Team Flame, which investigates digital sex crimes, she has spent much of this year infiltrating roughly 50 Telegram chat rooms alongside investigative outlet Newstapa, documenting how AI tools have swelled the ranks of anonymous perpetrators and lowered the age of victims.

“Even today, many initial leads in these investigations often come from victims themselves,” she said. “The police need to further specialise and strengthen their capabilities.”

Kim, of the AI Safety Institute, said the government needed to prepare for the unintended consequences of increasing access to AI.

“Once AI becomes embedded in society, it is difficult to remove it,” he said, describing it as “an irreversible change”.

“We need to conduct thorough impact assessments from the beginning, considering what effects the technology might have and whether it could be misused, abused or overused.”

To combat crime, Kim said he would support police undercover investigations “depending on the circumstance” alongside greater use of invisible watermarking to trace AI-generated content back to its creator or means of distribution.

“Online platforms should take more active steps to identify online crimes” and prevent abuse material from being circulated, he said, adding the children “need to receive education on these issues as part of broader civic education and AI literacy”, starting in primary school.

Generation chatbot

Yet in the classroom, an upside-down hierarchy of knowledge has begun to emerge, according to Moon Sung-ho, the 16-year-old editor-in-chief of Tokipul, an independent student-run newspaper.

“In many cases, students actually know more about AI than teachers, resulting in students using AI to complete all of their assignments while teachers don’t really know how to stop them,” he said.

Song Keun-sang was among the educators who protested last year against the government’s short-lived 1.2 trillion-won plan to roll-out AI-powered textbooks.

“Once we actually tried using AI in the classroom, we realised that it wasn’t as useful as we had expected,” said the fifth-grade teacher at a school in South Chungcheong province.

While good teaching pushes students to learn more about the world, AI short-circuits this process, according to Song.

“It simply gives you the answers,” he said. “It doesn’t have much educational value.”

Song had once thought that AI might be useful to help isolated students or those struggling to make friends, but that changed after a child in neighbouring North Chungcheong province died by suicide following conversations with a chatbot.

“I wonder whether it is really beneficial for students to be exposed to chatbots that constantly cater to them and reassure them,” he said. “They are essentially designed to tell you what you want to hear, so you will never be challenged or face disagreements.”

The effects of this may already be starting to be felt. South Korean 15-year-olds topped global reading charts in 2006, as measured by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development’s Programme for International Student Assessment.

Yet in 2025 they posted their lowest average reading score since the country first began taking part in the assessments in 2000, the OECD reported earlier this month.

“Other countries are starting to ban social media and other online devices for adolescents, but South Korea is moving in the exact opposite direction,” Song said. “We can already expect serious declines in academic achievement and literacy skills.”

The more pressing concern for him, however, is social rather than academic.

“Cooperation and communication between students ultimately develops the skills they will need to succeed in society later on,” he said, predicting that interacting with AI chatbots might make it “much more difficult to form relationships with other people.”

Moon has seen this happen among his own classmates and friend group, who once went to internet cafes and played football together, while also asking for help with homework assignments.

“Students these days increasingly ask AI chatbots about these questions,” he said. “It feels like it’s become more difficult to talk with people.”

This Week in Asia contacted South Korea’s Ministry of Education for comment on this article.

If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

item.title: [SCMP] Wing Shya: photographer to Wong Kar-wai on working with the great and good of Hong Kong cinema
item.description:
I WAS BORN in Hong Kong in 1964. My parents came from Shandong province, in mainland China, arriving illegally, later legalised – a common story for that generation. I went to the all-boys Salesian School, in Chai Wan, and was not a good student. I spent all my time messing around with friends. Then, at 17 or 18, I watched a film called Boat People (1982) and there was a character holding a camera who looked cool. Something happened in me. “I want to be that,” I thought. Not the actor – the photographer. I saved every dollar I made from part-time jobs until I could buy a camera, then I started to photograph everything: friends, family, the street, skateboarders. I didn’t really have a plan. I just liked looking through that little window.

MY ENGLISH WAS so bad and I didn’t do well in my exams, so university in Hong Kong wasn’t possible. Art school was the only door open to me and, I’ll admit, a good excuse not to get a real job yet. I went to a technical college, the Lee Wai Lee Technical Institute (in Kowloon Tong), before I found the Emily Carr College of Art and Design, in Vancouver, Canada – the only overseas school I could afford, where tuition for international students was the same as for local students.

I WORKED THREE or four jobs at a time, sometimes illegally, as I was on a student visa. I delivered food for a Chinese restaurant, waited tables and even cleaned houses that were a two-hour drive from the city. On weekends, I would sell my drawings in Stanley Park.
item.content:encoded:
I WAS BORN in Hong Kong in 1964. My parents came from Shandong province, in mainland China, arriving illegally, later legalised – a common story for that generation. I went to the all-boys Salesian School, in Chai Wan, and was not a good student. I spent all my time messing around with friends. Then, at 17 or 18, I watched a film called Boat People (1982) and there was a character holding a camera who looked cool. Something happened in me. “I want to be that,” I thought. Not the actor – the photographer. I saved every dollar I made from part-time jobs until I could buy a camera, then I started to photograph everything: friends, family, the street, skateboarders. I didn’t really have a plan. I just liked looking through that little window.

MY ENGLISH WAS so bad and I didn’t do well in my exams, so university in Hong Kong wasn’t possible. Art school was the only door open to me and, I’ll admit, a good excuse not to get a real job yet. I went to a technical college, the Lee Wai Lee Technical Institute (in Kowloon Tong), before I found the Emily Carr College of Art and Design, in Vancouver, Canada – the only overseas school I could afford, where tuition for international students was the same as for local students.

I WORKED THREE or four jobs at a time, sometimes illegally, as I was on a student visa. I delivered food for a Chinese restaurant, waited tables and even cleaned houses that were a two-hour drive from the city. On weekends, I would sell my drawings in Stanley Park.

I DID A double major: graphic design and fine art. In the summer, I’d drive to San Francisco, or fly to New York on the cheapest ticket I could find. I could earn a few dollars drawing people in Washington Square Park, in Greenwich Village. I had so much energy then.

AFTER GRADUATING IN 1991, six classmates and I opened a graphic-design company in Vancouver. Eight months in, we were doing well. One afternoon at a restaurant in Chinatown, I picked up a Hong Kong gossip magazine and looked at the layout. I said to my friends, “I have to go back – this design is terrible. I want to do something in the city.” They tried to talk me out of it. But within a week, I’d sold my car and bought a ticket home, without telling my mother. I flew back and rang the doorbell. She opened it and said, “Why are you here? You’re not welcome. We have no space.” I slept on the sofa.

WORK WAS HARD to find, but in 1992, I won a biennial photography prize and gave the money to my mother – it’s the right order of things. In 1993, I got a job at J. Walter Thompson (JWT), the advertising agency, but only lasted about a year; I had too much ego and was always fighting clients. I ran into an old school friend, Jan Lamb Hoi-fung – a singer who DJ’d at Commercial Radio Hong Kong – on the street by chance and he got me hired as the creative director there. It was a tiny department, just two of us, responsible for everything – stage design, ads, CD covers, concerts. I worked hard and I loved it. I got to know the biggest Cantopop stars: Jacky Cheung Hok-yau, Andy Lau Tak-wah and Faye Wong – she was there all the time.

THROUGH A FRIEND, Eric Kot Man-fai, my portfolio landed in front of Wong Kar-wai, in 1996. He said I could shoot some promotional pictures. On a Japanese commercial he directed, I hid behind a sofa so the crew wouldn’t throw me out of the tiny set – and when the official photographer could not get enough pictures, my photos were the only ones that worked. Because of that, Wong Kar-wai sent me to Argentina a year later, for Happy Together, starring Tony Leung Chiu-wai and Leslie Cheung Kwok-wing.

I HAD NEVER done film stills professionally. I didn’t even own a sound blimp – the soundproof box for your camera so you can’t hear the shutter going off. Because of this, I mostly shot between takes. I captured the actors sitting, waiting, hanging out: Tony and Leslie just breathing, not performing. One afternoon, on a rooftop, the street noise was so loud that my shutter was no longer an issue and I could finally shoot freely. Most of my images that you know from that film came from that one afternoon.

THEN, THE COLOUR. I was shooting slide film. Wong Kar-wai demanded to see the images immediately, but there were no labs where we were in Argentina that could process slide film. We found a shop that only did negative film. Because slide film is positive film, they ran mine through the wrong chemicals, and that turned everything green. Argentina’s grey walls became luminous. In the end, Wong Kar-wai loved it. It became the visual language of the whole film. I can call it a mistake, or I can call it, “I had no choice. It ended up like this.” After that, I left the radio station and started my company, Shya-la-la Workshop.

ONE DAY, WE were shooting in a train station – it was too noisy for sound recording – so I could shoot freely. Leslie was annoyed at me for distracting him. My shutter was too loud, but I kept going. I explained to him, “I’m only scared of Wong Kar-wai, not you. Because he hired me, only he can fire me.” He looked at me for a long moment, then said, “I like your attitude. When we get back to Hong Kong, you’ll work for me.”

HE MEANT IT. From that day until he died, I shot almost every photograph of Leslie for his work, his concerts, behind the scenes, albums and tours. He was the most considerate person I’ve known in this industry. He remembered everyone’s habits, every name, if you took milk in your coffee. He looked after the whole crew, from driver to delivery boy. We travelled together for concerts, shot in countries I’d never been to. I still think about him.

FOR In the Mood for Love (2000), Wong Kar-wai gave me one instruction: the film is about red. He gave me some music to listen to, and that was it, initially. So, in 1999, I went to Tokyo, bought 40 or 50 different rolls of film, shot test after test and laid every print in front of him. He picked one: an old, obscure film – barely still in production, its colour deeply reddish. I called the manufacturer; they were closing the following month because nobody was buying their film any more. “How many rolls remained,” I asked. “Two hundred,” they said. I bought every single one.

THAT PHOTO FILM was made in the 1960s or 70s, and its dyes were slowly failing – that’s why my shots for In the Mood for Love look the way they do. After we finished the film, there was none left anywhere in the world.

THERE ARE PEOPLE who I learned almost everything from. One, of course, is Wong Kar-wai, who gave me access to everyone, all these famous faces. I learned how to crop a photograph by watching him on the monitor. But another one of my real teachers is William Chang Suk-ping – the famous production designer and art director. Even now, we work together regularly. Just the other day, I was on a shoot, with William beside me. I learned what makes a picture by watching what Wong Kar-wai and William chose to keep and what they threw away. I don’t think of my work as mine alone. It is a long conversation with two people I deeply respect.

IN 2010, FOX came to Hong Kong to make a Chinese film – my feature-film directorial debut, Hot Summer Days. Stars such as Jacky Cheung, Maggie Cheung Man-yuk, Nicholas Tse Ting-fung and Daniel Wu Yin-cho all appeared in it, for very little money, as a favour to me because we had 20 years of trust.

DIRECTING FELT LIKE another universe. You have to think about logistics, 80-people crews, egos, dangerous rigs, scenes and even the crew lunches! I’ve made more films since. I still shoot fashion campaigns, recently for Chanel and Bottega Veneta, and – fingers crossed – I am now writing a television drama.

MY FIRST BOOKS came about because cultural curator Shelly Verthime told me at a dinner many years ago that she wanted to make a book. One day, in 2015, she called from Hong Kong International Airport, so I put a hard drive with every photo I owned into a taxi and sent it to her, at the terminal. She spent a year and a half editing alone. An investor funded the printing and an exhibition in Shanghai, in 2017. My shows in Japan (in Tokyo and Kyoto), the books (Chaos [2020], Solace [2024], Is [2026] and more) – they happened all because someone pushed. I never start these things myself.

MY WORK HAS been in the Mori Art Museum, in Tokyo, and in the V&A, in London. I don’t think about it much. I’ve done it already, and the future is more exciting to me than the past. What I still love is being on set – the mess, the crew eating together, the gossip, the waiting. I think the universe already has a script written. My job is only to follow my heart and see what page it turns to next.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] Up in smoke: why Southeast Asia failed to halt the haze
item.description:
Dr Asma Zafirah doesn’t need satellite images to know when Kalimantan is burning. She sees it in the watery eyes and laboured breaths of the patients at her clinic in Sarawak, and the children who are kept home from school to protect them from the toxic air.

Southeast Asia’s transboundary haze crisis was meant to have been brought under control six years ago.

But Borneo is once again belching out dangerous emissions, as fires in the peatlands and forests of Kalimantan – Indonesia’s section of the island – send a wall of pollutants across Malaysia’s Sarawak and on to the wider region.
item.content:encoded:
Dr Asma Zafirah doesn’t need satellite images to know when Kalimantan is burning. She sees it in the watery eyes and laboured breaths of the patients at her clinic in Sarawak, and the children who are kept home from school to protect them from the toxic air.

Southeast Asia’s transboundary haze crisis was meant to have been brought under control six years ago.

But Borneo is once again belching out dangerous emissions, as fires in the peatlands and forests of Kalimantan – Indonesia’s section of the island – send a wall of pollutants across Malaysia’s Sarawak and on to the wider region.

Repeated, prolonged exposure to haze wreaks havoc in the human body, triggering inflammation, asthma attacks and other respiratory problems.

“That is already a signal that their body is not simply being irritated,” Asma said. “It is having a clinically significant response to the exposure.”

Left unchecked, that exposure can scar lungs, cause cardiovascular illness and lead to cancer, as PM2.5 particles small enough to cross into the bloodstream spread the damage far and wide.

In Sarawak, the Air Pollutant Index (API) Malaysia uses climbed as high as 519 this week, surpassing a level so hazardous it triggered a state of emergency in the Bornean state’s Serian district that was lifted only once the air was clear enough to breathe.

Singapore, which had gone three years without air quality breaching unhealthy levels, restarted daily haze alerts and in the Philippine capital, more than 2,000km (1,240 miles) from the wildfires, schools were forced to shut their doors.

Climate experts warn of a meteorological double-whammy conspiring to make this the hottest year on record for Southeast Asia. “Super El Nino” – a massive warming of the Pacific Ocean that chokes off regional rainfall – is being stacked on top of a developing positive Indian Ocean Dipole, which cools regional waters, further cutting off moisture.

Together, they act as a force multiplier, fuelling droughts, heatwaves and wildfires from Indonesian Borneo and Sumatra to the Mekong nations of Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar.

Extreme weather is only part of the story, however. The fuel for the fires is the land cleared, year after year, for palm oil, pulpwood, corn and sugar cane, on plantations that drain water from the region’s peatlands until they become as dry as tinder.

It’s agribusiness vs the atmosphere, observers say – and for now, agribusiness is winning, despite decades of Asean pledges, a real-time satellite-powered fire-detection system and US$1.5 billion in funding to tackle the crisis that has yet to be raised.

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, facing an electorate once again struggling to breathe, called on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to take action. “Asean ministers must seriously look at it”, he told reporters, “because it is affecting lives, particularly of children and babies”.

The crisis is also decimating some of the world’s greatest stores of biodiversity. Pitiful photographs from Kalimantan of rescued pangolins curled into defensive balls and orangutans with their fur singed orange-black have refocused the world’s attention on the issue.

But climate advisers warn against a convenient narrative taking hold: that this is simply the fault of this year’s “super El Nino”, rather than the businesses making billions from the burning.

“El Nino and dry conditions are risk multipliers, not the root cause,” said Renard Siew, a climate change specialist at the Centre for Governance and Political Studies in Kuala Lumpur.

“We cannot govern El Nino away,” he added. “But we can manage land better, prevent fires, enforce regulations and reduce the underlying vulnerability. Climate change is effectively making the consequences of weak governance more severe.”

History repeats

By far Southeast Asia’s worst haze offender is its most populous nation and largest economy.

Indonesia’s peatland fires began alarmingly early this year, with hotspots detected way back in January – months before the typical dry season burn.

More than 202,000 hectares (780 square miles) have burned so far and police have named 138 arson suspects, including eight companies implicated in forest and land clearance.

But arrests are of little comfort to the families forced to live under a cloud of toxic haze.

Lina Rose, a mother of four in Sarawak, has had to keep her children indoors for most of the recent school holidays.

“I’m worried about my child who has asthma,’’ she said. “The sky looks so gloomy that you think it’s going to rain, but then it doesn’t.”

Residents hark back to 2015, when Indonesia’s worst haze crisis in decades – fuelled by the same slash-and-burn clearance for palm oil and pulpwood – released thousands upon thousands of tonnes of carbon into the atmosphere and blanketed tens of millions of people, from Sumatra to Singapore, in choking smog for months on end.

Jakarta, faced with international fury, labelled that year’s crisis a “crime against humanity of extraordinary proportions” and belatedly signed on to an Asean road map promising haze-fire skies by 2020.

But that deadline came and went – and still the haze continued. A second road map followed in 2023, with a new target year of 2030. Yet few believe this new framework will be any more effective than the first.

The reason comes down to Asean’s modus operandi: consensus and non-interference are not conducive to policing environmental crime across borders, analysts say.

Meanwhile, the palm oil, pulp and paper conglomerates whose business models depend on cheap land clearance have every incentive to keep enforcement weak.

“The fundamental shift has to be from ‘managing haze’ to preventing the conditions that create it,” Siew said. “That means stronger land-use governance, better fire prevention and peatland management, clearer accountability across supply chains and much greater investment in local capacity.”

To its credit, the newer haze-control road map does “contain something its predecessor lacked”, according to Dominique Nicky Fahrizal, a legal expert and researcher at Indonesia’s Centre for Strategic and International Studies – namely, measurable indicators, “including zero days at the highest alert level for two consecutive years”, as well as pledges to reduce burned area by 10 per cent and hotspots by 5 per cent, with a midterm review due in 2028.

But the mechanisms for holding anyone accountable remain weak.

“The consensus principle and the related ‘Asean Way’ approach have led to the creation of mechanisms that are ambitious but have been described as toothless,” said Helena Varkkey, an associate professor of political ecology at the University of Malaya. “This is because the mechanisms often lack strong operationalisation or punitive measures.”

Sanctions would not work, Fahrizal said, as Asean members would never agree to impose them on one another, adding that the latest road map “is not a binding instrument” with reporting done by member states themselves.

Asean’s consensus-based approach has allowed Jakarta to commit to haze-free targets with no penalty attached to missing them. After 2015, it did impose a moratorium on peatland clearance and created an agency to restore affected areas, eventually rehabilitating some 1.6 million hectares (6,177 square miles).

But Indonesia also produces more than half the world’s palm oil and its industry has found ways to adapt, securing permits for “sustainable” farming on the one hand while surreptitiously clearing protected areas on the other. The peatland restoration agency, for all the good it did, was dissolved last year.

Fahriza said the most “realistic” option for enforcing anti-haze measures was to employ independent, third-party verification of data that could be reviewed collectively to impose “consequences for reputation and access to financing”.

Absent that, Asean’s credibility – and relevance – would “ultimately be judged by the citizens breathing the smoke, not by the number of documents signed”, he said.

Patchwork fixes

Advocacy groups are done waiting for another of the bloc’s road maps to fail.

On Monday, Asean Parliamentarians for Human Rights called for the region’s latest haze crisis to be treated as a “human rights emergency”, urging Asean member states to use an October summit in Vietnam to close enforcement gaps and hold corporate offenders to account by forcing companies to publish fire and land-use information for independent scrutiny.

Some smaller-scale bilateral cooperation has also emerged. Thailand and Laos signed a data- and resource-sharing agreement on Wednesday aimed at pre-empting wildfires before they spread, echoing a similar arrangement Bangkok struck with Myanmar last month.

External pressure is building too, with mixed results. The European Union’s threatened ban on palm oil linked to deforestation has been delayed to 2027, after Indonesian objections and Brussel’s own need to lock in a new trade deal amid rising US tariffs.

Then there are the built-in weaknesses in Asean’s own crisis-response tools: under the bloc’s latest haze agreement, accepting emergency firefighting help from abroad remains entirely voluntary.

“At the moment, the arrangement exists, but ultimately it cannot function without the explicit invitation of the host country,” Varkkey said.

“This should be a scientific decision, when the haze is bad enough to warrant external help, not a political one.”

Singapore perhaps best captures the tension between profit and public safety: its companies are heavy investors in Kalimantan’s palm oil sector, yet its people – the region’s wealthiest – no longer tolerate haze imported from beyond their borders.

The city state’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act 2014 lets it prosecute companies for haze pollution regardless of where the fire was lit, a legal reach that was tested after the 2015 pollution crisis when six companies, including Indonesia’s Asia Pulp & Paper Group, were investigated – a move Jakarta called an affront to its sovereignty.

As of 2021, four of the cases remained open, Singapore’s environment minister told parliament. There has been no public confirmation of their closure in the years since.

Meanwhile, Singapore still wheezes whenever Borneo burns.

Wildlife photographer Eddie Vanderloot, 47, has learned to recognise a tight chest and itchy eyes as unmistakable signs that the air has turned.

“Constantly planning activities around the air quality gets tiring and it’s hard not to feel worn down by it,” he said.

“Even with all the windows closed, a mask on, an air purifier and air conditioners switched on, the haze still affects me for hours.”

item.title: [SCMP] Talk is growing of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Will geopolitics throw a spanner in the works?
item.description:
One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world.

The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour.

In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year.
item.content:encoded:
One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world.

The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour.

In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year.

But because of its location, this highly efficient manufacturing powerhouse could present a vulnerability in Washington for Tesla CEO Elon Musk, whose sprawling empire spans EVs, autonomous driving, rockets, satellite internet, humanoid robots, artificial intelligence and brain-computer interfaces.

While his EV business relies heavily on China’s supply chain to fulfil global demand, Musk’s commercial aerospace company SpaceX has become a core national security contractor for the Pentagon.

That poses a dilemma for the CEO, as he looks to navigate the geopolitical waters between the world’s two biggest economies.

Musk must perform a balancing act between the competing interests, which would require a complicated, ring-fenced strategy for his China operations to satisfy regulators in both Washington and Beijing, according to industry observers.

“Musk is not yet choosing between the United States and China. He is trying to establish a balance between several tracks of [his] offerings,” said Marina Yue Zhang, associate professor at the Australia-China Relations Institute at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS).

“But the danger to maintain this balance lies in an uncertain geopolitical landscape.”

The challenge could intensify if Musk were to bring his businesses closer together.

Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another

Seth Goldstein, Morningstar

Currently, Wall Street is abuzz about a possible merger between SpaceX, whose close ties to the US government and Pentagon heighten national-security sensitivities, and Tesla, due to an ever deeper technology overlap between the two firms, from AI to robotics.

While Musk has not commented on a merger, the usually outspoken tech mogul has also not publicly denied the speculation.

“Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another,” said Seth Goldstein, senior equity analyst at Morningstar.

Tesla supplies solar panels, batteries and potentially cargo casings for SpaceX’s Starship launch vehicle, while SpaceX provides its Grok AI model and Starlink satellite internet for Tesla’s cars and potentially its humanoid robot Optimus, according to Goldstein.

The merger would make “operational sense” as it would allow Musk to transfer engineering talent between Tesla and SpaceX projects more smoothly without triggering corporate compliance concerns, Goldstein said.

Tesla’s China footprint could complicate such a move, with a merger raising concerns on both sides of the Pacific: Washington’s wariness towards a core partner maintaining a major manufacturing base in China, as well as Beijing’s misgivings about allowing a US defence contractor to operate within its borders.

The concerns sparked speculation that Musk may be forced to decouple from China. A Wall Street Journal report in late July, citing unidentified sources, said Tesla had been instructed to separate its China business to pave the way for a potential merger with SpaceX. However, Musk was quick to dismiss it as “absurdly fake news”.

“This has never even come up in a discussion ever,” Musk said on his social media platform X, formerly Twitter.

Tesla and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the subject.

Can Tesla do without China?

At stake is Tesla’s sprawling Shanghai manufacturing ecosystem, which accounted for over half of the company’s total global EV deliveries in 2025.

Lingang does not just host the Gigafactory, China’s first wholly foreign-owned car plant. It also has the still-expanding Megafactory, Tesla’s energy-storage manufacturing plant, as well as a dense network of Chinese suppliers capable of meeting the company’s standards on cost, quality and scale.

Nearby are plants operated by – among others – automotive supplier Joyson Electronics, which provides Tesla with steering wheels and airbags; battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) and Faway Dongyang, a producer of car bumpers.

Inside Tesla’s own factory, crates bearing the names of Chinese suppliers such as Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls, Suzhou Current Power Technology, Lingyun Industrial and Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing can be seen along the production line.

Many are based within the manufacturing belt that stretches across the country’s east coast, through Shanghai and the provinces of Jiangsu and Zhejiang.

Tesla says more than 95 per cent of the parts used at its Shanghai factory are locally sourced. It works with more than 400 Chinese suppliers, more than 60 of which have gone on to enter Tesla’s global supply chain.

China is critical to Tesla in three interconnected ways: scale, cost efficiency and speed of innovation, said Zhang of UTS.

“Shanghai is not simply an inexpensive assembly base. It sits inside an unusually dense network of battery, electronics, casting, motor, tooling and automation suppliers,” she said.

“That proximity allows Tesla to alter designs, resolve manufacturing problems and scale production much faster than it could through a dispersed supply chain.”

Divesting China “would impair Tesla’s production volume, cost structure and manufacturing-learning loop”, Zhang added.

Musk himself was once a frequent visitor to Shanghai. Over a roughly 18-month span between 2018 and 2020, he met Li Qiang – then Shanghai’s Communist Party chief, and now China’s premier – four times, according to a city government account.

Musk returned to Shanghai in 2023. His later public visits to China in 2024 and 2026 were centred largely on Beijing. Most recently, he joined US President Donald Trump’s entourage for a state visit to China’s capital in May.

Over those years, Musk’s role changed within China and globally. With the establishment of the Shanghai facility, he became one of the country’s most important foreign manufacturing investors.

And in the years since his purchase of Twitter, he has accrued immense influence over public discourse and geopolitics, especially in the world’s two largest economies.

The more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised

Marina Yue Zhang, University of Technology Sydney

Between Washington and Beijing

Musk’s geopolitical calculus now must include the stringent obligations for SpaceX that come with being a US military contractor.

Among the multibillion-dollar agreements the company has made are a US$4.16 billion deal for satellites designed to track airborne missiles, and a US$2.29 billion contract to build a space-based network for satellite communications, both signed with the Space Force of the US Department of Defence in May.

Contracts from the US government accounted for around 20 per cent of SpaceX’s total revenues in 2025, the company said in its prospectus.

The relationship between SpaceX and the US government is perceived as symbiotic, with each side reliant on the other. Musk said his company had become a “vital element” of the country’s national defence in June.

But Zhang said Washington would expect significant compartmentalisation in Musk’s China business. “[The US] may tolerate civilian Tesla manufacturing in China under the same ultimate holding company, but only if that activity is demonstrably isolated from classified programmes, military-relevant AI, controlled technical data and sensitive defence supply chains”.

Questions will also be raised from the Beijing side, although China values Tesla as a flagship foreign investment, she said, adding that China could require a ring-fenced Chinese subsidiary or restrictions on data, algorithm and technical access to maintain leverage over the EV maker’s local operations.

How Musk plans to navigate between Washington and Beijing will be “the real bottleneck” in a potential merger, according to Zhang.

“The commercial case is relatively easy to articulate. The harder question is whether those synergies can be realised without creating unacceptable channels between an American defence contractor and Tesla’s Chinese operations.”

She said the CEO would need to “construct an exceptionally clear institutional firewall”, but added this could create a paradox: “the more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised.”

Tesla lays the first bricks

Tesla could be taking early steps to build such a firewall within its production network. A former engineer who worked on battery development for the company said the firm had, years ago, launched an internal effort aimed at building a supply chain that was less dependent on China.

It was, in practice, “almost an impossible task,” the engineer said, speaking on condition of anonymity, because Chinese companies were present at almost every layer of the industry.

Tesla did ask some suppliers to build production capacity outside China in this effort, the former engineer said.

CATL was among the companies that were approached, but the battery maker shelved its direct investment plan in the US in 2022 as geopolitical tension mounted. Japan’s Panasonic and South Korea’s LG Energy Solution, however, have deepened their ties with Tesla in the US market.

Still, the former engineer cautioned against reading every effort to diversify production through a geopolitical lens. Hardware companies routinely build parallel supply chains, the engineer said, often for more pragmatic reasons: cost, efficiency and resilience.

“A patchwork of regulations and economic incentives has increasingly pushed companies such as Tesla to build a more ‘China-free’ supply chain, or scrutinise suppliers much more closely, sometimes several tiers down,” said Leah Yu, a partner at Jincheng Tongda & Neal Law Firm.

Sources of pressure included import restrictions linked to forced labour, national security rules covering connected vehicles, tariffs and tax incentives favouring US-made batteries and components, Yu said.

SpaceX faced a harder technology firewall, she added, as export controls were layered on top of supplier-security requirements associated with its aerospace and national security work. These controls could restrict not only sourcing, but also which suppliers and personnel were allowed access to the necessary technology.

Goldstein of Morningstar said that ring-fencing Tesla’s Chinese EV and battery operations could address the demands of both governments.

However, to allow a merger to proceed, regulatory authorities in both the US and China might still demand that Tesla sells off its Chinese operations or move to a non-controlling stake.

While a China divestment could hurt Tesla’s cost efficiency, the EV maker traditionally competes on its autonomous driving technology as a differentiator rather than price, Goldstein said.

Gearing up for the ‘biggest product ever’

However, even compared with EVs, China could prove more indispensable for the production of Optimus, which Musk has called “the biggest product ever”.

“So far, the largest reliance on China is likely the rare earth metals used to produce magnets for motors that are required for every joint in a humanoid robot,” Goldstein said. “Tesla will likely try to source rare earth metals from suppliers outside China, but this may be difficult as China controls the vast majority of supply today.”

Musk addressed the rare earth issue in April, admitting that Beijing’s restrictions on exports of the critical minerals affected the production of Optimus. “We’re working through that with China,” Musk told investors in an earnings call.

A continued grip on rare earth elements – and the crucial magnets made with them – could hurt Musk’s ambitions for the humanoid robot, which he projected to be a US$10 trillion sales generator.

Beyond rare earth magnets, Optimus remains heavily reliant on China’s supply chain, even with its primary manufacturing rooted in the US.
