“There has been a lot of hype generated,” Tan Tee Khoon, Knight Frank Singapore’s head of auction and sales, said after the first seven properties failed to find buyers. “Some of them literally tell me, ‘I just want to come and see.’”

item.title: [SCMP] Anti-South Asian online hate surges in US under Trump 2.0, study finds
item.description:
Anti-South Asian hate in the United States has spiked since Donald Trump returned to the Oval Office for a second term, with racist, dehumanising and xenophobic slurs and narratives proliferating across both mainstream and fringe social media platforms, a US-based report has revealed.

The report, titled “The Rising Tide of Anti-South Asian Hate in the United States”, by the Washington-based Centre for the Study of Organised Hate (CSOH), found that the monthly volume of hate towards South Asians in the United States on the social media platform X rose 240 per cent between January 2024 and June 2026, from 12,904 posts to 43,843.

The hate speech is largely aimed at Indians, Bangladeshis and Pakistanis, according to the report, which traces the surge to Trump’s immigration crackdown, economic anxiety and the South Asian community’s growing visibility in American life.
item.content:encoded:
Anti-South Asian hate in the United States has spiked since Donald Trump returned to the Oval Office for a second term, with racist, dehumanising and xenophobic slurs and narratives proliferating across both mainstream and fringe social media platforms, a US-based report has revealed.

The report, titled “The Rising Tide of Anti-South Asian Hate in the United States”, by the Washington-based Centre for the Study of Organised Hate (CSOH), found that the monthly volume of hate towards South Asians in the United States on the social media platform X rose 240 per cent between January 2024 and June 2026, from 12,904 posts to 43,843.

The hate speech is largely aimed at Indians, Bangladeshis and Pakistanis, according to the report, which traces the surge to Trump’s immigration crackdown, economic anxiety and the South Asian community’s growing visibility in American life.

Similarly, South Asian political figures from both major US political parties have faced racist and xenophobic attacks, the report found, including Kamala Harris, former vice-president and Democratic presidential nominee; Usha Vance, current second lady of the US; Kash Patel, director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation; Zohran Mamdani, the first Muslim mayor of New York City; and Democratic representative Raja Krishnamoorthi.

CSOH executive director Raqib Naik said the research, which focused on online sentiment towards South Asian Americans since December 2024, showed a clear and significant rise in targeting of the demographic, particularly Indians, since Trump’s second term.

“The administration is part of the problem. Our report has outlined how incendiary rhetoric from top offices in the country is contributing to anti-South Asian hate, especially the federal government helping to fuel harmful and hateful narratives,” Naik said.

He added that though some states were putting in place measures to mitigate the hate, most members of the South Asian community felt vulnerable as online hate manifested in real life.

The report warned that the enormous scale of online hate showed the wide reach of social media platforms and algorithms that amplified hateful content.

“It also reflects the growing alignment of powerful technology executives and owners like Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg with the Maga movement and the rollback of hate speech policies, fact-checking programmes, and other trust and safety measures by platforms,” it said, adding that the transformation of X – formerly Twitter – after its acquisition by Musk led to the “normalisation of a violent and racist discourse” that was previously largely restricted to fringe online spaces.

Naik urged the US government to take the lead, especially in controlling social media platforms, which he said had been weaponised to fuel hate.

Citing the CSOH study, Indian-American congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi accused the Trump administration and the Maga movement of contributing to the rise in hate speech and what he described as systemic racism.

“The 240 per cent surge in monthly anti-South Asian hate on X did not come out of nowhere. We have watched politicians demonise South Asians over something as ordinary as attending a college-football game and the Trump administration traffic in racist stereotypes targeting people named Singh,” said Krishnamoorthi on X in reference to tirades by Texas Republicans against brown people and a racist poster used by the administration.

“Americans of every background, and leaders of both parties, need to speak out against racism and xenophobia wherever they appear. South Asian Americans are as much a part of the fabric of America as anyone else, and no amount of hate can erase the contributions we have made to this country,” Krishnamoorthi said.

According to the report, more than half a million anti-South Asian posts appeared on X between January 2025 and June this year. The volume rose 75 per cent over this period and 240 per cent from January 2024 to June this year. Five of the six highest-volume months occurred between November 2025 and June 2026, showing that anti-South Asian hate continues to intensify.

The report identified 397,522 hateful and dehumanising mentions targeting South Asians across the 4chan, 8chan, and Gab bulletin boards in 2025, with monthly volume remaining at a persistently high baseline for much of the year.

Last month, Indian travel YouTuber Paramvir Singh Beniwal said he was subjected to racist remarks during a recent visit to Las Vegas.

Beniwal, known online as Passenger Paramvir, shared a 57-minute YouTube vlog in which three men approached him and his friend, with one claiming to own 73 7-Eleven stores across the US before offering Beniwal a job as a cashier.

Beniwal said he believed the offer was intended as a racist joke rather than a genuine job offer. He said the exchange was a reference to a stereotype that Indians often worked as cashiers at 7-Eleven stores.

The video has garnered 6.8 million views in eight days, with viewers praising Beniwal for confronting the men over the remarks.

According to the report, six key factors collectively drove the surge in anti-South Asian hate, including posts portraying South Asians as “invaders, job thieves, and a demographic threat” on X.

The report identifies the H-1B visa programme, the American Tech Workforce Act of 2025, and the Visa Cap Enforcement Act as major triggers for anti-South Asian hate, especially against Indians, who in 2024 constituted 71 per cent of H-1B visa workers.

An H-1B visa is a temporary US work permit that allows companies to hire foreign professionals in specialised fields. Indians are the largest beneficiaries of the H-1B programme, accounting for 71 per cent of approved H-1B petitions in the 2024 financial year, according to data from the US Citizenship and Immigration Services.

The Trump administration has curbed new H-1B visas by raising the fee for workers in this category by US$100,000. Of those subject to the higher H-1B fee, 82 per cent were Indian nationals, according to an analysis from the Penn Wharton Budget Model at the University of Pennsylvania.

About 30 per cent of all posts on X and 45 per cent of mentions on fringe platforms with references to South Asians contained the word pajeet and its variants, according to the CSOH report. Pajeet is a slur mocking the sanitation habits of South Asians.

item.title: [SCMP] Days after Xi-Trump summit, the US marks China’s National Day with pared-down note
item.description:
Five days after Chinese President Xi Jinping left Washington, the US State Department marked the 77th anniversary of the People’s Republic of China with a greeting short enough to fit on a calling card.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s congratulatory statement landed on Wednesday, a few hours before dawn on National Day in Beijing. It made no mention of Xi’s visit, the trade understandings reached during the trip or the meetings the two leaders have scheduled for later this year.

Washington continued its tradition of marking China’s National Day before October 1 arrived in the United States. But it pared down the message.
item.content:encoded:
Five days after Chinese President Xi Jinping left Washington, the US State Department marked the 77th anniversary of the People’s Republic of China with a greeting short enough to fit on a calling card.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s congratulatory statement landed on Wednesday, a few hours before dawn on National Day in Beijing. It made no mention of Xi’s visit, the trade understandings reached during the trip or the meetings the two leaders have scheduled for later this year.

Washington continued its tradition of marking China’s National Day before October 1 arrived in the United States. But it pared down the message.

“On behalf of the United States of America, I congratulate the people of China on the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China on October 1,” it said.

“The United States wishes the people of China goodwill, along with peace, health and happiness in the coming year.”

Unlike Rubio’s greeting last year, this year’s version dropped the word “prosperity”. The previous statement wished the Chinese people “health, happiness, prosperity and peace in the year ahead”.

That wording change sits against the backdrop of a week of high-level contact. Xi just completed a state visit to Washington, while US and Chinese officials announced outcomes on trade and other topics. Hours before Xi’s arrival in the US, Rubio himself described the US-China relationship as one that would “define the 21st century”.

Atul Kumar, a fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi, said Rubio’s note introduced “goodwill” while dropping “prosperity” and made no reference to the summit between Xi and US President Donald Trump or their planned meetings later this year.

“As Xi seeks strategic persuasion and a constructive, stable relationship with Trump and the US administration, the inclusion of goodwill seems noteworthy,” he said. “However, the omission of ‘prosperity’ underscores deeper bilateral economic rivalry.”

He added that the framing kept the State Department’s “formal, ceremonial language of diplomatic courtesy without explicitly endorsing or institutionalising Trump’s leader-level summit diplomacy”.

Speaking at the Chinese embassy’s National Day reception in Washington on Wednesday, Chinese ambassador Xie Feng called the Xi-Trump rapport the “most valuable strategic asset” in the bilateral relationship, adding that head-of-state diplomacy anchored ties. The personal connection between the two leaders had “helped keep China-US relations on course at critical moments”, he added.

Manoj Kewalramani, chair of the Geostrategy Programme at the Takshashila Institution in Bengaluru, said the latest statement still pointed to engagement.

“The signal essentially remains that the US is looking to build some sort of a working relationship with China rather than simply manage difficult issues or compete intensely,” he said.

From cooperation to competition

The National Day greeting has been more than a holiday courtesy. Its wording has offered a small annual snapshot of how Washington describes its relationship with Beijing, with the length and tone broadly tracking the state of ties.

During Barack Obama’s presidency, the messages contained references to cooperation.

In a September 29, 2011 statement, then US secretary of state Hillary Clinton said the two countries were “developing the positive, cooperative and comprehensive relationship envisioned by our presidents”. She cited the state visit by then Chinese leader Hu Jintao in January of that year as well as the Strategic and Economic Dialogue that May.

“A thriving China is good for America and a thriving America is good for China,” she added.

John Kerry, who succeeded Clinton as secretary of state, took a similar tone. In 2013, the year of the Sunnylands summit between Xi and Obama, Kerry said the relationship had “grown by historic measures since President Nixon’s visit to China 41 years ago”. He added that “a prosperous China is good for the United States, and a prosperous United States is good for China”.

In 2014, marking the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations, Kerry called cooperation on climate change, Ebola fever and nuclear proliferation “indispensable”.

And in 2015, just a week after Xi’s previous state visit to Washington, Kerry wrote that the two sides had “shown how much we can accomplish through cooperation”. He closed with a wish for “peace and prosperity over the coming year”.

The messages became shorter as tensions deepened during Donald Trump’s first term as US president.

On September 30, 2017, the US State Department issued a statement while then secretary of state Rex Tillerson was in Beijing, ahead of Trump’s November state visit. It said that “a strong, constructive relationship between the United States and China is important for the prosperity and stability of our two countries as well as the world”.

Tillerson also wished the Chinese people “peace and prosperity”.

By 2019, in the middle of the US-China tariff war, references to the bilateral relationship largely disappeared from the holiday greeting. Former secretary of state Mike Pompeo’s message wished the Chinese people “happiness, health, peace and prosperity in the year to come”.

His 2020 message came a few months after Washington closed China’s consulate in Houston and Beijing closed the US consulate in Chengdu. It wished the Chinese people “health, prosperity, happiness and peace in the coming year”.

Blinken returns to ties

Antony Blinken, secretary of state under former US president Joe Biden, brought the relationship back into focus.

After a frosty meeting with top Chinese diplomats in Alaska in 2021, Blinken said Washington sought to “work cooperatively to solve the challenges we all face” and wished the Chinese people “peace, happiness and prosperity”.

A year later, just weeks after then US House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan, he pointed to areas where the two sides could work together, including “health, climate change, counternarcotics and other areas where our interests intersect”.

That language continued in 2023, following controversy over an alleged Chinese surveillance balloon and a summer of high-level US visits to Beijing. Blinken highlighted cooperation on “the climate crisis, public health, counternarcotics, food security and global macroeconomic stability”.

Then, in 2024, the message arrived after October 1. It said the US was “committed to responsibly managing our bilateral relationship with the [People’s Republic of China] and will maintain open lines of communication”.

item.title: [SCMP] Why US Himars missile shortfalls raise stakes for a potential Taiwan Strait conflict
item.description:
A potential conflict in the Taiwan Strait could see crossfire exchanged between two mobile rocket systems: the US-made High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (Himars), and its mainland Chinese counterpart, the PHL-16, also known as the PCL-191.

Taiwan is set to receive all 29 Himars systems from its initial orders by the end of this year, with another 82 systems approved for purchase in a follow-on deal, bringing the planned total to 111. This does not include the US military’s Himars systems already deployed in the region.

Meanwhile, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) is estimated to have deployed more than 200 PHL-16 systems.
item.content:encoded:
A potential conflict in the Taiwan Strait could see crossfire exchanged between two mobile rocket systems: the US-made High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (Himars), and its mainland Chinese counterpart, the PHL-16, also known as the PCL-191.

Taiwan is set to receive all 29 Himars systems from its initial orders by the end of this year, with another 82 systems approved for purchase in a follow-on deal, bringing the planned total to 111. This does not include the US military’s Himars systems already deployed in the region.

Meanwhile, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) is estimated to have deployed more than 200 PHL-16 systems.

The real question, however, is ammunition.

Two long-range missiles fired from the Himars platform – the Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS) and the Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) – are among the US munitions most heavily depleted during the war with Iran.

The US Army has used “virtually all” of its global stockpile of these two missile types, according to a Reuters report in August, citing people familiar with the data.

The draining of US stocks raises questions about Taiwan’s plans to expand its ATACMS inventory.

The island’s military has received 64 of the systems and is expecting 20 more this year as part of its initial order. Washington approved the sale of an additional 420 in December last year, which would bring the total number ordered to 504.

At the same time, Lockheed Martin, which makes the ATACMS, is in the process of phasing out its production. How fast the stocks can be replenished and delivered to Taiwan remains highly uncertain.

Meanwhile, although exact ammunition stockpiles remain classified, the PLA has recently released footage of live-fire training exercises involving the PHL-16 system, showcasing two distinct munition types.

These were an airburst “steel rain” guided rocket designed to disperse large quantities of high-velocity fragments over a wide area and a 750mm tactical ballistic missile with a 500km (311-mile) strike range, making the modular PHL-16 the world’s longest-range rocket artillery platform.

More broadly, mainland China’s defence industry appears to be operating at an elevated tempo.

The Pentagon estimates that, as of 2024, China had at least 3,150 ballistic missiles and 300 ground-launched cruise missiles. From 2015, those represented 147 per cent and 50 per cent increases respectively.

A Bloomberg analysis in May identified 81 companies in China’s missile supply chain – more than double the 32 firms identified in 2013, when President Xi Jinping first took office. Moreover, it found that nearly 40 per cent of these companies reported record sales in 2025, also the highest proportion since 2013.

“The build-up indicates that China is flush with missiles just as US stockpiles have been depleted,” it said.

The United States’ growing munitions shortfalls were explicitly acknowledged by the Pentagon’s inspector general in a recent report on the war in Iran.

Of the estimated US$33.4 billion spent on Operation Epic Fury between February 28 and June 30, some US$22.3 billion – 67 per cent of the total – went towards munitions, according to the inspector general’s first-of-its-kind report to the US Congress released on Monday.

“The munitions expenditure on [Operation Epic Fury] has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” the report said, referring to the joint US-Israeli military campaign targeting Iran.

This marked a rare official acknowledgement by the US Defence Department regarding its depleted munitions supplies and pressure on the industrial base.

Until recently, US President Donald Trump and top Pentagon officials had repeatedly denied reports concerning US munitions shortages.

In recent months, media outlets and think tanks have repeatedly warned of the rapid depletion of America’s critical munitions during the conflict with Iran, such as long-range precision-strike missiles and air-defence interceptors, noting that this exposed a vulnerability in the event of a western Pacific confrontation with Beijing.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Besides the “virtually all” used up ATACMS and PrSM, nearly 80 per cent of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defence (THAAD) missile inventory and about half of the Patriot interceptors had also been depleted compared to pre-war stockpile levels by August, CNN reported.

The Washington Post detailed some consumption figures for key munitions during the first month of the conflict, which included more than 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles, over 1,000 Patriot and THAAD interceptors, and more than 1,300 army tactical ballistic missiles.

Although Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has been urging the US defence industry to increase weapons manufacturing, it may take over three years for the inventories of Tomahawk, THAAD and Patriot systems to be restored to their pre-conflict levels, according to estimates by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

Beyond these advanced munitions, the US has faced difficulties expanding production of lower-technology conventional ammunition because of a diminished industrial base, despite efforts to rebuild capacity in response to rising demand since the Ukraine war.

An example is a newly built artillery-shell plant in Mesquite, Texas. As part of the US Army’s effort to increase 155mm production, the US$469 million facility was intended to produce 30,000 projectiles a month by October last year, but as of March, nearly two years after coming online, it had yet to produce a single one.

According to Chinese military researcher Liu Yi, the origins of the problem can be traced back to a 1993 dinner hosted by then-US defence secretary Les Aspin, when the Bill Clinton administration outlined plans for post-Cold War defence budget cuts. This led to a wave of consolidation in the US defence industry in the following years.

Soon after the so-called last supper, the number of major US defence contractors fell from 51 in the 1980s to just five by 2000, Liu said in an article in Chinese military magazine Modern Ships in September.

The continued dominance of the “Big Five” – Lockheed Martin, Raytheon (now RTX), Boeing, General Dynamics and Northrop Grumman – has since left the industry highly concentrated.

Since the early 21st century, demand for these high-performance munitions had remained weak for an extended period, Liu said, as the US military shifted its focus towards counterterrorism operations.

“The profit margin on munitions is relatively low, and the procurement orders were limited for much of the time, with roughly half of them coming from overseas,” he added.

“This has driven the ‘Big Five’ to scale down their ammunition-production capacity,” Liu added, noting that the broader decline in America’s manufacturing base had left smaller contractors either unable or unwilling to fill the gap.

Military commentator Song Zhongping argued that the concentrated structure of the industry was keeping prices artificially high, weakening the US military’s bargaining power and making it difficult to bring down the cost of weapons, which had ultimately contributed to the lack of inventory.

“Excessively high costs per unit limit the quantities the US military can afford to procure, even as the defence budget continues to rise,” said Song, a retired PLA officer.

He also cited the large share of munitions production for overseas buyers, saying that foreign customers generally paid higher prices, giving contractors an incentive to prioritise exports.

Although China’s defence industry was similarly concentrated within a few mega contractors, its state-owned nature ensured strategic alignment with the PLA’s demands rather than pure pursuit of profit as happened within the US military-industrial complex, Song added.

One example highlights the difference.

The US Navy effectively abandoned plans to field the 155mm main guns on its Zumwalt-class destroyers, largely because the custom Long-Range Land Attack Projectiles, developed jointly by BAE Systems and Lockheed Martin, reached an estimated cost of about US$800,000 per round.

Meanwhile, Chinese defence reports have suggested that a 155mm naval gun under development could leverage the PLA’s existing 155mm artillery ammunition and technology base. If so, it could reduce duplicate research and development and supply-chain costs while accelerating development and deployment.

“There is still internal competition among state institutes and private companies are increasingly participating to improve drive efficiency,” Song said of the Chinese defence industry.

“By achieving full domestic sourcing across the supply chain and complete indigenisation of its defence production, China has ensured full control over production capacity, unit costs and delivery timelines.

“This means China’s war potential is immense.”

During the 1993 dinner that reshaped the US defence industry, China “wasn’t even on the cards”, according to attendee Norman Augustine, who at the time was chief executive of defence contractor Martin Marietta and later served as Lockheed Martin’s CEO from 1996 to 1997.

But 30 years later, Augustine warned in a 2023 interview that the US no longer had “as many companies as we need in the defence world … particularly with the evolution of China and aggression from Russia”.

“We may have to restructure the industry,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] Xi-Trump rapport is ‘most valuable strategic asset’ in US-China ties, envoy Xie says
item.description:
The Chinese ambassador to the United States, Xie Feng, has described the personal rapport and “mutual respect” between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump as the “most valuable strategic asset in our bilateral relations”.

“Their personal connection and in-depth dialogue have helped keep China-US relations on course at critical moments,” Xie said during a speech on Wednesday marking National Day celebrations at the Chinese embassy in Washington.

“Head-of-state diplomacy anchors the bilateral relationship.”
item.content:encoded:
The Chinese ambassador to the United States, Xie Feng, has described the personal rapport and “mutual respect” between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump as the “most valuable strategic asset in our bilateral relations”.

“Their personal connection and in-depth dialogue have helped keep China-US relations on course at critical moments,” Xie said during a speech on Wednesday marking National Day celebrations at the Chinese embassy in Washington.

“Head-of-state diplomacy anchors the bilateral relationship.”

The ambassador’s comments come days after Xi’s state visit to the US, during which Trump pulled out all the stops to make the trip a grand affair.

It included an airport welcome, a formal White House reception, a state dinner attended by leading American business executives, a meeting over tea and a visit to the National Archives.

During the meetings, both sides agreed to build a “constructive relationship of strategic stability” based on “respect, fairness and reciprocity”.

Xie also highlighted expected meetings between the two leaders at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) gathering in Shenzhen in November and the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami in December. He said their “support for each other” gave “fresh momentum to Asia-Pacific cooperation and global governance”.

The relationship Xie described dates to April 2017, when Trump first hosted Xi at Mar-a-Lago in Florida, saying they had “developed a friendship”.

That personal channel survived a trade war, the pandemic and a four-year interruption under president Joe Biden, before being revived last October on the sidelines of the Apec meeting in Busan.

Repeated phone calls kept the contact alive until Trump travelled to Beijing in May, the first visit by a sitting US president to China in nearly a decade.

At the White House arrival ceremony last week, Trump said: “From the time of my first election in 2016, President Xi and I have forged a friendship, a truly great friendship, actually, built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people.”

Xi returned the favour, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.” He said he had come to Washington “to carry on our friendship”.

This year’s National Day celebration at the Chinese embassy had more invited speakers and more emphasis on people-to-people connection between the two countries than last year.

In keeping with tradition, the US State Department issued a congratulatory note on its website: “The United States wishes the people of China goodwill, along with peace, health and happiness in the coming year.”

During his speech on Wednesday, the Chinese ambassador highlighted China’s advances in technology, pointing to developments by tech giant Huawei and AI start-up Kimi as evidence of the country’s progress despite US restrictions on access to advanced technology.

“The Tau Scaling Law gives a new approach to improving chip performances,” Xie said.

In May, Huawei unveiled the Tau Scaling Law and chip architecture that it said could deliver 1.4 nanometre-level performance in coming years without relying on advances in chipmaking equipment tools.

As part of a US-led campaign to restrict China’s access to advanced semiconductor technology, Chinese companies are barred from acquiring the most advanced extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, traditionally required to produce powerful chips at the 3nm and lower process nodes.

While last week’s summit produced no breakthrough on easing US chip controls, the two leaders covered a wide range of issues.

In their meeting on September 24, Xi urged Trump to explicitly oppose Taiwan independence, saying he hoped the US side would “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, according to a statement from Beijing’s foreign ministry. The White House did not mention Taiwan in its statement.

On Monday, Trump denied discussing US arms sales with his Chinese counterpart, disputing US ambassador to China David Perdue’s account in a Fox News interview a day earlier that the US president had proposed selling weapons to China.

“I never heard of that one,” Trump said. “I am gonna have to ask him. You mean we’re going to sell? No, they’d probably like to buy it because we do make better equipment than that, so maybe it’s a good idea. But we didn’t discuss.”

Speaking to Fox News after Xi’s visit, Perdue said: “[Trump] actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.”

Perdue did not say when Trump raised the question, what prompted it, or how Xi responded.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States – Taiwan’s main international backer – do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

According to the Chinese embassy, the two militaries also agreed to conclude a memorandum of understanding on “crisis communication and prevention as soon as possible”. The US side made no mention of military cooperation.

The South China Morning Post reported earlier this month that the two sides were expected to announce measures to improve military-to-military communication.

Among the economic deliverables, both sides extended the Busan trade agreement for two more months, until January 10, 2027.

The deal signed in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025 lowered US tariffs on some Chinese goods, suspended additional US restrictions on Chinese-affiliated companies, paused certain Chinese rare earth export controls, and secured new Chinese commitments to buy American soybeans. The arrangement was due to expire on November 10.

At the summit last week, Beijing and Washington also launched the Board of Trade mechanism and on Sunday announced a range of products in non-sensitive sectors, capped at US$30 billion each, for tariff reduction.

The White House released tariff-reduction lists that included 77 categories of Chinese imports into the US and 1,619 US imports into China.

The US import list covered a range of consumer goods, including microwave ovens, electric irons, Christmas ornaments and toys. China’s list was dominated by agricultural products, including beef and vegetables, but also included coal, timber and medical devices such as hearing aids and pacemakers.

On artificial intelligence, the two sides announced an AI dialogue to exchange views on the technology’s “risks and benefits”, with the next meeting scheduled for November. They also agreed to establish a “bilateral communication channel” to discuss AI-related incidents.

item.title: [SCMP] Beijing slams ‘harassment’ after Manila challenges research ship near Batanes
item.description:
China and the Philippines have launched a war of words after their coastguards challenged each other in the waters off the Batanes Islands, an area that has become the latest maritime flashpoint as Beijing ramps up pressure against Manila-Tokyo delimitation efforts.

The Philippine coastguard said on Thursday it had sent one of its biggest vessels and an aircraft to “disrupt and drive away” a Chinese research ship – the Jia Hai Ke 7 – which has been operating in the waters off the islands over the past several days.

“At 7.55am, BRP Teresa Magbanua closed in on Jia Hai Ke 7 to less than 100 yards (91 metres) and launched a rigid-hull inflatable boat to disrupt the research vessel’s illegal marine scientific research and compel it to leave the area,” coastguard spokesman Jay Tarriela said in a post on social media.
item.content:encoded:
China and the Philippines have launched a war of words after their coastguards challenged each other in the waters off the Batanes Islands, an area that has become the latest maritime flashpoint as Beijing ramps up pressure against Manila-Tokyo delimitation efforts.

The Philippine coastguard said on Thursday it had sent one of its biggest vessels and an aircraft to “disrupt and drive away” a Chinese research ship – the Jia Hai Ke 7 – which has been operating in the waters off the islands over the past several days.

“At 7.55am, BRP Teresa Magbanua closed in on Jia Hai Ke 7 to less than 100 yards (91 metres) and launched a rigid-hull inflatable boat to disrupt the research vessel’s illegal marine scientific research and compel it to leave the area,” coastguard spokesman Jay Tarriela said in a post on social media.

The Jia Hai Ke 7 has spent more than a week conducting operations near the Philippines’ Batanes archipelago, located between the country’s Luzon island and Taiwan.

Footage posted by Tarriela showed the Philippine coastguard issuing radio warnings and one of its inflatable boats circling the Chinese vessel.

He added that the coastguard aircraft, the PCG Islander 251, circled the area several times at low altitude to support the operation, vowing to continue to “challenge, disrupt and drive away the survey vessel until it leaves Philippine waters”.

During the operation, a Chinese coastguard vessel “abruptly” arrived in the area to shield the survey ship and moved towards the Philippine ship while repeatedly issuing radio challenges, Tarriela said.

The Philippine ship then “shadowed” the Chinese coastguard vessel from about 1,000 yards away while remaining close to the research ship, he added.

He said the presence of the Chinese coastguard “raises serious questions about who Jia Hai Ke 7 is really working for” and “what data the vessel has collected over the country’s undersea cable corridors”.

In response, Beijing denounced Manila’s “harassment” and insisted its research vessel was conducting “normal operations in waters under Chinese jurisdiction” in accordance with international law.

“China has taken, and will continue to take, resolute measures to safeguard its legitimate rights and interests,” Guo Wei, deputy spokesman of the Chinese embassy in Manila, said in a social media post on Thursday.

Guo also urged the Philippines to cease its “provocative interference with China’s normal scientific research activities”.

Tarriela fired back on social media, telling Guo to stop “meddling” and saying that the Philippine coastguard “will continue to oppose and drive away Chinese research vessels that have no right to study our own seas without permission!”

Data recorded via the vessel’s Automatic Identification System (AIS) for September, tracked by MarineTraffic, revealed that the Jia Hai Ke 7 research ship departed from Xiamen on China’s southeastern coast on September 19, arrived near Itbayat in the province of Batanes on September 22.

The Philippine coastguard confirmed the survey ship’s presence on Monday. Tarriela said the vessel was around 38 nautical miles (70km) northwest of Itbayat and displaying behaviour inconsistent with innocent passage.

“Rather than steaming on a steady course and speed, Jia Hai Ke 7 has been loitering and holding position in the same area – the movement pattern of a vessel conducting marine scientific research, not transit,” Tarriela previously said on social media.

The vessel’s presence has stirred concerns in Manila over critical subsea telecommunications cables traversing the seabed of the Luzon Strait, which connect Southeast Asia to North America and northeast Asia.

Philippine aerial patrols issued three radio challenges demanding that the ship declare its mission and cease unauthorised surveys, but received no response.

The deployment comes amid heightened friction over the Batanes Islands.

Some Chinese researchers argued in June that the islands were a natural geographical extension of Taiwan and therefore fell under Chinese sovereignty. The assertion is not officially endorsed by Beijing.

The ship’s deployment has also raised concerns over China’s use of research vessels to assert claims, map seabed terrain for potential military applications, and gather intelligence on undersea infrastructure in disputed waters.

Beijing’s concerns about the area have risen following Manila and Tokyo’s decision in May to launch formal negotiations on delimiting their overlapping exclusive economic zones and continental shelves.

Beijing said the bilateral initiative was unlawful and void, arguing that the waters formed part of Chinese maritime zones projected from Taiwan.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, Japan and the Philippines, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state.

The state-run Global Times said the Jia Hai Ke 7 was conducting “legitimate and lawful” offshore marine geological surveys and scientific investigations in waters under Chinese jurisdiction.

“By forcibly overstretching the concept of security and militarising civilian research, the Philippines not only interferes with China’s normal navigation and scientific operations, but also deliberately stokes regional tension,” the newspaper said.

According to the China Classification Society, the 70-metre (230-foot) vessel is China’s first privately owned research ship equipped with a Dynamic Positioning Class 2 system, tailored for precision station-keeping and offshore marine geological surveys.

It was built for Zhuhai Jiahai Marine Technology Co and entered service in April last year.

The incident marks the latest in a pattern of Chinese research vessel deployments to sensitive maritime areas that have generated controversy across the region.

These operations typically involve research activities inside the exclusive economic zones and contested waters near Taiwan, the Philippines and Japan.

Since May, mainland Chinese research vessels have appeared in waters east of Taiwan on multiple occasions, raising alarms in Taipei.

Last month, the Philippine Coast Guard accused another Chinese survey vessel, the Haiyang Dizhi 10, of conducting “illegal” operations for 25 days within the Philippine exclusive economic zone, including the territorial sea of Scarborough Shoal. The disputed shoal, known as Huangyan Island in China and Panatag Shoal in the Philippines, has become a frequent maritime flashpoint in South China Sea disputes between Beijing and Manila.

Manila also said the Haiyang Dizhi 10 occasionally switched off its AIS transponder in what it described as an attempt to evade detection.

Meanwhile, the Chinese coastguard patrolled the disputed Scarborough Shoal, Second Thomas Shoal and Sabina Shoal on Thursday, marking the country’s National Day holiday with a display of its claim to the South China Sea regions.

item.title: [SCMP] China-US dialogue will ease concerns, but competition will remain, Paul Chan says
item.description:
Competition between China and the US will persist, but increased dialogue between the two economic superpowers will provide greater global certainty and ease geopolitical concerns, with Hong Kong positioned to play a unique role, the city’s financial secretary has told the South China Morning Post.

In a wide-ranging interview, Paul Chan Mo-po said more communication and dialogue between the two nations would be “good for everyone”, as Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart, Donald Trump, wrapped up a historic summit in Washington last Friday, local time.

Chan also shed light on his expectations for the coming Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting, which takes place in Hong Kong on October 20 and 21, and will bring together hundreds of global leaders in the city. He anticipated that visiting political leaders would see Hong Kong and its vibrancy with their own eyes.
item.content:encoded:
Competition between China and the US will persist, but increased dialogue between the two economic superpowers will provide greater global certainty and ease geopolitical concerns, with Hong Kong positioned to play a unique role, the city’s financial secretary has told the South China Morning Post.

In a wide-ranging interview, Paul Chan Mo-po said more communication and dialogue between the two nations would be “good for everyone”, as Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart, Donald Trump, wrapped up a historic summit in Washington last Friday, local time.

Chan also shed light on his expectations for the coming Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting, which takes place in Hong Kong on October 20 and 21, and will bring together hundreds of global leaders in the city. He anticipated that visiting political leaders would see Hong Kong and its vibrancy with their own eyes.

The event will take place ahead of this year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, which will be held in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19.

Chan said Beijing supported Hong Kong’s hosting of the finance ministers’ meeting, as the central government wanted to elevate the city’s profile as a global financial centre.

With the current Hong Kong administration having less than a year before the new term, Chan was also asked about his future plans.

He said that officials had worked hard under the “capable leadership” of the chief executive.

“At the moment, we are concentrating our energy and efforts on pushing forward the various policy agendas and initiatives. So this will remain our priority focus,” he said.

Chan also touched on the three-day China-US summit last week, which saw tensions ease and a trade truce extended by two months until January.

“We do believe more communication and dialogue are good for everyone,” he said.

“And this is important, not just for the two countries or Hong Kong but for the global community, providing more certainty and removing some of the geopolitical concerns.”

But Chan anticipated China-US competition would persist in areas such as financial services, adding that Hong Kong would strengthen its status as an international financial centre to further attract foreign capital and connect mainland China to the rest of the world.

“So for us, under the ‘one country, two systems’ arrangement, we play the unique role of connecting the mainland with the rest of the world,” he said.

Despite geopolitical tensions, Chan said Hong Kong had become a destination for investors to park their money over the past two years.

Net inflows into Hong Kong-domiciled funds stood at HK$118 billion (US$15 billion) in the first five months of 2026 following a 118 per cent year-on-year surge to HK$357 billion in 2025.

Total assets under management also grew by 20 per cent to HK$42.2 trillion in 2025 from a year earlier, with most coming from outside the mainland and Hong Kong.

“Capital investors really vote for Hong Kong with their feet,” Chan said.

He said China-US relations were bound to have “ups and downs,” and Hong Kong’s top priority was to ensure financial stability while taking advantage of development opportunities.

At the core of Hong Kong’s financial development was the city’s stock market, which had recorded robust trading volumes and a larger number of new listings in recent years, Chan said.

The stock market is also set to benefit from a series of measures floated in the policy address and the city’s first five-year plan, which were both released earlier this month.

Proceeds raised in initial public offerings (IPOs) in the first eight months of 2026 were 153 per cent higher than in the same period last year, at HK$342.4 billion.

The eight-month total has already surpassed last year’s IPO proceeds of HK$286.9 billion. The 2025 figure already represented growth of 226 per cent year on year.

“So all these indicate that we remain focused on doing the right thing, enhancing our competitiveness, improving our listing regime, for example, expanding the possibility of attracting additional liquidity. Then, quality companies will come,” Chan said.

“We are taking this window to further build, further strengthen our equities market. But at the same time, develop FIC [fixed income and currencies], develop commodities, trading and gold. This takes time, but we move on; we’ll invest in it.”

Chan also highlighted plans to expand the global use of the yuan.

While Hong Kong currently served as “a firewall” for the wider nation’s financial security, the city also planned to drum up yuan product offerings to raise liquidity and act as a testing bed for yuan products, the finance chief said.

Hong Kong has the world’s biggest pool of yuan outside the mainland, sitting at about 1.1 trillion yuan (US$163 billion).

“Our idea is that if we want to gather more liquidity, gather more investors coming to our market, then we need to enrich the product offering. We need to build the necessary infrastructure. We also need to provide the liquidity that is needed,” Chan said.

He added that several central banks were planning to increase their yuan holdings in an effort to pursue diversification, which would generate more investment opportunities.

Asked whether the push risked diminishing the role of the Hong Kong dollar – which is pegged to the US dollar – amid so-called de-dollarisation, Chan said “no”, and remained adamant that the linked exchange rate system, which debuted in 1983, had worked well and was an anchor for the city’s currency regime.

“This is very core to us in terms of strength,” he said. “We have no intention at all to change this. This is very fundamental.”

As the city is fast-tracking its push into gold trading and storage and a commodity ecosystem, Chan said the government planned to launch a “gold connect scheme” to facilitate more cross-border trade.

Hong Kong and the mainland already operate various connect schemes that grant global financial institutions access to mainland stock and bond markets through the city.

“The competition is keen,” Chan said, referring to competition between gold markets in Hong Kong, London and Singapore.

“But our advantage is the strong hinterland. China is a major user of gold. The Shanghai gold exchange is very keen and has a strong market, but it needs to have an international connection. Hong Kong can play the role.”

item.title: [SCMP] How Hong Kong’s old businesses are adapting to new times
item.description:
In the second of a two-part series on Hong Kong’s economic transformation, Ambrose Li and Wynna Wong profile three established enterprises that have rejuvenated their brands and reinvented their businesses. Read part one here.

Late into the night, Hong Kong football fans in their twenties, thirties and forties sat in Lin Heung Lau restaurant on Wellington Street watching World Cup matches over dim sum rather than pints at a sports bar.

The historic restaurant, traditionally associated with elderly morning-tea regulars, extended its operating hours during the World Cup in the summer, drawing on the expertise of chairman Rocky Wong Hei-yan, a nightlife industry veteran behind once-bustling Lan Kwai Fong venues such as Club No 9, Club Beijing and Magnum.
item.content:encoded:
In the second of a two-part series on Hong Kong’s economic transformation, Ambrose Li and Wynna Wong profile three established enterprises that have rejuvenated their brands and reinvented their businesses. Read part one here.

Late into the night, Hong Kong football fans in their twenties, thirties and forties sat in Lin Heung Lau restaurant on Wellington Street watching World Cup matches over dim sum rather than pints at a sports bar.

The historic restaurant, traditionally associated with elderly morning-tea regulars, extended its operating hours during the World Cup in the summer, drawing on the expertise of chairman Rocky Wong Hei-yan, a nightlife industry veteran behind once-bustling Lan Kwai Fong venues such as Club No 9, Club Beijing and Magnum.

“On that occasion, we were not calculating money only,” he said. “We were looking at brand-building and opening another channel through which we could find customers.”

The century-old Lin Heung Lau brand has been rejuvenated with new marketing and business strategies since 2024, when its management was revamped amid a decline in the tradition of people going out for dim sum.

The restaurant has hosted a series of “dim sum raves”, taking social media by storm with its tea-infused cocktails and electronic music paired with steaming towers of pork buns and shrimp dumplings.

Lin Heung Lau’s football and rave nights illustrate one solution to a question confronting established Hong Kong businesses: how can they follow changing customer habits and find new sources of revenue without discarding the identity that made them valuable?

Interviews with family-business scholars and companies ranging from a traditional dried-seafood retailer to a long-established transport operator suggest that transformation does not follow a single formula.

It can involve creating new experiences, rebuilding unglamorous back-end systems, adopting artificial intelligence (AI) or allowing a younger generation to experiment.

Winnie Peng Qian, director of the Roger King Centre for Asian Family Business and Family Office at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, cautioned against assuming that every established company needed to pursue rapid or radical innovation.

“People always think you need to innovate, need to react fast,” she said.

“But you see a lot of century-old family businesses in Japan. They’re very small, fewer than 10 people, just a store doing the same thing.”

Such companies could instead innovate gradually, she said, while adapting their traditions to remain relevant to the environment they faced.

Nightlife meets yum cha

Wong saw an opportunity in Lin Heung Lau when it closed during the Covid-19 pandemic, believing its brand had untapped potential despite the difficult environment facing Hong Kong’s catering industry.

Wong, the restaurant’s chairman and primary investor, was granted the perpetual right to use the Lin Heung Lau brand in Hong Kong rather than ownership of the underlying intellectual property.

He had known the restaurant for more than 25 years, having regularly visited for morning tea after finishing work at his clubs.

“I was very familiar with the brand and knew its strengths and weaknesses,” he said.

“It was not simply a matter of me taking over and benefiting from a powerful brand. It had already closed. I was setting out with it again and that was a major challenge.”

Despite the obvious differences between running nightclubs and operating a traditional Chinese dim sum restaurant frequented in the morning, Wong said both businesses ultimately depended on the same thing: management.

“If you manage people properly and they naturally follow the organisation’s instructions, you can succeed in even selling salted crispy peanuts,” he said.

“But if management is poor and everything becomes too personalised, it will destroy the entire management system.”

Since taking over the operation, Wong has sought to preserve Lin Heung Lau’s traditional yum cha atmosphere and handmade dim sum while reaching beyond the predominantly elderly clientele historically associated with such restaurants.

“We are not taking a single direction and targeting only the silver-haired market,” he said.

“We are adding new elements to attract different customers – middle-aged people, young people and even children.”

Wong did not provide figures for the investment, sales or footfall generated by the football screenings but said they were profitable and attracted a largely younger crowd.

He argued that their greater value was promotional, estimating that the equivalent publicity would have cost millions of dollars to reproduce through conventional advertising.

Lin Heung Lau had opened or substantially redeveloped five outlets in just over two years, Wong said.

Its latest restaurant occupies about 13,000 sq ft at the airport, while other locations include Mong Kok and Tsim Sha Tsui.

About 95 per cent of the menu is shared among its restaurants, but each has distinctive dishes or design features.

Wong said operators could no longer simply open their doors and assume customers would arrive.

“You have to catch the trend,” he said. “A business has to change. If it does not change, customers will not come.”

More affordable ready-to-eat abalone

At On Kee Dry Seafood, founded in the 1930s, transformation has been less visible to customers but no less extensive.

The family business has made traditionally expensive dried gourmet seafood such as abalone more affordable by creating mouth-sized snacks that proved popular with younger shoppers at the city’s signature food fair.

As preparing and cooking items like abalone, sea cucumber and duck’s feet can take a couple of days, the group has diversified into ready-to-eat offerings such as frozen and pre-cooked seafood, as well as ready-to-consume soups and desserts.

“Our ready-to-eat products have proved to be very popular because they cater to the busy lives of Hongkongers who have a preference for convenience,” said Henry Poon, 27, the fourth generation of the family business.

“About two years ago, we developed an individually wrapped abalone snack that could be consumed right away, designed for when people are feeling peckish.”

The company was still relying heavily on handwritten notes and fax machines as recently as five years ago.

Its six retail stores also handled about 1,000 online orders a day, forcing employees to pack e-commerce purchases on crowded shop floors while serving customers.

“After all, we are a very traditional company,” Poon said.

“Even five years ago, we weren’t a particularly digital company, relying heavily on handwritten notes and using fax.”

Over the past two years, Poon has led a digital transformation, describing it as a “timely catch-up” with the market amid the growing popularity of e-commerce.

An enterprise resource planning system consolidates orders placed through On Kee’s website and third-party platforms, streamlining stocking, packing and delivery.

The company can process about 1,800 online orders a day, an 80 per cent increase from before.

On Kee also introduced a point-of-sale system capable of handling more complex promotions, such as a 10 per cent discount on a second item and 20 per cent off a third.

AI has reduced the time needed to calculate how much stock should be taken to exhibitions – important events for the business – from several days to minutes.

“We’d typically look at the trend from the past three to four times we took part, as well as our previous orders,” Poon said.

“The press of a button generates you a very good forecast table.”

The transition remains unfinished. Poon estimated that it could take another three to four years for all the new systems to operate smoothly.

‘Standing still means falling behind’

At Kwoon Chung Bus Holdings, one of Hong Kong’s largest franchised and non-franchised bus operators, the changes in its business and strategies have been sweeping.

Founded in 1948 as a car-cleaning service by the late entrepreneur Wong Kwoon-chung, the firm, which earned 82 per cent more year on year in net profit in 2025-26, at HK$268.4 million, is aiming high – literally.

It made a breakthrough in the 1990s, taking over bus operations on Lantau Island and coach companies that catered to hotel and tour group operators.

A landmark change took place in 2023, when third-generation family members Timothy and James Wong pushed through a new venture, KC Smart Mobility, by investing in electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft (eVTOL), alongside autonomous vehicles, drones and ride-hailing services.

In August, the company worked with mainland Chinese autonomous aerial vehicle manufacturer EHang and tech hub Cyberport to bring an eVTOL to Hong Kong, culminating in the city’s first successful demonstration flight of an unmanned heavy-duty aircraft.

“These are medium- to long-term investments that will not be profitable soon,” said Newton Ng, business development director of KC Smart Mobility.

“Standing still means falling behind. If we remain the same as we are today, there will not be expansion.”

The company plans to buy 30 eVTOLs from EHang for more than HK$70 million, although the aircraft remain at the testing stage. Charging can take more than an hour for a flight lasting about 20 minutes, while Hong Kong does not yet have regulations for commercial operations.

Ng said acting early could help the company capture market share.

“If government policies are also directed towards newer modes of transport, the earlier we act, the sooner we can possibly capture a larger market share,” he added.

Kwoon Chung has already encountered changing customer behaviour in its traditional passenger-transport operation.

Its existing limousine customers previously had to telephone the company to reserve vehicles, but increasingly wanted to arrange their journeys online.

The operator responded by partnering with ride-hailing company Uber to launch Uber Elite, a premium service combining Kwoon Chung’s vehicles, full-time chauffeurs and local operating experience with the US-based firm’s widely used booking platform and customer reach.

The service, Uber’s first of its kind outside the United States, offers pre-booked rides in Mercedes-Benz vehicles for groups of up to six passengers, targeting C-suite executives and business travellers.

Customers can book between two hours and 90 days in advance. Ng said demand during the first month was strong enough that the company could not always accommodate requests made at shorter notice.

“It’s a changing consumption pattern,” he said. “If we do not develop a model that caters to the trend, some customers will of course drift away over time.

“We’ll have to follow the habits of the younger generation and have a presence where they book their commutes.”

Space for the next generation

Kwoon Chung’s decision to place its experimental businesses in a subsidiary headed by third-generation members reflects one way family companies can pursue transformation without immediately disrupting their core operations.

Jeremy Cheng Chi-yeung, an adjunct associate professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s business school, said such companies could initially be slower to adopt the latest trends but often committed substantial resources once they decided to proceed.

One model, he said, was to allow the rising generation to establish a smaller agile unit, the kind created by Kwoon Chung.

“The rising generation will build their own team, a small unit, which is meant to be agile, and they can lead faster changes,” Cheng said.

“Once they are successful with that particular experiment, they tend to cross-fertilise that in different units in the business itself.”

Victoria Wang, a professor at the same institution, said slower adoption did not necessarily mean a family business lacked the ability to survive.

“They change slowly to go faster,” she said. “Tradition is legacy, purpose and identity. They very much want to make sure their identity continues.”

Transformation, however, does not always require radical innovation.

“If a tradition remains relevant, it is valuable,” Peng of Hong Kong University of Science and Technology said. “But if the family is static, very traditional and refuses to change, of course it cannot survive in the long term.”

For Lin Heung Lau, this has meant continuing to serve handmade dim sum while challenging assumptions about who should eat it and when.

At On Kee, the dried seafood remains, but the handwritten orders and fax machines are disappearing.

For Kwoon Chung, the coaches continue operating while the next generation explores modes of transport extending from smartphones to the skies.

Peng said the family businesses that endured tended to share two deeper characteristics – a long-term outlook and a sense of responsibility towards society.

Their experience of surviving economic and political upheavals helped them look beyond immediate difficulties, while a broader purpose gave future generations a reason to continue beyond preserving their own wealth.

“Sometimes you need to stick to who you are and your family values,” Peng said. “The first thing that stands out is a long-term perspective. The other is altruism. You need to care about society.”

item.title: [SCMP] US families ramp up efforts for loved ones’ release from China ahead of Xi’s visit
item.description:
Chen Youlin, a Chinese-American scientist, travelled back to China in October 2024 for a month-long holiday, including to celebrate his mother’s 80th birthday. As he prepared to leave, authorities arrested him at the airport in Beijing.

For more than 670 days, his wife, Rong Yufang, and other family members have not been able to see or speak with him.

“Sometimes I realise I can no longer clearly remember the sound of his voice, and that breaks my heart,” Rong told the South China Morning Post. “Our home feels empty without him and the uncertainty surrounding his future has become a prison for our family as well.”
item.content:encoded:
Chen Youlin, a Chinese-American scientist, travelled back to China in October 2024 for a month-long holiday, including to celebrate his mother’s 80th birthday. As he prepared to leave, authorities arrested him at the airport in Beijing.

For more than 670 days, his wife, Rong Yufang, and other family members have not been able to see or speak with him.

“Sometimes I realise I can no longer clearly remember the sound of his voice, and that breaks my heart,” Rong told the South China Morning Post. “Our home feels empty without him and the uncertainty surrounding his future has become a prison for our family as well.”

Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected visit to Washington next week, cases of several US citizens detained in China are gaining greater attention as their families step up pressure on the Trump administration to press Beijing for their release.

As well as Chen’s family, the relatives of Americans Min Zin, Dawn Michelle Hunt and Nelson Wells Jnr are pressing Washington to intervene with Beijing – but their cases vary. Chen and Zin are being held on national security-related allegations, while Hunt and Wells Jnr have spent over a decade in Chinese prisons over drug convictions.

Families like Chen’s face a dilemma: pursue quiet diplomacy or go public to pressure Washington and Beijing. Many initially favour a low-profile approach, but turn to public advocacy when private efforts fail.

The cases highlight the risks American citizens can face in China’s legal system, even as US President Donald Trump and Xi seek to stabilise ties and Beijing courts foreign investors, academics and tourists.

US government lists individuals as being ‘wrongfully detained’

Chinese authorities have accused Chen of espionage, likely linked to his previous work analysing seismic data, including North Korean nuclear tests.

Another recent well-publicised case involves American scholar Zin, who was detained in China in June. Chinese authorities accused him of espionage and endangering China’s national security.

Both Chen and Zin have been formally designated as “wrongfully detained” by the US government, a status that means officials will prioritise efforts to secure their release.

A lawyer has been hired to represent Chen and US consular officials have been allowed to visit him.

Rong, Chen’s wife, raised concerns about his health and weight loss during his detention. She told the SCMP that senior US officials had assured her that Trump would raise Chen’s case.

“President Trump and his senior team have been 100 per cent on my side,” Rong said.

The State Department’s Office of the Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs has also publicly addressed the issue, saying: “Hostage diplomacy has no place in the US-China relationship.”

Chen’s family initially worked behind the scenes, according to its representative, Eric Lebson of Global Reach. It went public after Trump raised Chen’s case with Xi in May but secured no breakthrough.

Trump also raised the cases of Pastor Ezra Jin, who was later freed, and jailed Hong Kong media boss Jimmy Lai Chee-ying. Lai’s family and supporters want Trump to raise his case again next week.

For Zin’s case, the circumstances are less clear. The Wall Street Journal reported that US officials believe his background as a former student activist in Myanmar and his US-funded academic work may have drawn the attention of Chinese security services.

Edgard Kagan, a China expert at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, said the detention of Chen and Zin is likely linked to their academic work, and he expects Trump to press for their release.

Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey is leading a bipartisan resolution condemning China’s wrongful detention of American academics.

The James W. Foley Legacy Foundation says 12 Americans are currently wrongfully detained in China, including some subject to exit bans. It has assessed 42 cases since 1998, though the total number of Americans caught up in China’s legal system may be higher.

In 2024, US diplomacy secured the release of three Americans held for years; Beijing said the US returned four people to China.

The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.

Beijing has firmly rejected the “wrongful detention” designations. Asked about Chen’s case, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said there is no “wrongful detention” in China and that judicial agencies handle cases in accordance with the law.

The embassy spokesperson offered more detail on Zin specifically, telling the Wall Street Journal that he is subject to “criminal coercive measures,” meaning he is under investigation, and that his “legitimate rights have been fully guaranteed.”

Two other high-profile cases involving Americans

Two other high-profile cases involve Americans Hunt and Wells Jnr, both of whom have been imprisoned in China for more than 12 years after being convicted on separate drug charges.

Unlike the scholars’ cases, which have been designated as “wrongfully detained”, the families are pursuing the humanitarian release route and say that they are speaking on behalf of ordinary “rank-and-file” Americans.

The families have joined forces, saying both detainees unknowingly carried drugs out of China. Dawn Michelle’s brother, Tim Hunt, said scammers lured her there with a purported competition prize, then gave her purses with drugs sewn into the lining. Wells Jnr was arrested after agreeing to carry someone else’s suitcase containing hidden narcotics, his family said.

Both have worsening health problems, their families say. Wells Jnr’s father said his son has seizures, high blood pressure and diabetes, and was recently diagnosed with hepatitis C.

Peter Humphrey, a former SCMP China correspondent and fraud investigator who was imprisoned in China with his wife from 2013 to 2015, is working with the families. Since his release, he has advised foreign detainees and their families on how to navigate China’s system.

“We have been constantly hearing from our lobbying contacts in Beijing that the Chinese side is very ready to consider a humanitarian release, so long as there is a request from the American president,” Humphrey said.

Joi Chaney, a legal expert working with the families, called the lack of a US-China prisoner transfer treaty a “blockade” the US has placed on itself. Chinese law allows transfers through bilateral negotiations in special cases, but Washington has historically maintained that US law does not, said Humphrey. He said the US State Department asked China in May 2025 to release Wells Jnr and Hunt on humanitarian grounds.

In response to an SCMP inquiry, a US State Department spokesperson said it has repeatedly raised serious concerns about Wells Jnr and Hunt’s health with Chinese officials.

“We have called upon the Chinese to release them unconditionally on humanitarian grounds, at every opportunity, and we will continue to do so,” it said, while adding that decisions on humanitarian release are at the discretion of the host government.

Additionally, in 2025, bipartisan lawmakers introduced the “Nelson Wells Jnr and Dawn Michelle Hunt Unjustly Detained in Communist China Act”, seeking to strengthen the government’s response to Americans detained in China and support their families. The bill has stalled since its introduction.

“We’re not famous people, we’re not sports stars,” Chaney said, arguing that ordinary Americans should be able to count on their government to bring them home. Both families have histories of military and public service. “If you say you respect the people who serve, show us,” Tim Hunt said in a plea to Trump. “Ask for their release.”

When asked about Hunt and Wells, the White House offered a general response rather than addressing the individual cases.

Families put faith in Trump as Xi summit approaches

“President Trump is always concerned about Americans detained abroad. That is why he has brought over 100 individuals – a record number – home from around the world,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said.

Both families said they were disappointed when their loved ones were not released after the last Xi-Trump summit.

Wells Snr described feeling out of it in the weeks after, not wanting to talk. Tim Hunt found it hard to speak to his sister, who felt she had false hope in the lead-up to the meeting.

Addressing the US president directly ahead of next week’s summit, Wells Snr said: “I would tell President Trump that he’s a father. If he had a child that was in the same situation as our child or Tim’s sister, he would do everything in his power to try to bring them home.”

item.title: [SCMP] China, US may unveil measures to boost military ties when Xi visits Washington
item.description:
China and the United States are discussing possible announcements to strengthen military-to-military ties during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington next week, multiple sources familiar with the discussions told the South China Morning Post.

Another item that is being discussed, and a possible deliverable, is restarting the arms-control talks that were suspended in 2024 over US weapons sales to Taiwan, with the dialogue potentially including military personnel.

In a phone call on Thursday to make final arrangements before the summit, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that both sides should prepare for the next stage of high-level exchange in the spirit of equality, respect and mutual benefit.
item.content:encoded:
China and the United States are discussing possible announcements to strengthen military-to-military ties during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington next week, multiple sources familiar with the discussions told the South China Morning Post.

Another item that is being discussed, and a possible deliverable, is restarting the arms-control talks that were suspended in 2024 over US weapons sales to Taiwan, with the dialogue potentially including military personnel.

In a phone call on Thursday to make final arrangements before the summit, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that both sides should prepare for the next stage of high-level exchange in the spirit of equality, respect and mutual benefit.

“[We should] strengthen communication, advance cooperation and manage differences, respect each other’s core interests, and send a positive message that China and the United States are committed to advancing a constructive and strategically stable relationship and to jointly promoting world peace and development.,” Wang said, according to Xinhua.

The two also discussed the situation in the Middle East, Xinhua reported.

Sources said both sides were discussing ways to activate more military communication channels and bolster the existing ones – marking a rare bright spot in an otherwise fiercely competitive relationship.

They said officials in the two militaries were interacting at various levels, with the frequency and level of engagement increasing substantially in the past few months.

Despite a still-contentious economic relationship marked by tit-for-tat tariffs, export controls and sanctions, military ties between Washington and Beijing have moved in a more positive direction, with regular dialogue and public commitments to maintaining peace and increasing mutual understanding.

Sources said both sides were rebuilding military channels to speak frequently and prevent any misunderstanding and miscalculation about each other’s intentions.

Ending a two-year hiatus, China and the US held command-level talks late last month in Canada, with a meeting between Chinese General Yang Zhibin, commander of the Eastern Theatre Command, and US Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of the Pacific Command.

The US Pacific Command said Yang and Paparo discussed the importance of maintaining open lines of communication between senior American and Chinese military leaders to reduce the risk of miscalculation and to promote safe and professional conduct between forces.

One source said China and the US were seeking military dialogue at three levels. Those talks would be between the two presidents, who are also commanders-in-chief of their countries’ armed forces; also at the ministerial level, including the US Department of Defence and China’s Central Military Commission; and between frontline commanders, in particular the US Pacific Command chief and the PLA’s Eastern Theatre Command chief.

“The presidential-level and frontline commander-level talks are progressing,” the source said, referring to recent meetings between Xi and US President Donald Trump and the talks between Paparo and Yang.

“But actual ministerial-level talks might take a while. One problem has been China’s anti-corruption campaign that [almost] wiped out the CMC, leaving Zhang Shengmin [as the only uniformed official in the body],” he said.

“But we believe they will take place in the near future.”

Another person familiar with the matter said both sides had made clear they wanted new communication channels.

One of the channels could be to revive dedicated arms-control talks between the US State Department and China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which gained momentum in 2023 before being suspended in July 2024 over Washington’s continued arms sales to Taiwan.

A source described the talks as a give from the Chinese side that could eventually be broadened to include military personnel – a long-standing US request – “if things go well”.

Washington had planned to send a more senior Pentagon China official to Beijing’s Xiangshan Forum this week, after last year dispatching only the defence attache. But the official withdrew before the forum, with the US delegation instead led by Brigadier General Stacy Kihara of the embassy in Beijing, leaving the official level unchanged from 2025.

A third source said military-to-military contact under Trump’s second term had become more stable but remained “shallow”. The source said deliverables for the Xi-Trump summit were discussed and locked in when Yang and Paparo met face to face in Canada – their first in-person meeting.

The person called that progress “unique” under a Republican president, describing Trump as “a different sort of Republican president”.

A fourth source said the two militaries were working to follow the “strategic stability” guidance agreed by Trump and Xi during their May meeting in Beijing.

After the summit, the two sides referenced the concept of “strategic stability” in their statements, while differing over its phrasing and interpretation.

In July, a senior Pentagon official – for the first time in more than five years – attended and spoke at a reception at the Chinese embassy in Washington marking the 99th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Liberation Army.

“Under the leadership of Secretary [Pete] Hegseth, we are actively repairing a once broken military-to-military channel and making clear, steady progress,” said Alvaro Smith, deputy assistant defence secretary for China, Taiwan and Mongolia.

He added that US-China military communication was “stronger than it has been in years” and said Washington was not seeking a “conflict with China”.

“This is how two powerful militaries should engage, and over the last year and a half, we made this a reality.”

US undersecretary of defence for policy Elbridge Colby also hosted Chinese Foreign Vice-Minister Ma Zhaoxu at the Pentagon, later saying on social media that the US interacted with its “Chinese counterparts in a spirit of respect, candour, and realism”.

In another sign of closer military engagement, China is cooperating with the US military to recover the remains of American soldiers who went missing in China during World War II.

As part of those efforts, US defence recovery teams travelled to China in early July to resume searches for missing service members.

The renewed engagement marks a significant shift from the Joe Biden administration, when a series of incidents escalated tensions and left military-to-military communication largely stalled.

Beijing suspended several key military dialogue mechanisms with Washington in 2022 after then-House speaker Nancy Pelosi travelled to Taiwan on a high-profile visit.

Taiwan has been the most sensitive issue between Beijing and Washington. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary.

Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent nation, but Washington opposes any attempt to seize the self-governing island by force and has pledged to supply it with weapons.
