item.title: [SCMP] Golden years: in Southeast Asia, growing old is big business
item.description:
Helen Fung’s home felt empty. After her husband died last October, she found herself rattling around a house in Singapore with only a domestic helper she could not get along with for company.

She turned down her children’s invitations to move to England, put off by London’s grey winters, and instead checked herself into an assisted living facility.

On a recent Monday afternoon in St Bernadette Lifestyle Village at Trevose Crescent, tucked away in the leafy residential estate of Bukit Timah, Fung celebrated her 92nd birthday.
item.content:encoded:
Helen Fung’s home felt empty. After her husband died last October, she found herself rattling around a house in Singapore with only a domestic helper she could not get along with for company.

She turned down her children’s invitations to move to England, put off by London’s grey winters, and instead checked herself into an assisted living facility.

On a recent Monday afternoon in St Bernadette Lifestyle Village at Trevose Crescent, tucked away in the leafy residential estate of Bukit Timah, Fung celebrated her 92nd birthday.

Carers wheeled and walked eight fellow residents to the dining table before breaking into song. Goaded into a speech, Fung kept it brief: “I’m very happy to be here.”

The home, a refurbished two-storey bungalow, is one of a growing number of assisted living facilities springing up as Singapore’s population ages. The city state officially became a “super-aged” society this year, with more than one-fifth of its population over 65.

These facilities offer a much-needed middle ground for older people who can no longer live independently but do not require the round-the-clock medical care of a nursing home.

Staff help residents with daily tasks such as dispensing medication and writing letters, while some facilities include memory care units for those experiencing cognitive decline.

Assisted living is a nascent but fast-growing segment of Singapore’s multibillion-dollar silver economy. The government has provided more than 1,100 such flats since 2021, and private real estate operators are also increasingly entering the market.

For residents like Fung, what matters most is feeling part of a community, keeping their independence and being treated with dignity. Despite her early-stage osteoporosis, she moves around the home without a walking frame, sometimes forgoing afternoon sessions of mahjong to journal in her room instead.

“I’m fitting in little by little – I’ve learned to get to know more of the residents and our different timetables,” she said. “I told my family I’ll probably stay here until the time comes.”

For fellow resident Soo Soo Cheng, 90, her single room is a world away from the six-bedded ward she shared at her previous nursing home. “It was like a dormitory and nothing private like this. I was getting really uncomfortable,” she said.

Now she spends her days in a bright orange armchair by the window, walking frame within reach, while carers take care of tasks like printing copies of bills and helping her to bed when her spine acts up.

“I’m thankful for a place like this, where I can do things on my own and yet never have a dull moment,” she said. “Time seems to fly.”

A middle ground

Southeast Asia is ageing rapidly and its social welfare systems are increasingly grappling with a thorny question: what happens to the people who can no longer manage entirely on their own, but do not need a hospital bed?

Assisted living – offering medical and social care scalable to residents’ needs – has emerged as an answer.

It was designed for people whose needs fell somewhere between the intensive clinical care of a nursing home and what a domestic helper, who cannot reasonably be expected to manage a medical emergency, could provide, said Janice Chia, founder of Ageing Asia, a Singapore-based social enterprise focused on the business of growing old.

In Singapore, more people are ageing alone – an estimated 83,000 by 2030, according to the Ministry of Health – while shrinking family sizes are increasing the caregiving burden shouldered by adult children.

“Assisted living provides independence and privacy without the seeming unpopular burden of managing foreign domestic helpers,” said Kelvin Tan, who heads the applied ageing studies programme at the Singapore University of Social Sciences.

Options in the city state range from government-run flats to private luxury apartments, with monthly bills ranging anywhere from three to five figures, depending on location, room size and level of care required.

In 2021, Singapore introduced community care flats aiming to support independent ageing in a social environment. Five such projects have launched so far.

The Housing Development Board announced in July that from its sixth project, launching in October, the eligibility age for assisted-living public housing estates would be lowered from 65 to 55, alongside lower fees aimed at improving affordability.

Estimated fees for a 15-year lease – currently S$40,000 to S$49,000 (US$31,400 to US$38,500) for a basic package – will drop to between S$26,000 and S$28,000 from next year, according to Vanguard Healthcare, which operates the developments.

“The cost is a big advantage for average Singaporeans looking for an accessible offer,” Tan said.

Private operators are also scaling up their operations. St Bernadette Lifestyle Village, which runs eight facilities island-wide, offers a mid-tier option priced from S$3,000 to S$6,000 a month.

Care homes were “less a business venture than a necessity”, said founder Belinda Wee, who has observed elderly residents growing unsettled in nursing homes due to a lack of socialising. About 80 residents lived in St Bernadette’s homes last year, up from 19 in 2023.

Well-heeled pensioners gained a luxury option last month with the opening of Perennial Living, a S$260 million, 195,000 sq ft development in northeastern Singapore featuring a hydrotherapy pool, a traditional Chinese medicine clinic and a karaoke lounge.

A basic package for a 330 sq ft studio flat starts at S$8,000 a month, while a 565 sq ft two-bedder costs more than S$13,000.

The hefty price tag has raised concerns about the affordability of retirement, though experts note the project is aimed squarely at the upper end of the market.

Chia said its prices should be viewed in the category of premium hospitality and care, rather than general assisted living.

Sign-ups have been gradual and interest has been “positive”, according to Perennial Holding’s chief executive Pua Seck Guan, who projected a 30 per cent occupancy rate after a year and 80 per cent after two.

More new entrants were expected to join the assisted living sector, Chia said, as Singapore’s shift from live-in caregiving to mainstream services gave firms the confidence to invest. But she urged regulators to pace approvals carefully given the dearth of healthcare workers.

Singapore needed to recruit about 6,000 nurses, healthcare professionals and support staff every year to meet demand, the Health Ministry said in 2024. It previously estimated that a healthcare workforce of 82,000 would be needed by 2030.

“This figure is the one worth dwelling on, because it shows care capability cannot simply be commissioned. Sites can be approved considerably faster than carers can be trained, deployed and retained,” Chia said.

Ageing in luxury

With its circular driveway and plush lobby, Perennial Living looks more like an upscale hotel than a home for the elderly.

The development aimed to set a “new benchmark for senior living in Singapore”, Pua said – reflecting a surge in luxury senior living facilities across Asia as operators recognise their target demographic wants more than just care and medical services.

More than US$500 billion is expected to pour into the silver economy across six Southeast Asian markets – Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines – by 2030, according to Ageing Asia.

Retirees today were wealthier, healthier and more assertive than any generation before them, the social enterprise said in a report released last month, making the business of ageing the Asia-Pacific’s “largest commercial opportunity”.

“Baby boomers, the biggest savers of all generations, have spent their lives making choices and are expected to hold onto that autonomy into their older age,” it said.

At Homerly International Senior Living in Thailand, residents walk long, tree-lined avenues within a large, serene gated community, accompanied by nurses, with their pets padding along behind them. The resort, which provides assisted living and nursing care, is one of hundreds of retirement communities popping up across a country with abundant land and a growing healthcare workforce.

A month’s stay – including round-the-clock medical care, physiotherapy, pool villas shaded by trees and two staff members in attendance – starts at US$2,200, with the top-end pool villas commanding a price tag of around US$4,500.

“Here you’re not a patient, you are a resident. We treat people with dignity,” general manager Rene Pisters said. “You have somebody with you all the time if you need it and the feeling that if something happens to you, there is a nurse sitting here.”

Malaysia is seeing a similar boom in luxury homes for the elderly, driven by changing expectations of ageing, according to N. Raaj Selvarajan, group chairman of regional healthcare infrastructure investor Hemrish Group and founder of its flagship senior living brand Sukha Golden.

Residents increasingly wanted privacy, wellness and access to care without the institutional feel traditionally associated with elderly care, he said.

Demand for its luxury Sukha Senior Resort has surged since it opened in March last year – all rooms are fully occupied, with interested residents placed on a waiting list.

Capitalising on the boom, Selvarajan said plans to expand regionally were under way, with projects in Indonesia and Vietnam in the pipeline. “The opportunity is not simply that Asia is ageing; it is that people want to age differently,” he said.

Crossing borders

For Singaporeans who feel priced out of their own super-aged society, homes for the elderly have become an unlikely engine of Malaysia and Thailand’s recent tourism boom, as families shop for similar care standards at a fraction of the cost.

The Straits Resorts Medini, a retirement home in Johor just a 15-minute drive from the border, has built its business around Singaporean demand.

“Consistent and encouraging” is how founder Elvira Tan describes cross-border interest in the facility, which offers rooms from S$4,300 a month, bundling in personalised care and grooming services, arts activities and social programmes.

Industry insiders expect the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone and Rapid Transit System Link, set to open in January, to further boost demand.

“You can obtain the most expensive level of care in Malaysia for about one-third the price of the same level of care in Singapore,” said Kashif Ansari, group CEO of real estate market intelligence group Juwai IQI.

Cultural familiarity and the absence of a language barrier eased the transition for would-be residents considering homes across the causeway, he added.

“Families with a senior who needs potentially years or even more than a decade of care, naturally want the highest quality service and the lowest cost they can possibly obtain,” he said. “Malaysia has a real competitive advantage in this sector and operators hope to make the most of it.”

Money goes further in Thailand too. Facilities in Bangkok and Chiang Mai are attracting a growing number of Asian retirees, including from Singapore and Hong Kong, looking for care comparable to what they can get at home at a fraction of the cost.

Thailand hopes the care and wellness industry will become a defining part of its economy in the years ahead, as more people grow old and spend money on a curated retirement.

Care standards were high, Homerly’s Pisters said, adding that his company helped elderly residents with bureaucratic hurdles such as visas and bank accounts.

“The demand is huge, and it will only get bigger,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] How Wilson Cheng’s start-up is cutting in-flight food waste
item.description:
Young minds, big ideas: meet five laureates of the AIA Scholarships programme, which was founded on the belief that education can open doors not only for individuals, but for the communities they will one day serve. See our other features, on Zara Chui Siu-wa, King Chan Kai-man, Selina Wong Yuen-shan and Atta Yu Yee-ting

There is a 7mm gap between the main body and the handle of an airline trolley – that is the space Wilson Cheng Wui-sum’s camera has to fit into without disrupting the in-flight service.

Cheng, 21, majors in computer science at Polytechnic University with a minor in information security. In August 2025, he and four friends incorporated a start-up that helps airlines reduce food waste using artificial-intelligence-powered devices. It is, by design, unglamorous: a compact gadget, mounted on a service trolley, running offline at cruising altitude. As trays are returned to the trolley, the device’s camera records the leftover contents and the AI-driven tracking app identifies what has (and hasn’t) been eaten – half a portion of the main course, a bread roll, a drink barely touched.
item.content:encoded:
Young minds, big ideas: meet five laureates of the AIA Scholarships programme, which was founded on the belief that education can open doors not only for individuals, but for the communities they will one day serve. See our other features, on Zara Chui Siu-wa, King Chan Kai-man, Selina Wong Yuen-shan and Atta Yu Yee-ting

There is a 7mm gap between the main body and the handle of an airline trolley – that is the space Wilson Cheng Wui-sum’s camera has to fit into without disrupting the in-flight service.

Cheng, 21, majors in computer science at Polytechnic University with a minor in information security. In August 2025, he and four friends incorporated a start-up that helps airlines reduce food waste using artificial-intelligence-powered devices. It is, by design, unglamorous: a compact gadget, mounted on a service trolley, running offline at cruising altitude. As trays are returned to the trolley, the device’s camera records the leftover contents and the AI-driven tracking app identifies what has (and hasn’t) been eaten – half a portion of the main course, a bread roll, a drink barely touched.

Born from a sustainability hackathon held by a local airline in 2024, his start-up’s solution addresses a pressing issue: more than US$5 billion worth of in-flight meals are wasted each year. Roughly 30 per cent of all food and drink goes uneaten, according to Cheng. He and his team placed third in the competition, and are now partnering with the airline to launch a smart waste-tracking system.

You find the problem, take it apart and try different ways to solve it

Wilson Cheng

Computer science “is a problem-solving puzzle”, says Cheng. “You find the problem, take it apart and try different ways to solve it.” He has been taking things apart since childhood, his toys becoming disassembled components. In secondary school, he chose chemistry, physics and information and communications technology, then immersed himself in robotics.

Even when life throws him curveballs, he doesn’t slow down. In Form Five, he developed a weakness in his lower limbs. A walking frame came first; a wheelchair followed. He sat the Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE) on schedule anyway, and took up his undergraduate studies at PolyU. Because traditional engineering – with its labs and physical demands – would have been difficult, coding began as a compromise, but it quickly became a calling.

He admits “the adversity was daunting”, but his friends kept him going – the classmates who went through DSE with him and the members of his start-up, for which one person designs, another manages the business, a third leads strategy and a fourth oversees finance, leaving Cheng as the coding brain. “I might think something won’t work, until someone else looks at it from another angle,” he says, referring to the team’s synergistic advantages.

Cheng believes that university projects should be about more than just ticking boxes. It wasn’t until he joined the robotics club at PolyU and worked on motor-tuning for a robotics competition that he took on his first challenge outside the conventional curriculum.

Cheng’s device came from an almost comical prototype: a robotic arm affixed to the service trolley to sort rubbish in the aisle, followed by a brief phase using millimetre-wave sensors. What survived is a portable tool with a camera, used offline, at a slightly tilted angle, and an app that goes along with it as the tracking intelligence. “I wouldn’t say it was a very mechanical or very clever method,” he says. “It was simply a product of experimentation.”

But the moment the device is placed into the hands of a flight attendant, everything changes. Abstract design instantly gives way to real-world stakes. With the tracking system at work, the captured data is the true asset. Cheng’s long-term play is to leverage anonymised consumption trends, such as overall meal popularity, to help airlines stock in-flight meals with greater precision. Cabin service has “optimised so many steps, but nobody has asked whether you actually like chicken”, he says. Sustainable waste reduction, as he sees it, is a consequence of understanding preferences. “In one sentence: it is a data-driven solution.”

Cheng’s faith in data, however, does not make him an unquestioning evangelist for AI. He uses it regularly, but warily, treating its results as something to test rather than accept. “You can’t take it at face value,” he says. For him, the real question is not whether a technology is clever, but whether it is useful to the person who has to live with it. An airline’s head office may love a new tool that fulfils an environmental, social and governance mandate, but a flight attendant asked to host it on their service trolley might feel differently about its practical uses within already limited space.

For him, doing good means remaining invisible. “Truly good tech is when the user doesn’t even realise it’s there,” he says. “Ideally, zero user friction.”

Cheng is expected to graduate in 2027, and is mapping out a career in IT and AI while continuing to work on the start-up. As an AIA Scholar, he has access to events that AIA hosts across the year, and has volunteered at wheelchair-cleaning sessions and the annual AIA Community Day, held at the Central Harbourfront, that brings together hundreds of children from underprivileged families. He moves fast in his motorised wheelchair; the kids like to run after him. Cheng appreciates these opportunities as motivation to socialise and connect with the community. Receiving financial support through the AIA Scholarships programme for his undergraduate degree has also allowed him to channel other funds towards upgrading his wheelchair and improving his quality of life.

At home, his room is filled with Snorlax plush toys because, he jokes, the Pokemon looks like him. While the comparison is playful, it’s not entirely misplaced. Snorlax is known for its ability to take hits and remain in the game. Cheng, too, absorbs the friction of a world not entirely built for him, but doesn’t allow it to define his limits. Unlike his cuddly Pokemon counterpart, however, his analytical mind never idles – it is always focused on finding the problem, taking it apart and trying and trying again.

item.title: [SCMP] Xi projects confidence in National Day speech, with rallying call for economic growth
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping projected a message of confidence about the country’s ability to overcome challenges during his annual National Day address, issuing a rallying call for robust economic growth and more certainty amid geopolitical complications.

Xi’s address, delivered at a state reception in Beijing on Wednesday evening to mark the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic, was his first to the nation following his state visit to the US last week. It came weeks ahead of a key Communist Party conclave next month.

In a resolute tone projecting confidence about the nation’s growth trajectory despite a complex global environment, Xi’s speech included a forceful push for economic resilience and stability.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese President Xi Jinping projected a message of confidence about the country’s ability to overcome challenges during his annual National Day address, issuing a rallying call for robust economic growth and more certainty amid geopolitical complications.

Xi’s address, delivered at a state reception in Beijing on Wednesday evening to mark the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic, was his first to the nation following his state visit to the US last week. It came weeks ahead of a key Communist Party conclave next month.

In a resolute tone projecting confidence about the nation’s growth trajectory despite a complex global environment, Xi’s speech included a forceful push for economic resilience and stability.

“We are extremely proud of the world-renowned achievements of New China and full of confidence in the bright future of Chinese-style modernisation,” he said, according to state news agency Xinhua.

Noting that this year marked the beginning of the 15th five-year plan, which covers 2026-2030 and is crucial for cementing China’s footing in the global tech race and advanced industrial chain, Xi called for steady approaches to “reform and opening up” while striking a balance between growth and national security.

“Our country’s economy has forged ahead under pressure, shifting towards new drivers and higher quality, and demonstrating strong resilience and vitality,” he said.

Acknowledging China was facing “a complex and intricate domestic and international landscape”, he ordered the Chinese government to “strive to meet the year’s targets and tasks”, and ensure a strong start for the five-year plan.

He also pledged to “unswervingly” implement the “one country, two systems” principle and better support Hong Kong and Macau in integrating into China’s overall national development and long-term stability and prosperity.

On cross-strait relations, the Chinese leader maintained a tough line. Xi reiterated Beijing’s pledge to “resolutely combat ‘Taiwan independence’ separatist forces” and to “oppose interference by external forces”.

But he also explicitly called for efforts to “promote the peaceful development of cross-strait relations and advance the great cause of national reunification”. This specific phrasing was not part of his National Day address last year, when cross-strait tensions were high.

Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary, and considers it the core of its core interests. Most countries, including the US, do not acknowledge the self-ruled island as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is legally committed to supplying it with arms.

The fifth plenary session of the party’s 20th Central Committee will be held from October 26 to 29. It is the most important gathering ahead of next autumn’s national party congress, a five-yearly event marked by top-level reshuffles. The party is also gearing up for a seamless leadership transition next year.

At the fifth plenum, officials will discuss and approve a draft policy decision by the Central Committee to strengthen party governance and discipline. Consultations on the document have already been held, and it will be submitted to the Central Committee for final deliberation and approval, according to a Politburo meeting held last week.

At the reception, Xi also said China would continue to adhere to an independent foreign policy of peace to “inject greater certainty and positive energy into an uncertain and turbulent world”, according to Xinhua.

The recent warming of US-China ties, marked by Xi’s state visit and commitments for two more summits this year, has injected renewed certainty into what had been a deeply strained relationship. The two leaders will meet again at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen in November and the Group of 20 (G20) meeting in Miami in December.

“Chinese and American leaders meeting four times within a year is unprecedented in the history of US-China engagement,” said Xin Qiang, deputy director of the Centre for American Studies at Fudan University.

“Although the two powers have conflicting interests and structural frictions, they remain willing to meet and talk, seeking ways to manage their ties,” Xin said.

He suggested the detente could provide Beijing with a strategic window from late this year to early next year if ties remained calm.

Yet cordiality should not obscure the fundamental reality: competition in key areas such as artificial intelligence (AI) remains intense. US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he did not want to work with China to address AI risks, adding that cooperation might undermine America’s lead in the field.

Beijing, on the other hand, has unveiled detailed innovation action plans for the next five years, emphasising frontier areas such as AI, the life sciences and biotechnology, controlled nuclear fusion and talent training.

China’s economy is also at a critical point. Amid an intensified push for tech and innovation, Beijing faces domestic pressure to step up job creation, especially for young people, and incentivise investment and consumption.

Marking a shift in its assessment of the country’s economic performance, Beijing on Monday acknowledged emerging challenges in the economy and signalled that more policies were in the pipeline to revive faltering growth.

This was quickly followed by new supportive measures on Tuesday from the Chinese central bank and Ministry of Finance, including a new subsidy for the interest on home mortgages.

“Persistently weak domestic demand has this year been aggravated by the energy-supply shock from the Iran conflict,” said Gavekal Dragonomics in a research note on Wednesday.

“The artificial intelligence boom is lifting China’s exports, but there has not been much spillover into stronger domestic investment or consumption.”

Concluding his address with a sweeping declaration on the country’s trajectory, Xi proclaimed that the great rejuvenation of China was “unstoppable”.

“After a long period of exploration and practice, the socialist system with Chinese characteristics has demonstrated tremendous advantages, and the modernisation of our country’s governance system and capacity has continuously improved,” he said, according to Xinhua.

He urged the nation to “firm up our confidence, lock on to our goals and move forward steadily step by step” to realise China’s success.

Xi and other party and state leaders attended a ceremony to present flowers to fallen national heroes at Tiananmen Square in Beijing on Wednesday morning, marking Martyrs’ Day, which commemorates those who gave their lives for national independence and prosperity.

item.title: [SCMP] Border mine blasts show why both Koreas urgently need to restore communication
item.description:
The two Koreas urgently need to restore military communication to prevent a landmine dispute in the demilitarised zone (DMZ) from escalating into an armed clash, according to observers.

The danger is growing as North Korea presses ahead with leader Kim Jong-un’s order to fortify its side of the 4km (2.5 mile) wide buffer zone separating it from the South.

South Korea views the works, including the laying of mines near the sparsely marked Military Demarcation Line (MDL) running through the centre of the DMZ, as a violation of the 1953 Korean war armistice agreement.
item.content:encoded:
The two Koreas urgently need to restore military communication to prevent a landmine dispute in the demilitarised zone (DMZ) from escalating into an armed clash, according to observers.

The danger is growing as North Korea presses ahead with leader Kim Jong-un’s order to fortify its side of the 4km (2.5 mile) wide buffer zone separating it from the South.

South Korea views the works, including the laying of mines near the sparsely marked Military Demarcation Line (MDL) running through the centre of the DMZ, as a violation of the 1953 Korean war armistice agreement.

Last Monday, two South Korean soldiers clearing routes south of the MDL to monitor North Korean activities were wounded when two anti personnel mines exploded.

“With the risk of an accidental clash growing, Seoul should strongly urge Pyongyang to reactivate emergency military communication channels to prevent further escalation,” said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies.

“Seoul should actively make the proposal and maintain pressure regardless of whether North Korea accepts it.”

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff on Wednesday urged North Korea to apologise and halt its border fortification work, warning that Pyongyang would otherwise be held responsible for all the consequences.

A team from South Korea and the US-led United Nations Command (UNC) concluded its investigations on Tuesday. It found three North Korean mines south of the MDL, including the two that injured the soldiers last week.

“Based on the findings of the investigation, UNC determined that an armistice agreement violation occurred,” it said in a statement.

North Korea flatly denied responsibility, accusing Seoul of fabricating the findings and warning of “immediate and merciless” retaliation if its troops came under fire.

Kim Yo-jong, the North Korean leader’s powerful sister, said in a statement on Wednesday that “the armed gangsters” of South Korea were shifting the blame to the North to justify future provocative actions.

She insisted that North Korean soldiers had “never crossed the border”, while accusing the South’s military of threatening them with warning broadcasts and gunfire.

Pyongyang is building what it describes as an impregnable “permanent” southern border, including erecting barriers, laying mines and blocking roads along the DMZ.

North Korean troops involved in the project have repeatedly crossed the MDL, said Oh Gyeong-seob, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification.

“This fuels concerns that even a simple exchange of warning shots in the border area could escalate into a conflict involving tactical weapons, albeit a localised one,” Lim said.

Building justification

North Korea’s actions suggest it intends to build a justification for retaliatory strikes, according to experts.

“It needs to portray South Korean warning shots or the findings of the mine investigation as interference with the construction project and an infringement of its sovereignty, while laying the groundwork for retaliation in the event of an exchange of fire,” Lim said.

Last week’s explosions recalled a similar incident in August 2015, when two South Korean soldiers on a routine patrol inside the DMZ were severely wounded by landmines.

In response, Seoul resumed anti-Pyongyang propaganda broadcasts through loudspeakers along the border for the first time in years. High-level talks eventually led to North Korea expressing regret over the incident, defusing the crisis.

This time, however, the chances of Pyongyang accepting responsibility were slim, Oh said, noting that in 2015 South Korea had presented compelling evidence – including footage showing North Korean soldiers laying mines south of the MDL.

“North Korea’s statement is intended to deter the South from taking military countermeasures as it continues with the border fortification work,” he said. “To prevent further escalation and an exchange of fire, the two sides should reopen communication channels for talks.”

Inter-Korean military communication channels were effectively severed in 2023, when North Korea began ignoring routine daily hotline calls. Pyongyang has since defined inter-Korean relations as those between two hostile states, rather than between two halves of a divided nation awaiting reunification.

Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies, said Kim’s swift statement, issued before the South Korean and UNC investigation had reached its final conclusion, appeared intended to “contain the fallout” from the incident.

It was also intended to pre-empt any resumption of psychological warfare operations by South Korea, including loudspeaker broadcasts along the border, Yang said.

Such broadcasts pose a challenge to Pyongyang’s efforts to prevent outside information from reaching its troops and undermining frontline morale.

South Korea’s opposition People Power Party has urged President Lee Jae Myung’s government to resume the broadcasts, even as Lee pursues dialogue and exchanges with the North despite Pyongyang’s refusal to engage.

North Korea appeared to view what it called a “staged incident” as Seoul’s attempt to “build a justification for military action against the North”, Yang said.

Pyongyang has cited South Korean warning broadcasts and shots since August as evidence of harassment of North Korean troops and alleged incursions across the border.

“By defining the incident as a deliberately planned ‘staged operation’, North Korea is rejecting a 2015-style approach to resolving the issue,” Yang said. “This suggests a rejection of subsequent procedures such as fact-finding, determining responsibility and demanding an apology.”

Heightened tensions along the DMZ and other border areas could also be intended to put pressure on Washington ahead of possible North Korea-US talks, he said.

Hong Min, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification, said North Korea appeared concerned about the possibility of personnel involved in the project being fired on, potentially forcing work to be suspended.

Kim’s intervention at such a high level, rather than a rebuttal issued through military channels, reflected Pyongyang’s confidence amid strengthened ties with Russia and China, as well as advances in its nuclear arsenal and modernisation of its conventional forces, Hong said.

“However, Pyongyang remains wary of a rapid escalation before the border fortification project is completed and ahead of possible talks with Washington.”

item.title: [SCMP] EU weighs sweeping new trade powers against China before make-or-break October
item.description:
Brussels and Berlin are steeling themselves for a make-or-break October with China, as the mood towards Beijing hardens in both capitals.

The month ahead could help set the course of the increasingly thorny EU-China relationship for years to come, as Europe gears up to present a slew of new tools for countering Beijing’s trade practices, likely to come in December.

Before then, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic travels to Beijing on October 8 and 9 for crucial meetings with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. These will assess how much progress has been made in rebalancing trade ties since the last showdown in June.
item.content:encoded:
Brussels and Berlin are steeling themselves for a make-or-break October with China, as the mood towards Beijing hardens in both capitals.

The month ahead could help set the course of the increasingly thorny EU-China relationship for years to come, as Europe gears up to present a slew of new tools for countering Beijing’s trade practices, likely to come in December.

Before then, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic travels to Beijing on October 8 and 9 for crucial meetings with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. These will assess how much progress has been made in rebalancing trade ties since the last showdown in June.

The European Commission is pushing China to set voluntary export limits on products such as plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, sales of which have soared in tandem with a downturn in Europe’s own automotive fortunes.

The bloc wants to put the brakes on a surge of Chinese imports that, combined with sluggish EU exports to China, have extended a gaping trade deficit.

Officials said talks had been progressing surprisingly well, and there might well be some deliverables from next week’s meetings. Nonetheless, Beijing has publicly rebuked any suggestion that it would curb its shipments.

These meetings will inform the agenda of an EU national leaders’ summit in Brussels the following week. The European Commission will present the outcome of its China negotiations and expects to receive the green light to propose new weapons in early-December.

Official and diplomatic sources say China is not expected to be named in the customary written conclusions of the European Council summit, as the bloc hopes to maintain diplomatic decorum with Beijing and draw less retribution.

However, multiple sources said that firm action was now expected this year, regardless of the outcome of next week’s meeting in Beijing.

“Nothing is going to happen in the meeting next week that prevents this train from leaving the station,” one official source said.

In her state of the EU speech this month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen asserted that while “some say the second China shock is looming … it’s already here”.

Fears abound that unfair Chinese trading practices are contributing to a deindustrialisation of Europe’s manufacturing heartland, including in Germany but also spreading through central and eastern Europe.

In recent weeks, Berlin has come closer to the long-standing view in Brussels and Paris that the trading situation is unsustainable and that something has to change.

“There is a sense of emergency … Germany has changed dramatically. There is this total destruction of employment, of factories. There is a lot of stress,” a diplomatic source said.

Among the planned tools are a diversification instrument that would oblige firms in critical sectors to have at least three suppliers spread across several countries, and a solidarity fund to compensate companies hit by retaliation from China or any other trading partner.

Speculation has been mounting in recent days that a third weapon is also in the works, one which could give broad tariffing powers to the European Commission, akin to those used by the US government through its Section 301 tool.

Various reports have described a commission-controlled emergency trade power that could rapidly restrict Chinese imports when dependency or overcapacity crosses a systemic threshold, without waiting for traditional product-by-product investigations or a positive vote from member states.

Two newsletters, Dossier Bruselas and Watching China in Europe, reported that a joint paper on China from France and Germany would propose achieving this through reworking the dormant anti-coercion instrument, which would provide broad retaliatory powers but have a high bar to be activated.

Diplomatic sources confirmed that the paper will be presented to the European Commission before the European Council summit.

“It is basically finalised … the instrument that we are calling for would allow us to cut China off from the European market within 24 hours,” one official was quoted as saying in the Watching China in Europe newsletter, written by analyst Noah Barkin.

A new 301-like tool would “risk weaponising trade policy”, the China Chamber of Commerce to the EU said in a statement on Wednesday.

“European industry has also experienced the negative impact of similar unilateral trade measures. International trade instruments should not become subject to a ‘race to the bottom’, nor should unilateral measures replace multilateral rules,” the chamber said, urging the EU to avoid “beggar thy neighbour approaches”.

In recent weeks, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz under huge pressure from the electoral gains of the far-right Alternative for Germany, Berlin appears to have shifted decisively on China.

Previously the main proponent of engagement, it is now signalling support for protectionist measures.

On Tuesday, the German government notified the European Commission of tighter telecoms security and certification rules aimed at further restricting certain vendors’ access to German networks.

Huawei Technologies is not named, but the Chinese company is widely understood to be the main target.

Some of the country’s major business lobby groups have come out in favour of a more protectionist trade stance towards Beijing, including those that have previously warned against action.

In a policy paper last week, the Federation of German Industries (BDI) – which has previously backed harsher policies on China – warned that the cost of doing nothing would outweigh that of any Chinese retaliation.

“Even if de-risking entails costs, including in the form of counter-reactions, passivity would in the long term be economically considerably more costly and irresponsible from a security policy perspective,” the BDI wrote.

While the group said it favoured WTO-compatible solutions, it also signalled that some flexibility might be required.

“Given the critical situation, particularly China’s state-induced massive overcapacities … WTO-compatible temporary defensive measures sometimes take effect too late or are insufficient,” it wrote.

“The advantages and disadvantages of possible instruments such as local-content requirements, tariff-rate quotas, sector-wide or even general tariffs must be carefully examined and weighed against each other.”

In contrast to the BDI, the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA) has been a strong opponent of defensive trade action against China, with its views proving influential across the German government. Now, however, it appears to have had a change of heart.

According to German business daily Handelsblatt, an internal VDA note said “imbalances have arisen in trade with China in recent years” and that “trade defence instruments” could be used “from a certain point of distortion of competition”, for example in cases of “proven unfair practices”.

“Germany, which has long been known for its opposition to a hardening of trade policy towards China, is beginning to shift its stance,” wrote Pascal Canfin, the European Parliament trade committee’s lead rapporteur on China, in an article for Le Grand Continent, a French magazine.

“The Germany that blocked tariffs on electric vehicles in 2024 is different from the Germany that is today open to discussions, alongside France, on how to respond to China’s aggressive industrial policy.”

item.title: [SCMP] Gaza on stage: concert activism meets Malaysia, Singapore red lines
item.description:
American rapper Macklemore lost his spot on British pop star Ed Sheeran’s US tour after speaking up for Palestinians, but in Malaysia it was Sheeran’s music which ended up being pulled from the airwaves.

In neighbouring Singapore, British band Massive Attack faced a different kind of fallout, barred from returning after members displayed a Palestinian flag during a July concert.

The contrasting cases highlight the competing pressures on foreign artists in Southeast Asia, where political expression can cross different red lines set by governments, promoters, venues and audiences, analysts and industry figures say.
item.content:encoded:
American rapper Macklemore lost his spot on British pop star Ed Sheeran’s US tour after speaking up for Palestinians, but in Malaysia it was Sheeran’s music which ended up being pulled from the airwaves.

In neighbouring Singapore, British band Massive Attack faced a different kind of fallout, barred from returning after members displayed a Palestinian flag during a July concert.

The contrasting cases highlight the competing pressures on foreign artists in Southeast Asia, where political expression can cross different red lines set by governments, promoters, venues and audiences, analysts and industry figures say.

In Malaysia, where public support for the Palestinian cause runs deep, promoters must still weigh an artist’s politics against commercial considerations and concert rules. Singapore, meanwhile, draws a sharper line between humanitarian expression and what it considers political advocacy.

The disputes come amid demands for musicians to speak out against Israel’s actions in Gaza. A UN commission of inquiry concluded last year that Israel had committed genocide, a finding Israel rejected.

Macklemore’s removal from Sheeran’s tour after declaring “Free Palestine” at a New Jersey concert this month prompted other supporting acts to quit. Promoter Messina Touring Group said stadium owners would not accept him on the bill, while stadium owner Robert Kraft cited allegations of antisemitic rhetoric, which the rapper rejected.

On September 15, Sheeran said the decision to remove Macklemore was the promoter’s, after venues on the tour threatened to pull their shows if the rapper remained.

Three days later, Malaysian radio station Fly FM pulled Sheeran’s songs, declaring that “some things matter more than music”.

Sheeran apologised for his handling of the dispute at a Philadelphia concert the following day, calling the situation in Gaza “catastrophic and unjustifiable”.

The pressures on foreign artists in Malaysia extend beyond the airwaves. Foreign acts must also comply with concert rules, leaving promoters to balance an artist’s political stance with commercial considerations and authorities’ requirements.

Rohit Rampal, founder and CEO of Malaysian concert organiser Hitman Group, said an artist’s political stance would not automatically rule out a booking, but ticket demand was only part of the decision.

“Their public perception, suitability for the Malaysian market, and brand all come into play,” he told This Week in Asia. “A decision that’s considered acceptable or necessary in another market may be perceived very differently in Malaysia.”

Asked how he would respond if an overseas partner wanted a pro-Palestinian performer dropped, Rampal said he would raise the prospect of a Malaysian backlash and explore alternatives.

“International tours involve many stakeholders, and not every decision is ultimately within the control of the local promoter,” he said.

Stage directions

In Singapore, two members of Massive Attack received stern police warnings after displaying the Palestinian flag at their July 29 concert, with one shouting “Free Palestine”. Both were banned from re-entering the country, and authorities said future applications for the band to perform would not be accepted.

Abraham Vergis, managing director of Providence Law Asia, said Macklemore’s actions could be considered political advocacy in Singapore and invite a similar reaction from authorities.

“At the very least, I would expect a police investigation and some difficulty getting approval to perform here again,” he said.

The purpose of an artist’s intervention mattered, Vergis said. “Expressing sorrow for those caught in a war, or calling for peace, is unlikely to trouble anyone. Leading a crowd in political slogans or waving a flag on stage is different, because that is asking the audience to take a side in a foreign conflict.”

Singapore does not allow the open display of foreign flags, national emblems or banners without a permit.

Tan Kiat How, senior minister of state for digital development and information, said earlier this month that while Singapore did not prohibit artists from “expressing concern” for those affected by global conflicts, the city state “should not be used by foreigners as a platform to further political causes, including those relating to conflicts or political issues overseas”.

Sociologist Tan Ern Ser said most Singaporeans probably opposed mixing politics and entertainment, although some welcomed artists speaking about causes they supported.

“While I don’t think there is any serious polarisation in Singapore, there would be some who are fine with, even encouraging of, having an entertainer with a message on Palestine and Gaza,” he said.

Concert conditions

In Malaysia, American gospel singer Israel Houghton’s proposed October appearances in Sabah state have drawn objections over his support for Israel.

Sabah Police Commissioner Jauteh Dikun said on Monday that police would advise postponement if a formal application were submitted, state news agency Bernama reported. None had reached the state government despite publicity advertising the shows.

Houghton had expressed support for Israel in a social media post on October 8, 2023, according to Bernama. Checks by This Week in Asia found the post was no longer available.

Foreign performances require approval through the Unit for Application for Foreign Filming and Performance by Foreign Artiste, known as Puspal. Organisers must also be able to halt shows that breach conditions.

The “kill switch” measure followed British band The 1975’s performance at the Good Vibes Festival in 2023, when frontman Matty Healy criticised Malaysia’s anti-gay laws and kissed a male bandmate, prompting authorities to cancel the rest of the festival.

Later that year, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim defended Coldplay against calls to cancel its Kuala Lumpur concert, citing the band’s support for Palestinians, while organisers agreed to a kill switch.

Korean-American singer Eric Nam cancelled a planned Kuala Lumpur show in 2023, citing threats after liking a post about the Israel-Gaza war. Bruno Mars performed there in 2024 despite Muslim student activists’ objections over his previous concerts in Israel.

Benjamin Loh, a communication and media studies lecturer at Monash University Malaysia, said authorities would be mindful of protecting the country’s standing as a concert destination even when public pressure mounted.

“Musicians are bound by their popularity, and any hit to their reputation will directly impact their income,” he said.

A Pew Research Centre survey published in June found that 89 per cent of Malaysians and 86 per cent of Indonesians viewed Israel unfavourably.

Musicians from both countries have used their work to raise money for Palestinians. Cholil Mahmud, vocalist of Indonesian band Efek Rumah Kaca, and Malaysian artists Noh Salleh and Kayda collaborated on Our Power, released in July with royalties pledged to Palestinian aid.

“We hope this song encourages people in Indonesia and Malaysia, and their governments, to care more about this issue,” Cholil told Indonesian outlet Medcom.

Malaysian singer-songwriter Azmyl Yunor, who also lectures at Sunway University, said treating Palestinian solidarity as an unwelcome intrusion of politics missed the depth of support for the cause at home.

“It’s beyond politics – it’s about being human,” he told This Week in Asia. “The Malaysian public, from what I’ve observed, has a clearer and broader understanding of the issue, albeit with some confirmation bias based on your own personal beliefs and faiths.”

While commercial pressure still discouraged mainstream musicians from speaking out, “pop artists who have a broader potential to influence their audiences can do more”, Azmyl said.

item.title: [SCMP] Slow is beautiful: China launches war against AI drama, goes beyond algorithms
item.description:
China’s broadcasting regulator has called for greater support for live-action dramas as the government seeks to steer the booming microdrama industry towards higher-quality production and tighter rights safeguards amid the rapid rise of AI.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has created innovation and production possibilities for microdramas, while also posing challenges over content quality and rights protection, according to Wang Xiaoliang from the National Radio and Television Administration.

“Faced with this new challenge … our position is very clear. Live-action dramas are the mainstay of high-quality production and should be strongly supported,” said Wang, who heads the department overseeing online audiovisual content.
item.content:encoded:
China’s broadcasting regulator has called for greater support for live-action dramas as the government seeks to steer the booming microdrama industry towards higher-quality production and tighter rights safeguards amid the rapid rise of AI.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has created innovation and production possibilities for microdramas, while also posing challenges over content quality and rights protection, according to Wang Xiaoliang from the National Radio and Television Administration.

“Faced with this new challenge … our position is very clear. Live-action dramas are the mainstay of high-quality production and should be strongly supported,” said Wang, who heads the department overseeing online audiovisual content.

AI has rapidly expanded the scale and efficiency of microdrama production in China while intensifying concerns over copyright and the mounting pressure on human creators.

Wang’s remarks, made at a press conference on September 17, follow a proliferation of formulaic and derivative content as producers race to churn out more dramas in pursuit of hits and profits.

The scale of the shift is striking. Around 430,000 microdramas were released in China in the first eight months of 2026 – as much as 13 times the figure for the whole of last year – with AI dramas accounting for more than 90 per cent of new releases, Wang said.

According to Wang, the regulator will step up its initiative to promote and distribute high-quality microdramas, guiding platforms to create dedicated sections for live-action dramas while providing financial support so that quality productions can find audiences and generate returns.

Microdramas or duanju, meaning short or mini dramas, have exploded in popularity in China in recent years.

Built for mobile screens and short attention spans, the fast-paced, scripted and often melodramatic shows are divided into dozens of episodes, usually in a vertical format, with each lasting just a few minutes.

AI is moving beyond a supporting tool and into almost every stage of production – from story adaptation and scriptwriting to character and scene generation, and onwards to post-production – upending an industry that supports more than 2 million jobs nationwide.

The change has spawned a new format known as AI microdramas – AI-generated animation and live action-style dramas featuring lifelike digital characters that reduce the need for conventional filming.

Companies can now churn out AI-generated content at a pace that was previously impossible, lowering production costs and technical barriers while allowing producers to test more titles in the hope of finding hits.

Johnny Chan, a senior lecturer in information systems at the University of Auckland in New Zealand, said microdrama platforms created a self-reinforcing cycle: the more you watch, the better the algorithm learns what keeps you hooked.

Creators keep refining the cliffhangers and paywalls that work, while the platforms invest more money to make the experience even stickier, he wrote in a paper published in August by the journal Systems Research and Behavioural Science.

Chan wrote that while people would usually get bored eventually by the formula, the ability of AI to rapidly generate endless fresh stories and variations meant the natural “boredom brake” might never fully kick in, causing viewers to keep scrolling for longer.

According to data from the China Netcasting Services Association, more than 275,000 AI microdramas were released online in the first half of 2026, an average of about 1,500 each day.

The explosion in numbers has created a broader regulatory challenge for Chinese authorities: how to encourage this form of cultural production while preventing speed, scale and platform-driven consumption from coming at the expense of quality, originality and rights.

The expanded use of the technology has given rise to various types of regulatory abuse, including content plagiarism and repackaging, as well as AI face-swapping and voice cloning, along with copyright infringement involving online literature.

Many high-profile actors and the general public alike have accused AI microdrama producers of using their likenesses without consent.

The speed at which AI is reshaping the industry has also exposed a growing gap between production capacity and the quality and originality of what gets made.

In the first half of 2026, only 0.48 per cent of new AI microdramas released on the social media platform Douyin surpassed 100 million views, according to industry data provider DataEye.

Lydia Chen, a 30-year-old AI microdrama writer and director producing live action-style dramas for overseas audiences, said the industry’s rush for hits had made copying almost routine.

Platforms and production companies often copied each other’s hits and were used to taking dramas that had already gone viral in China, tweaking the plot and transplanting the story to a foreign setting, she said.

For example, a Chinese tale of a ba zong – internet slang for a bossy president or a powerful, domineering businessman – and a female lead from the countryside can be repackaged as a New York billionaire falling for a woman from rural America.

“You can see the productions becoming increasingly like internet products,” said Chen, who worries that as real-world filming declines, the craft itself will stagnate while AI models will have fewer new examples of real filmmaking to learn from.

“If everyone keeps copying past hits, where will the new ideas of the future come from?”

Chen also noted that some storylines adapted for overseas audiences reproduced traditional and conservative Chinese cultural attitudes towards gender, relationships and family – as they catered to the tastes of the mass-market microdrama audience.

She pointed to the plotline of a “bossy president” falling for a rural woman whose virginity is portrayed as part of her appeal, along with plots idealising women as stay-at-home mothers with multiple children.

“Sometimes I wonder whether this is really the kind of culture we should be exporting,” she said. “To me, some of these ideas feel quite outdated.”

Beijing has responded to the challenges by tightening oversight of both the content and the systems through which it reaches audiences.

The National Radio and Television Administration launched a two-month campaign in June targeting “harmful, lowbrow and pirated” microdrama content.

The campaign focused on material harmful to children as well as sexually suggestive scenes, wealth-flaunting, “distorted” views on marriage and relationships, along with superstitions, violent revenge, sensationalist titles and copyright violations.

Everyone was working themselves to the limit just to … make money.

Shiliu, microdrama director

Wang told the press conference that since the beginning of the year, regulators had removed 68,000 microdramas that violated the rules and guided platforms to punish more than 1,200 accounts.

More than 90 per cent of the problematic content involved AI dramas, he said.

The government has also introduced rules specifically addressing the use of AI in production.

The microdrama development and management measures, which took effect on September 1, require clear labelling for every episode of AI-generated microdramas, along with “respect for original works, copyright protection, fair competition and more orderly industry development”.

Platforms must also regularly review and assess their recommendation algorithms, models and data, give priority to high-quality microdramas and prohibit suggestions that are designed to encourage user indulgence or excessive consumption.

The pressure is also being felt by people working inside the industry, with microdrama actors facing a harsh reality.

Since the beginning of the year, many have said they are struggling to find roles, with some actors taking on part-time work as AI-generated dramas increasingly replace live-action productions.

For those still working in AI microdrama production, greater efficiency has not necessarily meant an easier workload.

Shiliu, a 28-year-old AI microdrama director who joined the industry 2 ½ years ago, said his team was expected to complete five dramas a month, each running for 50 to 70 episodes.

As the team shrank, he found himself taking on multiple roles and working 14 to 16 hours a day, said Shiliu, who asked not to be identified by his real name.

“Because AI is so convenient, bosses only focus on efficiency,” he added. “Everyone was working themselves to the limit just to [fulfil demand] and make money.” The workload eventually took its toll, prompting him to quit the industry.

The state-run Economic Daily urged the industry last month to move away from scale-driven growth in favour of higher quality, more original and professionally produced content.

Familiar formulas were being repeatedly recycled while a flood of lookalike content competed for limited attention, the paper said in an article published on August 13.

“Promotion and computing costs rise, leaving producers caught in a cycle of producing more without earning more,” it noted. “Audiences’ willingness to pay is further eroded while the industry’s reputation is bound to suffer.”

DataEye estimates that the overseas market for Chinese microdramas will exceed US$6 billion in 2026, with AI-generated animated and live-action style dramas accounting for more than US$4 billion.

The netcasting services association said that China’s AI microdrama industry was reaching a turning point, shifting from rapid, loosely regulated expansion towards more disciplined and quality-driven growth.

In Chen’s view, as AI lowers the technical barriers to content creation and more people without a professional background are able to turn their ideas into original works, individually created non-formulaic projects will have a better chance of standing out.

“We must strike a balance between encouraging innovation and upholding safeguards,” Wang said.

“Ultimately, AI is a tool, while people remain the creators. The faster AI dramas develop, the more important it is to ensure content quality.”

item.title: [SCMP] How Hong Kong firms are future-proofing business in challenging times
item.description:
Hong Kong’s economic transformation is at a critical juncture, and the private sector must adapt along with it, as Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has noted. In the first of a two-part series, Ambrose Li and Wynna Wong examine the forces driving change among established enterprises.

Before visiting a vendor in mainland China’s Jiangsu province, a salesman from Hong Kong bottling giant Swire Coca-Cola can now use a mobile phone to see which drinks customers in the neighbourhood are most likely to buy.

The recommendations, generated by artificial intelligence (AI) and based on factors such as the area’s consumer profiles, turn information held across the firm’s operations into what Swire Coca-Cola calls “suggested orders”.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong’s economic transformation is at a critical juncture, and the private sector must adapt along with it, as Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has noted. In the first of a two-part series, Ambrose Li and Wynna Wong examine the forces driving change among established enterprises.

Before visiting a vendor in mainland China’s Jiangsu province, a salesman from Hong Kong bottling giant Swire Coca-Cola can now use a mobile phone to see which drinks customers in the neighbourhood are most likely to buy.

The recommendations, generated by artificial intelligence (AI) and based on factors such as the area’s consumer profiles, turn information held across the firm’s operations into what Swire Coca-Cola calls “suggested orders”.

Swire Coca-Cola’s mainland plants are also using AI-powered robots that can make decisions and adapt to changing operating conditions as they pick and sort heavy, shrink-wrapped loads of drinks from pallets at high speed – a breakthrough in the labour-intensive industry.

These were some of the cutting-edge technologies Swire Coca-Cola had piloted on the mainland to transform its business, while looking to scale them to other provinces and even to Southeast Asia through and in Hong Kong, chief executive Karen So told the South China Morning Post.

“Due to our geographic coverage, we’re exposed to many geopolitical risk factors which we have to manage,” So said, adding that one of the most obvious recent impacts had been rising raw material costs, including those of aluminium and sugar.

“We have to stay very vigilant. Overall, we’ve had to make sure our brand and operations stay relevant in the past few decades to mitigate our external risks,” she said.

The company, which started business in 1965, is now the fifth-largest Coca-Cola bottling partner in the world.

As Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan sets out the blueprint for the city’s economic upgrade, businesses like Swire Coca-Cola are working to future-proof themselves against geopolitical headwinds and compete in an increasingly challenging environment.

City leader John Lee Ka-chiu last week urged Hongkongers and businesses to adopt a long-term vision, saying enterprises had to stay competitive even as the government rolled out measures to cultivate new growth drivers for the city.

“While the government works hard, business operators need to think of ways themselves because, after all, this is a highly competitive society,” he said.

An uneven economic recovery

Hong Kong’s economy has powered ahead in recent months, with merchandise exports hitting record highs on the back of overseas demand for AI-related products.

The government has consequently upgraded its 2026 full-year economic forecast to 3.5 per cent to 4.5 per cent, from an earlier projection of 2.5 per cent to 3.5 per cent.

Despite the stronger overall performance, streets are dotted with shuttered shops while retailers and restaurant operators continue to struggle.

In a high-profile warning, real estate advocacy group Momentum 107 said the sharp decline in shop values in recent years had rapidly eroded the pool of available capital, undermining confidence in investment and consumption.

It noted that shop prices had fallen by more than 40 per cent from their 2018 peak, while the overall vacancy rate had reached a 40-year high of 12.5 per cent in late 2025.

The retail and food and catering sectors have also been hit by the continuing trend of Hongkongers crossing the border to spend their leisure time and money.

Meanwhile, inflation has been on the rise.

After war broke out in the Middle East on February 28 and triggered a global oil crisis, the city’s inflation rate jumped from 1.1 per cent year on year in January to 1.7 per cent in February and has hovered above 1.7 per cent as of August.

‘Companies are forced to change’

Vera Yuen Wing-han, a lecturer in economics at the University of Hong Kong, noted that looking solely at struggling high-street shops overlooked the bigger picture, as high-value sectors such as professional services and finance continued to drive the economy.

However, consumer-facing sectors are undergoing structural shifts as mainland competitors catch up and local consumers spend more elsewhere.

“Hong Kong’s local consumption market is relatively small, so retail and catering suffer from northbound spending and changing habits,” Yuen said.

“Conversely, high-end services, technology and finance are holding up strong. But across the board, businesses rely heavily on international trade and foreign clients, leaving them exposed to global geopolitical frictions.”

Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of Our Hong Kong Foundation think tank and executive director of its Public Policy Institute, said companies faced three main challenges – high operating costs, disruption to global supply chains and geopolitical risks and barriers to technological transformation caused by shortages of funding and skilled workers.

He said Hong Kong’s rents, wages and logistics costs were relatively high, placing pressure on companies’ cash flow, while AI was creating another divide.

Large corporations often had money to invest but struggled to integrate new technology with legacy systems and secure cooperation across departments. While smaller businesses could be more agile, they frequently lacked capital and technical expertise.

Shui cited a Productivity Council survey suggesting about 90 per cent of responding companies intended to increase their use of AI.

The problem, he said, was not a lack of interest but uncertainty over how to turn that intention into practical transformation.

“Many people think of technology or AI as something that can help companies reduce costs and save money,” he said.

“But what is more important is how they can use AI to upgrade and transform themselves, innovate their business models or open up new markets.”

Hong Kong appeared to be performing relatively well in adoption.

Shui cited a survey by Hong Kong University of Science and Technology that found that about 72 to 73 per cent of respondents used AI at work daily or weekly, compared with a global average of around 30 per cent.

Another study put AI adoption among Hong Kong firms at about 41 per cent compared with less than 30 per cent in Singapore, he said.

But widespread use did not mean that companies were applying the technology effectively.

Shui said the ideal outcome was “human-machine collaboration,” in which AI performed repetitive research, data processing and preliminary analysis, while employees devoted more time to decision-making and setting the company’s direction.

“If your competitor is already doing this while you are making very limited use of AI, it will be very difficult to catch up,” he said. “This is something that many companies and employees will need to learn.”

Yuen echoed this view, saying that true AI adoption required a complete overhaul of corporate workflows rather than superficial daily tasks.

“The real productivity boost from AI isn’t just using it to write an email or draft a report – it comes when companies reshape their entire workflow from top to bottom,” Yuen said, comparing the current transition with earlier technological shifts such as the invention of the printing press, personal computers and the internet.

“Legacy businesses face a dilemma because changing established processes while serving existing clients carries risk. It could take eight to 10 years for industries to truly integrate AI into their bottom line,” she added.

Shui said Hong Kong needed a coherent AI development blueprint and stronger cooperation between the government, universities and industry.

The planned Hong Kong Artificial Intelligence Research and Development Institute could provide a platform through which companies test applications, academics provide expertise and the government coordinates resources.

Transform, transform and transform

In Swire Coca-Cola’s case, So said transformation was robust across mindsets, strategies and business practices, pointing out that the 61-year-old business had in recent years embarked on a sweeping revolution.

“The future of our business lies in moving from reactive, manual operations towards proactive, data-driven ecosystems that respond to modern consumer habits,” she said.

The company’s “suggested order” system in Jiangsu province produced 20 per cent higher monthly sales volumes during a year-long pilot that ended earlier this year.

She said it would be gradually rolled out to other markets, but conceded that it would take time for staff to get used to the AI tool.

“Our employees need time to adapt to tools designed to change how they make decisions and approach customers,” So said.

The project forms a key part of a transformation at Swire Coca-Cola, whose franchise bottling and distribution operations reach more than 940 million consumers across the western United States, 11 mainland Chinese provinces and Shanghai, Hong Kong, Taiwan and four Southeast Asian countries.

The company’s transformation became more complicated as it expanded beyond its two main markets – Greater China and the US – into Southeast Asia.

It acquired Coca-Cola bottling businesses in Cambodia in 2022, in Vietnam in 2023 and in Thailand and Laos the following year.

“When we acquired businesses from local operators of Coca-Cola in Southeast Asia, they had their respective enterprise resource planning systems,” So said. “We faced a challenge but also an opportunity to form a consistent operating system.”

Even basic data definitions varied among markets, including what constituted a home market sales channel and how revenue was calculated.

The company had to clean up and standardise the information before it could perform reliable analysis to improve the decision-making process and help salespeople make more targeted calls.

“The data alignment will take two to three years,” So said.

Another tool transferred from the mainland to Southeast Asia was the smart cooler – a drinks refrigerator which customers unlock using an electronic payment code.

Scales and cameras identify which drinks are removed and customers are charged accordingly.

“The solution adapts technology and operating concepts proven in mainland China to the Hong Kong market, which combines digital payment and product-recognition capabilities to offer a seamless cashless purchasing experience,” So said.

In Hong Kong, the group has deployed 120 coolers across a broad mix of locations including sports and entertainment venues, workplaces, residential communities, educational institutions and industrial settings.

So said the company aimed to replace traditional vending machines with these smart coolers.

Swire Coca-Cola’s regional expansion has also helped Chinese suppliers go global.

Baosteel, China’s biggest listed steelmaker and a supplier of aluminium cans to Swire Coca-Cola on the mainland, established a factory in Ho Chi Minh City as the company expanded its presence there.

“It is a win-win situation – we have a stable supply of aluminium cans while Baosteel expands out of China for the first time,” So said.

“Hong Kong is where our ambition is set and our global system is run. A purpose-built solution developed in the Chinese mainland, and now ready to scale across the global markets we serve, shows the super value-added, superconnector role Hong Kong is positioned to play.”

Shui said Hong Kong could also turn the technological rivalry between China and the West into an opportunity by developing a “dual-model” environment in which businesses could access systems from both sides.

“Hong Kong has always been a bridge connecting mainland China with the rest of the world,” he said. “If both systems can be used here, companies coming to Hong Kong can choose the tools that best meet their needs or potentially use both.”

To raise efficiency and reduce manpower, Swire Coca-Cola has teamed up with a Hangzhou-based tech company, Seth Robotics, to develop its own AI-powered solution for its bottling plant in Zhengzhou, Henan province.

The plants boasts the world’s first AI-powered intelligent picking-and-sorting robot, according to So.

Capable of picking 600 pallets of drinks an hour with 100 per cent accuracy in executing orders, and handling loads as heavy as 40kg, the robot works at twice the speed of manual labour.

“Normally after the first hour of work, workers need to take a rest. The robotic deployment will enhance efficiency and minimise any work-related injuries of workers, too,” So said.

She added that Swire Coca-Cola’s technology development also showed what a Hong Kong-headquartered company could contribute to embodied intelligence.

Against the backdrop of these operational investments, the group reported solid financial results for the first half of the year – net profit rose 5.35 per cent to HK$846 million (US$107.9 million) while revenue increased 8.36 per cent to HK$23.3 billion, compared with the same period last year.

Yet, as economist Vera Yuen noted, the rising cost of uncertainty left businesses with little choice but to adapt their models or risk falling behind.

Ultimately, she said, the question was no longer simply whether companies adopted new technology, but whether they could restructure their core operations to deliver genuine value to consumers.

item.title: [SCMP] Paul French lifts veil on final months of China’s last emperor in the Forbidden City
item.description:
On a recent afternoon, Paul French – British author, broadcaster, blogger but definitely not, as he always stresses, an academic – is explaining his technique.

“My trick, which I suppose is reasonably successful, is to try and write Chinese history linked to a genre that lots and lots of people read, [because] there’s that many people” – his finger and thumb indicate a space so narrow you’d hardly be able to pass a sliver of paper between them – “who read books on China. And there’s this many people” – his hands convey near-ceiling height – “who’ll read about true crime or gangsters or royalty.”

Such an approach has, indeed, made him reasonably, and internationally, successful. In 2011, he published Midnight in Peking: How the Murder of a Young Englishwoman Haunted the Last Days of Old China, which made it onto the New York Times’ bestseller list, won both the 2013 Edgar Award for “Best Fact Crime” in the United States and Britain’s Crime Writers’ Association’s “ALCS Gold Dagger for Non-Fiction”, and was named “International Success of the Year” at the 2012 Australian Book Industry Awards.
item.content:encoded:
On a recent afternoon, Paul French – British author, broadcaster, blogger but definitely not, as he always stresses, an academic – is explaining his technique.

“My trick, which I suppose is reasonably successful, is to try and write Chinese history linked to a genre that lots and lots of people read, [because] there’s that many people” – his finger and thumb indicate a space so narrow you’d hardly be able to pass a sliver of paper between them – “who read books on China. And there’s this many people” – his hands convey near-ceiling height – “who’ll read about true crime or gangsters or royalty.”

Such an approach has, indeed, made him reasonably, and internationally, successful. In 2011, he published Midnight in Peking: How the Murder of a Young Englishwoman Haunted the Last Days of Old China, which made it onto the New York Times’ bestseller list, won both the 2013 Edgar Award for “Best Fact Crime” in the United States and Britain’s Crime Writers’ Association’s “ALCS Gold Dagger for Non-Fiction”, and was named “International Success of the Year” at the 2012 Australian Book Industry Awards.

In 2018, his City of Devils: A Shanghai Noir was a Kirkus Reviews’ “Best Book of the Year”. In 2024, Her Lotus Year: China, The Roaring Twenties and the Making of Wallis Simpson received much coverage and quotably upbeat reviews (“Her Lotus Year stays in the mind as a bright, shining, lively snapshot,” says The Spectator. “Delightful to read.”).

Now, it’s the turn of Puyi in The Last Emperor of China: Twilight of the Forbidden City, which falls into a royalty subgenre that French calls “doomed monarchy”.

Although he’s writing – primarily – for a Western audience, as a category, it has promising global reach.
