Earlier this year, French was told by his Chinese publisher that only one other foreigner has shifted (and signed) more books in China: British author and historian Simon Sebag Montefiore, whose 2016 work on those quintessential doomed monarchs, The Romanovs: 1613-1918, was a massive hit.

Puyi, of course, didn’t meet his doom with an execution in a cellar. He was six years old in 1912, when the Manchu empire ended and the new Republican government decided to leave him behind the walls of the Forbidden City – an oddity, roaming around the “Great Within”, attended by eunuchs (“teapots without spouts” was the local term). With his peculiar upbringing and background, that child would grow into the adult who, during the second Sino-Japanese war (1937-1945), would become his country’s “Great Traitor”.

French, who was a language student in 1980s Beijing and lived in Shanghai for many years before returning to Britain in 2014, had been marinating this story for a while. He sensed that – “a bit like Wallis Simpson”, the American socialite whose relationship with Britain’s King Edward VIII led to his abdication – people sort of knew about Puyi but not really. He’d been struck by the blank stares he met when he mentioned him to Chinese-language students at a couple of British universities.

French realised that it’s been almost four decades since he, along with many others, had been “blown away” by the Bernardo Bertolucci epic, The Last Emperor (1987), which was – an amazing achievement – filmed inside the Forbidden City.

While he was wondering how to tackle the topic, he wrote an article about Puyi’s wife, Wanrong, in 2024, for this magazine. “Wanrong is so beautiful and there are so many pictures of her and I thought it would be fun,” he says. “I did mention, in a couple of lines, that she’d had a tutor and this was one of the things the film had missed.”

In fact, Joan Chen – who played Wanrong in the film – makes a single reference to her tutor as a “Miss Windsor”. Bertolucci, who co-wrote the screenplay with his brother-in-law, Mark Peploe, knew Wanrong was educated but not by whom, so they made up a name with British royal resonance. Wanrong’s tutor, however, was not British. Isabel Ingram was an American “mishkid” – a child of missionaries – born in Peking (Beijing) in 1902 and educated at Wellesley College, in Massachusetts, in the US.

After the PostMag piece came out, French was contacted by a man called Kenneth Mayer, who told him he was Ingram’s grandson. “He said, ‘Thank you so much for noticing Isabel; no one else does,’” French recalls. “And then he said, ‘By the way, you really should read her diary and she has some letters from this Johnston guy …’”

French was staggered. He hadn’t known about the diary, and the “Johnston guy” was Reginald Johnston, Puyi’s Scottish tutor, played in the film by Peter O’Toole.

Johnston had written a memoir which, in its 486 pages, makes a single reference to “the Empress’s American friend who had been her teacher of English both before and after the Empress entered the Forbidden City as a bride”; and his letters and journals had been destroyed after his death in Edinburgh, in 1938.

Diary! Letters! Such finds are history’s gold dust. Even better, Ingram, who died in Virginia in 1988, had typed up all of it. (French, who revels in his North London unacademic blokeishness, makes some cheerfully unrepeatable comments about the trials of handwritten research materials.) Once he’d read the Ingram documents, he knew he had his book. Ingram was 20 when she became Wanrong’s tutor, in October 1922. A few months later, on December 1, Wanrong, aged 16, married Puyi, also 16.

French decided to focus The Last Emperor of China on the 23 months between that five-day wedding – “the last burst of imperial pageantry Peking would ever see”, he writes – and the couple’s expulsion into the “Great Without” on November 5, 1924, which brought an end to more than 500 years of (occasionally interrupted) dynastic occupation of the Forbidden City.

Apart from sporadic chunks of necessary context, the book is like a wonderfully evocative play with four principal performers – a middle-aged Scottish man, a young American woman and two teenage Manchu royals – on a spectacular stage.

French says he’s only too aware that he joins a long line of Puyi biographers, but what Ingram brings to his version is the voice of modernity. Formal lessons with Wanrong, who had a golden fountain-pen and silver inkwell, rarely took up more than an hour or two. Afterwards, there would be hair-braiding, hat-selecting, wardrobe-rummaging, dancing to gramophone records, chocolates and cigarettes.

Ingram’s language – “I love her for life”; “cute little thing”; “the Empress is still darling”; “he nearly died on the spot” – could be that of a Californian blogger, and the film these scenes evoke isn’t the Bertolucci drama; it’s Clueless, in every sense. Her diary also testifies to Puyi and Wanrong’s genuine friendship as they go cycling and kite-flying and dog-walking around their vast, mouldering compound. Many happy photographs are taken.

For French, Ingram is an important witness to the growing intimacy between the newlyweds. As he says, a great debate among biographers concerns Puyi’s sexuality and whether he was asexual or homosexual. Famously, on his wedding night, the last emperor had sloped off to the Hall of Mental Cultivation for a think.

“He’s 16!” says French, and goes on to note that “the single most surprising thing [in the diary] is when Isabel writes about ‘the curtain being drawn’ and there are no lessons today … Obviously, like all young people, they work out what goes where”.

But Puyi and Wanrong’s isn’t the only unexpected romance in the book. It becomes clear through his letters that Johnston, 28 years older than Ingram, is attracted to her. French believes he was “heartbroken” when she refused him, which is why her name was never mentioned in his memoir. Perhaps. (On the other hand, this reader thinks it was more about Johnston’s considerable, publicity-hogging ego.)

At any rate, Johnston’s letters to Ingram veer in tone from housekeeper (“I am sorry to hear chewing gum has been introduced into the palace”) to stalker (“Who is the young man you kept looking at so earnestly all the time?”). Eventually, he becomes self-deludingly creepy. “Did you explain to the Lockharts how and why you refused to let me kiss you when we were on the Emperor’s swing together?” he writes. “And yet it would only have been a remote, innocuous fatherly salutation!”

By then, the quartet had broken up. On November 5, 1924, several hours after the early-morning palace coup, Ingram was taken by rickshaw to the Forbidden City as usual, but was barred from entering. At the Gate of Divine Prowess, the commandant told her that Wanrong had gone into the “Great Without” “hatless, coatless, baggage-less”. Ingram, who would leave China in 1927, never saw her dressing-up companion again.

In the Bertolucci film, when soldiers arrive to evict Puyi and Wanrong, they are playing tennis. In real life, he was peeling her an apple, that ancient symbol of expulsion, in the Palace of Gathered Elegance. Soldiers took a – distinctly unhappy – photo, which is in the book, of his abandoned bedroom: an adolescent muddle of kung fu novels and toys.

“Once they go outside the gilded cage, they’re lost,” says French. “You could write another book about Puyi in Manchuria and try and get into the psychology of what happened to that relationship when he’s manipulated, with no advisers, and she knows that they’ve made a horrendous mistake and slips into opium abuse.”

In this immensely readable book, however, French steps only briefly beyond the palace gates and into that future when Puyi was crowned the emperor of Japan’s puppet state, Manchukuo, in 1934 – another doomed monarchy.

Another sombre note is the contrast between Ingram’s spirited diary and the fate suffered by Wanrong in the final summary, which is heart-wrenching.

Puyi survived and, in the 60s, made several return visits to the Forbidden City. Premier Zhou Enlai liked to keep an eye on him.

Asked what he thinks of Puyi now, French replies, “I do take the Zhou Enlai line. He’s supposed to have invited Puyi to a lunch and told him, ‘You weren’t to blame for becoming emperor and what happened then. But you can be blamed for what happened after.’”

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore jails man for slapping preschooler at bus stop over rude gesture
item.description:
A man became angry after a four-year-old boy pointed his middle finger at him while he was picking up his son from preschool in Singapore.

He pursued the boy to a nearby bus stop that was crowded with other young kids, grabbed the boy by the arm and slapped him hard on both cheeks.

The boy, who was his son’s schoolmate, suffered bruises on his face and ringing in his ear, on top of emotional trauma that lingered for months and required his parents to change his preschool.
item.content:encoded:
A man became angry after a four-year-old boy pointed his middle finger at him while he was picking up his son from preschool in Singapore.

He pursued the boy to a nearby bus stop that was crowded with other young kids, grabbed the boy by the arm and slapped him hard on both cheeks.

The boy, who was his son’s schoolmate, suffered bruises on his face and ringing in his ear, on top of emotional trauma that lingered for months and required his parents to change his preschool.

The aggressor, Muhammad Firdhaus Mokhtar, was sentenced to 14 weeks’ jail on Wednesday. He was also ordered to pay S$170 (US$133) in compensation to the mother of the victim, who was in court to watch his sentencing.

Firdhaus pleaded guilty to one count each of voluntarily causing hurt and using criminal force on a minor, with a third charge taken into consideration.

At about noon on March 6 this year, Firdhaus went to his son’s preschool to pick the boy up. The name of the preschool was redacted in accordance with the gag order, which prevents the publishing of anything that can identify the victim.

Firdhaus’ son was playing with the victim when the victim pointed his middle finger at Firdhaus.

Firdhaus was angered and called the boy to come over but the boy ignored him and skipped towards his domestic helper.

The helper was at a bus stop outside the school where other preschool children, including the victim’s friends, were waiting.

Firdhaus followed the boy to the bus stop and grabbed him by the arm.

When the boy tried to break free, Firdhaus told the helper to tell his parents not to let him point his middle finger at others and threatened to slap him.

The boy tried to hide behind a pillar, but Firdhaus pulled him out by his collar and slapped him on the right cheek with the back of his hand.

He then slapped the boy’s left cheek and ear with such force that the child fell to the ground.

When the helper tried to help the boy up and pull him away, Firdhaus kept his grip on the boy’s arm.

He shoved a finger in the boy’s face, threatening to break his finger and shouting that he would return for him on Monday.

Firdhaus then swung the boy backwards, causing him to stumble backwards before leaving.

The assault was witnessed by members of the public at the bus stop, including several preschool children and captured on police camera footage.

The helper brought the crying boy home, where his mother noticed redness around his ears, cheeks and jaw.

At the hospital, he was found to have bruises on both cheeks and was discharged with a five-day course of paracetamol for pain relief. The hospital lodged a police report.

Shaken by the assault, the boy wept twice in his sleep that night and did not dare to attend school for the next few days.

In the months after the assault, he asked his mother anxiously whether the next day was Monday and whether he had to go to school.

He feared going to school because “I am scared the uncle will slap me hard again”.

His parents eventually transferred him to another school.

But he continued to have flashbacks of the assault and cried for prolonged periods. He also continues to have nightmares of the assault to this day.

Deputy public prosecutor Etsuko Lim sought four to six months’ jail, listing multiple aggravating factors including the sustained aggression and the viciousness of the slaps.

She said Firdhaus was brazen, slapping the child in broad daylight at a crowded bus stop, alarming and shocking bystanders.

The assault was also “deeply scarring” on the young victim, who would have taken the threat to break his finger seriously since he had also made good on the threat to slap him.

Firdhaus was represented by Daryl Lim from the Public Defender’s Office, who said there was no version of events that day that was “acceptable by any means”.

“A young child was hurt both physically and emotionally, and my client does own that fully,” he said.

The mother of the victim was in court with family members.

She told the court that although her son was recovering, he was not “recovering fully” as he still has nightmares. His confidence level has also gone down, she said.

“I must say that I’m very perturbed with this incident,” said the woman while Firdhaus stood stiffly in the dock.

“We had to engage in a lot of activities to keep him occupied to gain his confidence back again, to assure him that things are as normal,” she said.

“It also perturbs me to the fact that, now, it puts the puzzle into the picture on why my son has been asking [about] Monday,” the boy’s mother said.

“Because I’ve never known from him that he actually was being threatened to [have his finger broken] or [that the accused would] see him on the following Monday.”

She said she did not want to prolong her son’s distress, especially since the other child involved was his classmate and had been in the same class as her son since play group.

“As [his] mother, I felt that we want to have a closure for him,” the woman said. “And we also hope that the accused will acknowledge the harm that he caused and apologise to [my son].”

She said that while an apology cannot undo what happened or restore her son’s sense of safety, it is important to the family.

Firdhaus then apologised to the victim’s family in court.

“To the victim’s family and everybody in the court, I wish to sincerely apologise for the actions that I did, and I hope you really forgive me and also give me a chance to be a better man in the future,” he said.

The victim’s mother also asked to see the footage of the assault, but was told to ask the investigating officer.

District Judge Koo Zhi Xuan said inflicting such raw violence on a young victim was “a vile and intolerable act”.

“Such violence would not have been morally justified, had the accused committed the same acts against his own children at home, let alone a child he was not even acquainted with in a public and crowded setting where other children were present,” he said.

He agreed with the prosecution on several of the aggravating factors, saying the emotional turmoil suffered by the victim and his family was “particularly weighty”.

Firdhaus asked to defer his jail term until November 13, as his wife, who was also in court, is 23 weeks’ pregnant.

His lawyer said the couple have a hospital appointment on November 12, as the fetus remains in a breech position. They will obtain advice on whether that will necessitate an earlier delivery.

The judge noted that granting the request may lead to further applications for deferment, such as if Firdhaus’ wife requires surgery.

However, he granted the application when Firdhaus gave his word that he would surrender on November 13, and not seek further deferments.

The judge allowed the victim’s family to leave the courtroom first before allowing Firdhaus and his wife to leave.

For voluntarily causing hurt to a minor, he could have been jailed for up to six years, fined up to S$10,000, or both.

For using criminal force on a minor, he could have been jailed for up to six months, fined up to S$3,000, or both.

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] Can pay-as-you-earn funding fix Southeast Asia’s higher education debt problem?
item.description:
A Singapore-based education financing programme is testing whether income-linked funding can widen access to higher education without an unmanageable debt burden, a model analysts say could help ease repayment pressure faced by graduates across Southeast Asia.

Global Financing for Education’s (GFE) Pay It Forward scheme, publicly launched in September, provides students with funding for their education in return for 3 to 10 per cent of their subsequent income for one to 10 years.

The income-linked repayments graduates make to GFE are typically capped at twice the original funding amount.
item.content:encoded:
A Singapore-based education financing programme is testing whether income-linked funding can widen access to higher education without an unmanageable debt burden, a model analysts say could help ease repayment pressure faced by graduates across Southeast Asia.

Global Financing for Education’s (GFE) Pay It Forward scheme, publicly launched in September, provides students with funding for their education in return for 3 to 10 per cent of their subsequent income for one to 10 years.

The income-linked repayments graduates make to GFE are typically capped at twice the original funding amount.

The arrangement shifts the risk of weak employment or low earnings from students to the financing pool. But economists say its private-sector structure raises questions about selection criteria and whether students pursuing lower-earning careers could ultimately be excluded.

GFE founder Mario Ferro said the programme had already disbursed about US$25,000 among 11 students since May, while the total amount requested by students was more than US$3 million. Eight of the initial recipients are studying abroad, five of them in Thailand.

Ferro cited the case of one student who received US$5,000 for graduate studies in Singapore and agreed to contribute 10 per cent of income for three years, totalling US$3,600 by the end of the period.

“If the agreed term expires before contributions total US$5,000, the graduate does not owe the difference,” Ferro said, noting that the funding pool absorbed any shortfall while higher earners might contribute more up to the capped amount.

Selecting for outcomes

Ferro said GFE considered financial need alongside the field of study, institution and likely employment outcomes, as the objective was to fund “a credible path into work”.

Despite traditionally modest earnings in nursing, GFE was running an outreach drive for nursing training, Ferro said. This aimed “to support the growth of a profession that is in high demand given the current demographics and [offers] a solid career outcome”, he explained.

Bruce Chapman, the Australian economist who designed his country’s income-contingent student loan system, said public and private providers handled earnings risk differently. “The government pools the risk. [The] private sector wants a return on every person.”

Governments could verify earnings through national tax and payroll systems, but student loan providers from the private sector face an incentive to select applicants who are most likely to generate financial returns, according to Chapman.

While private income-linked contracts could help cash-strapped students, they could not finance higher education universally, as applicants pursuing lower-earning professions might be excluded, Chapman said.

“It can never be a general solution to finance the system,” he added.

Ferro said GFE required graduates to document earnings using payslips, employment records or bank statements.

While there was no fixed income threshold that automatically suspended contributions, graduates experiencing hardship could receive a temporary pause, extension or restructuring for repayments.

Chapman expressed reservations about case-by-case verification, saying hardship provisions depended on reliable income checks.

“They’ve got to set up an administrative system which verifies whether people are really in financial trouble,” Chapman said.

Filling the ‘missing middle’

Such trade-offs play out differently in countries where public help targets the poorest students but leaves middle-income households struggling to cover the full cost of higher education.

In Indonesia, economist Elza Elmira said income-linked finance could reach households that were too affluent for the government’s KIP Kuliah help programme but were unable to afford tuition and living expenses.

“An income-contingent model could reach the ‘missing middle’ that KIP Kuliah does not cover,” Elmira said. “Because repayments rise and fall with earnings, it lowers the risk of default.”

Indonesia’s KIP Kuliah provides tuition and living allowances for students with academic potential but limited financial means, with priority given in 2026 to those from the bottom 40 per cent of household incomes.

Elmira said an income-linked model could help incentivise both students and institutions amid ongoing debate over Indonesia’s large number of higher education institutions and their variable quality. Under such a system, students would evaluate course choices based on expected future earnings, while institutions would be forced to compete to attract more students.

However, Elmira warned that this could inadvertently favour stronger applicants, high-earning fields such as medicine and engineering and top public universities in Java.

“That has the risk of reinforcing regional and institutional inequalities in Indonesia,” Elmira said.

To prevent financing from concentrating in top-tier programmes, Elmira suggested that the government should take part as a lender or guarantor, restrict eligibility to accredited programmes and subsidise priority fields with lower expected financial returns.

“Fair terms should also include an earnings threshold, payments below 15 per cent of income, automatic suspension during unemployment, debt cancellation after a fixed period, death or permanent disability and regulatory oversight,” she said.

Public alternatives

In Malaysia, economist Geoffrey Williams said GFE resembled a privately administered graduate tax but was too small to replace a national student financing system.

“It is a nice scheme but is limited to a handful of people,” Williams said. “A private scheme would be difficult to scale up to hundreds of thousands of people burdened with PTPTN in Malaysia,” Williams said, referring to the country’s National Higher Education Fund Corporation.

PTPTN receives about 3 billion ringgit (US$735 million) annually through borrower repayments and government-backed bonds to support around 600,000 continuing and new students – equivalent to roughly 0.9 per cent of Malaysia’s 2026 operating expenditure.

Williams said GFE could serve as a model for reforming PTPTN by replacing traditional loans with government funding recovered through taxation.

Under this proposal, graduates earning more than 5,000 ringgit monthly could pay an additional 1 to 2 per cent in tax, while workers in socially necessary, lower-paid fields could be exempt.

“Those in higher-paid jobs pay more, even under a fixed-rate tax, because they are benefiting more,” Williams said.

He argued the best way would be to end PTPTN’s loan disbursement model entirely and transition to direct state funding.

He added that private education loans in Malaysia had limited take-up because students could draw on PTPTN or their Employees Provident Fund savings, making private financing more relevant for professional courses and overseas studies.

In the Philippines, students rely mainly on direct public support. Its Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education programme covers tuition and fees at state universities, complemented by the Tertiary Education Subsidy for priority students.

A supplementary government student loan programme offers short-term financing, but generally requires repayment within 12 months alongside a co-signer, who is equally and immediately liable for the debt. Unlike GFE, it does not link payments to subsequent earnings, leaving borrowers to absorb the financial risk if employment or income falls short.

According to Chapman, these models differ in who bears the financial burden when graduates earn too little: the borrower, the provider or the state.

“It’s the ones who don’t get it [financing] that the issues are about,” Chapman said.

item.title: [SCMP] Sell family jewels for latest iPhone? In India, craze dials up debate
item.description:
Tens of thousands of people thronged Apple stores in India this month to snap up the newest iPhone models – the 18 Pro and Pro Max – but the frenzy has kicked off public debate in the country about affordability and consumer debt.

The iPhone 18 Pro starts at 164,900 rupees (US$1,700) and goes up to 179,000 rupees, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at 179,900 rupees and maxes out at 329,900 rupees.

Apple also unveiled the iPhone Duo, its first-ever folding smartphone, essentially setting a new price benchmark with the top-end variant at 449,000 rupees (US$4,700), breaching the psychological threshold of 400,000 rupees for the first time in the Indian market.
item.content:encoded:
Tens of thousands of people thronged Apple stores in India this month to snap up the newest iPhone models – the 18 Pro and Pro Max – but the frenzy has kicked off public debate in the country about affordability and consumer debt.

The iPhone 18 Pro starts at 164,900 rupees (US$1,700) and goes up to 179,000 rupees, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at 179,900 rupees and maxes out at 329,900 rupees.

Apple also unveiled the iPhone Duo, its first-ever folding smartphone, essentially setting a new price benchmark with the top-end variant at 449,000 rupees (US$4,700), breaching the psychological threshold of 400,000 rupees for the first time in the Indian market.

The excitement among consumers – with some standing in line for hours – underscored how India, the world’s second largest smartphone market by volume, has emerged as one of the fastest growing sales sources for Apple.

There are no official sales figures for iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max yet, said Navkender Singh, an India-based analyst for IDC.

Pre-orders for the Duo will start on October 16 and Singh forecast that it would sell well in India despite its price tag. “It is a huge signal of wealth and affluence,” he said, pointing to what he called the “brand halo” of the tech giant.

The model was priced high because it was not being locally produced and was a luxury or aspirational product, he said. “It will tell the world that you have arrived – that you are rich enough to buy such an iPhone.”

Interest in the luxury devices has prompted scrutiny on social media over how young Indians with moderate incomes are increasingly relying on long-term, zero-cost monthly instalments to normalise spending beyond their means.

A man from New Delhi went viral on Monday after saying he had sold jewellery he inherited from his great-grandmother and grandmother to buy his wife an iPhone 18 Pro. In the interview outside an Apple Store in Noida, where he was queuing, he said he did it because he believed in enjoying life.

Social media users have also circulated memes juxtaposing the cost of an iPhone Duo against major financial milestones such as buying a car.

“An iPhone Duo top variant in India is priced around [450,000 rupees]. Just to put this into perspective, for this much amount, you can: fund a foreign family trip; front-load your Systematic Investment Plans which will give you 11-12 per cent returns; a couple of years of kids school fees; 30 grams (1oz) of gold; upgrade your house with four to five good quality white goods; house rental for a year in Tier 2 cities,” Kapil Vats Prince posted.

Another user, Aakash Yadav, pointed out that unless an individual earned at least an annual salary of 13 million rupees (US$135,400), buying the created a “substantially larger labour burden than it does for the average US worker”.

Price difference

Some questioned what the price disparity between the phones sold in India and those in the United States. An iPhone 18 Pro sells for between US$1,199 and US$2,399 in the US.

IDC’s Singh said part of the reason was India’s 18 per cent goods and services tax. Prices in the US do not show taxes, which vary from state to state in the country.

Also, a Duo is likely to cost about 70,000-80,000 rupees more in India than in the US because it is imported as a fully built unit, according to Singh.

Apple’s average selling price for phones had stayed above US$800, while India's overall smartphone average price sat between US$150 and US$250, Singh said. “That gap is the clearest evidence of Apple’s pull in India.”

And yet, despite the gripes about price, sales of iPhones keep growing, reflecting their utility. “This is one of the most important things we use every day,” Singh said. “We may forget our hankies or sunglasses when leaving our house but we can never forget our phones. It is part of our personality now.”

The price difference was part of the criticism against the phone’s affordability, said Samit Sinha, founder of Delhi-based Alchemist Brand Consulting. “It is causing more heartaches than the absolute price.”

India is Apple’s second-largest production base for iPhones globally, ranked only after China, but that does not automatically mean more competitive pricing in the Indian market, according to Sinha.

Given the size of the Indian market – estimated at 1.5 billion consumers – widely divergent reactions are likely. Buyers were those who had been iPhone users or had aspired to one for a long time, while critics were likely to be those who had not been users, he said.

The top 5 per cent who could afford the luxury gadget still amounted to around 75 million people. “That is a pretty large market and that is where luxury brands operate,” he said.

‘Emotional aspect’

The desire for the latest iPhone did not have to make sense, Sinha said. “Frankly, I don’t think an iPhone or any Apple product is bought strictly for rational reasons. There is certainly an emotional aspect to it. You sort of resonate with your own self-image.”

The affordability debate came into stark focus last month after a teenager who reportedly bought an expensive iPhone but was unable to afford the repayments jumped off a cliff. Both his parents, who had refused to give him the money for his repayments, followed him down the hilltop.

Apple always managed to create a sense of excitement about its products, said Lloyd Mathias, a Delhi-based angel investor and business strategist. That was why people were willing to go to great lengths to buy an iPhone.

They want the bragging rights and they tend to go to crazy extremes

Lloyd Mathias, a business strategist

“People who may be even conservative about their mode of transport are willing to strengthen their chequebook for an iPhone. They want the bragging rights and they tend to go to crazy extremes.”

India also has a large and growing market for used and refurbished iPhones – which adds longevity to the products more than in other markets, according to Mathias.

“There is always a consumer who says they want the joy of holding an Apple iPhone. India has a long track record of trading in second-hand phones. There is somebody who finds value in this.”

Some, though, said they did not get the hype. Rajender Nager, a Delhi-based real estate consultant, said he felt there was no need for anything more than an Android phone that costs under 40,000 rupees.

“That also lasts two to three years, so why should I spend so much? There is no limit to your spending if all you want is a status symbol,” he said.

Radhakrishnan Swaminathan, a recent college graduate who works as an intern at a motor and switchgear trading firm, said many of his friends were interested in getting the latest iPhone, but he was content with his iPhone 15 and a MacBook.

“I can get an iPad for 50,000 rupees and an Apple Pencil. People want to upgrade to the latest technology. What I feel is that if you are rational and you know what you want to achieve in life, you will not be blinded by luxury appeal,” he said.

“For 300,000 rupees, you can buy a car or bike.”

item.title: [SCMP] India-Europe trade corridor gets Trump’s backing, but can IMEC survive war?
item.description:
US President Donald Trump’s recent endorsement of a trade corridor connecting India to Europe via the Middle East has renewed focus on the three-year-old project, but analysts warn it must expand to withstand ongoing geopolitical conflicts.

The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) was first unveiled at the G20 summit in 2023 as an alternative to existing routes and China’s Belt and Road Initiative.

Backed by India, the United States, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Israel and the European Union, the project envisages combining shipping lanes, railways, energy pipelines and data cables into one corridor that is still largely a work in progress.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump’s recent endorsement of a trade corridor connecting India to Europe via the Middle East has renewed focus on the three-year-old project, but analysts warn it must expand to withstand ongoing geopolitical conflicts.

The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) was first unveiled at the G20 summit in 2023 as an alternative to existing routes and China’s Belt and Road Initiative.

Backed by India, the United States, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Israel and the European Union, the project envisages combining shipping lanes, railways, energy pipelines and data cables into one corridor that is still largely a work in progress.

Though some existing infrastructure can handle parts of the proposed route, key rail links, ports and other connections are still being developed.

Trump tied his support for IMEC to efforts to move Middle Eastern energy infrastructure away from vulnerable maritime routes amid the ongoing conflict with Iran.

“Iran’s terrorist attacks on commercial shipping in neighbouring countries have shown the need to shift Middle East energy infrastructure away from the Iranian checkpoints,” Trump said on September 22 at a meeting with Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

“That’s why my administration strongly supports the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor and other places of getting oil out, whether it’s pipelines or anything else,” he said, adding that “together we are on the verge of overcoming challenges that have plagued this region for a decade”.

The corridor represents a rare area of continuity between the second Trump administration and Joe Biden’s presidency, despite Trump’s backing having been erratic until recently, according to Alberto Rizzi, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations.

Trump’s recent endorsement helped build political momentum for the project, Rizzi said, even if “it is currently difficult to imagine that this political approval will translate any time soon into financial support from the US”.

He said conflict in the region had also exposed a fundamental weakness in IMEC: how resilient can a trade corridor be if its key gateways rely on the very chokepoints it was meant to bypass?

The near-total closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the Iran war was already changing the scope of the project, Rizzi said, creating an “IMEC on wheels” in which trucks crossed the Arabian deserts to transport goods to the Mediterranean.

Reliance on Omani and Emirati ports outside the strait had also grown, though this remapping had largely been spontaneous and not necessarily coordinated or interoperable, he said.

Rizzi said the crisis had added weight to the argument for turning IMEC into a network with built-in redundancies. “A single route can be disrupted easily; a network of lanes instead can deal with disruptions much better,” he said.

This weakness is clearest on IMEC’s eastern maritime leg, which connects Indian ports to UAE ports such as Jebel Ali and Khalifa before cargo travels overland through the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Jordan towards Israel and Europe.

Because UAE ports sit inside the Persian Gulf, ships arriving from India must pass through the Strait of Hormuz. At the other end, the corridor’s western gateway to the Mediterranean at Haifa in Israel is directly exposed to regional conflict.

Shanthie Mariet D’Souza, founder and president of the Mantraya Institute for Strategic Studies in Goa, said the Iran conflict had laid these weaknesses bare.

“The corridor’s design depends on ships carrying goods from India across the Arabian Sea to the UAE, and that route runs through waters where the Strait of Hormuz and the approaches to it are hostage to any escalation involving Iran,” D’Souza said.

“IMEC was conceived as a reliable alternative to the Suez route. But under the present circumstances, it can only become a corridor that swaps one chokepoint risk for another.”

The Gaza war, which erupted just weeks after IMEC’s launch, had already delayed the project amid regional tensions and logistical challenges. The Iran conflict has only added to the uncertainty.

Afaq Hussain, a non-resident senior fellow with the Project for Middle East Integration at the Atlantic Council, agreed with Rizzi that the IMEC’s geographic footprint needed to be diversified.

“It shouldn’t be a single-line corridor,” Hussain said. “Making it a network of corridors [will] be more secure and diversify risk.”

That could mean integrating ports such as Salalah in Oman, as well as routes through Egypt or Syria via Jordan, while addressing vulnerabilities at other regional chokepoints such as the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea, he said.

Samriddhi Vij, an associate fellow in the Middle East programme at the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi, called the problem IMEC’s “paradox of resilience”, adding that the crisis had validated the case for diversification while making the corridor harder to operationalise.

“Its eastern maritime architecture relies on Gulf ports inside or adjacent to Hormuz, while its western gateway around Haifa remains exposed to regional conflict,” Vij said.

“Higher war-risk insurance and geopolitical uncertainty raise the corridor’s cost of capital. The crisis has therefore made IMEC simultaneously more strategically necessary and commercially harder to implement.”

One response would be to build alternative gateways. Fujairah, on the UAE’s eastern coast outside the Strait of Hormuz, is one option. On September 20 – two days before Trump’s remarks – Etihad Rail and AD Ports launched a direct freight service connecting the Port of Fujairah with the Industrial City of Abu Dhabi.

Cargo arriving at Fujairah could now travel inland via the UAE’s national rail network, turning an outside-Hormuz gateway into an increasingly practical logistics route, said foreign affairs analyst Robinder Sachdev.

“Oman provides a second, potentially more structural option,” Sachdev said, noting that a 238km (148-mile) rail project was being built to connect the Omani city of Sohar to the UAE.

But moving the IMEC’s gateways “cannot by itself solve the geography of modern warfare”, he said. “I would call it less a redrawing of IMEC than a redesign of IMEC.”

The different components of IMEC need not follow the same geography, Sachdev said: freight could follow one alignment, while energy pipelines, electricity grids and digital cables follow others.

“The crisis has not weakened the logic of IMEC – it has weakened the logic of a single-gateway IMEC,” he added. “The next stage should transform IMEC from a corridor into a network, because a line can be broken at one point; a network can reroute.”

item.title: [SCMP] Philippine coastguard battles funding cuts amid bigger South China Sea role
item.description:
The Philippines is preparing to give its coastguard more responsibilities in the contested South China Sea even as the agency faces a more basic problem: whether it has enough ships, aircraft and personnel to carry them out.

The proposed overhaul comes as the coastguard is being stretched by increasingly demanding operations around Philippine-claimed waters, while funding constraints threaten to limit its ability to keep its existing assets at sea.

That tension is evident in the 2027 budget. The coastguard has sought funding for more vessels, unmanned systems, stations and personnel, while key allocations for patrols, intelligence and ship maintenance face cuts.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines is preparing to give its coastguard more responsibilities in the contested South China Sea even as the agency faces a more basic problem: whether it has enough ships, aircraft and personnel to carry them out.

The proposed overhaul comes as the coastguard is being stretched by increasingly demanding operations around Philippine-claimed waters, while funding constraints threaten to limit its ability to keep its existing assets at sea.

That tension is evident in the 2027 budget. The coastguard has sought funding for more vessels, unmanned systems, stations and personnel, while key allocations for patrols, intelligence and ship maintenance face cuts.

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) currently has a fleet of about 40 vessels, according to Coast Guard chief Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan, who said in June that the agency planned to add more than 40 vessels over the following five years.

But the number of vessels on the books does not necessarily reflect the number available for operations. Gavan told Senate finance committee chairman Joseph Victor Ejercito on September 18 that “it’s just a matter of time that we will run out of ships, with the cuts in the repair and maintenance budget”.

Gavan said the coastguard was “operating at almost 80 per cent to 90 per cent operational tempo”, leaving a short turnaround time between operations and overhauls. “The repair and maintenance requirement of our ships is already [at] dangerous [levels], you know. We might not be able to sustain [operations].”

The percentage Gavan cited “refers to the amount of time spent at sea”, according to Australian geopolitical analyst Dr Hunter Marston. “In that case, the vessels and service members would be at sea 80 or 90 per cent of the time and only ashore for resupplies, repairs or rest 10 to 20 per cent of the time, which is pretty high.”

In comparison, “I think the US navy aims for about 33 per cent”, Marston told This Week in Asia.

Gavan said the coastguard might also run out of planes since only one was operational while the second was under repair.

The cuts came on top of 3.3 billion pesos (US$52.7 million) in reductions for acquiring air and floating assets, which Gavan said were needed to address the shortage.

Its sea-based patrol funding under the Maritime Security Law Enforcement Programme was trimmed by 812 million pesos.

Political risk analyst Ronald Llamas told This Week in Asia the cuts were the result of “tight fiscal space” due to higher debt service and other priorities.

Independent budget specialist Zyza Suzara also said on television that “there is very little fiscal space” due to increased debt servicing, higher operational costs and the mandatory tax allotment to local governments.

Gavan warned that if the cuts took place, “we will be constrained [in our] daily operational response” and “obviously, it will have a very significant impact on our activities”.

The request for “unmanned tactical capability” consisting of surface and undersea drones was also cut by 600 million pesos, Gavan disclosed, while the agency’s intelligence funds were reduced by 150 million pesos for next year.

The PCG had also requested funds for fresh recruitment, 360 million pesos for hospital insurance for its personnel’s families and eight new coastguard stations worth 25 million pesos each, including on Palawan island and the Kalayaan Island Group in the Spratlys.

The pressure on the service could be seen in its recent encounters with Chinese vessels in the South China Sea.

On Thursday, Chinese coastguard and naval vessels intervened during a Philippine resupply mission to the grounded Philippine warship at Second Thomas Shoal, according to Manila. Beijing said its personnel were conducting lawful enforcement in response to a Philippine provocation.

On Sunday, the PCG challenged a Chinese coastguard vessel near Occidental Mindoro, while the following day a PCG aircraft tracked a Chinese research vessel near Batanes. Manila said the ships were operating within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone.

The two sides continue to dispute the legal status of the waters. China claims sovereignty over much of the South China Sea, including Second Thomas Shoal, and rejects a 2016 international arbitral ruling that found no legal basis for its claim to historic rights over resources within the sea areas covered by its nine-dash line. Beijing considers the ruling illegal and non-binding, while Manila relies on it in asserting its maritime rights.

Expanding mandate

The encounters illustrate why the coastguard’s capacity has become a strategic question for Manila. The agency is a civilian service, but it has increasingly been at the centre of the Philippines’ efforts to assert its maritime rights and maintain a presence in contested waters.

The proposed revised Coast Guard Law, which has already cleared the Senate and is moving through Congress, would formalise some of those responsibilities.

The measure seeks to address perceived gaps in the existing Republic Act 9993 by giving the agency a clearer mandate to enforce and maintain maritime security, as well as “prevent or suppress terrorism at sea”.

It would also empower the coastguard to directly “recommend” to the president regulations that would direct when and to what extent the Philippine military should extend support and assistance.

The proposed law would require a “minimum manning level” to ensure it could adequately patrol more than 36,000km of the country’s coastline.

It therefore envisages a coastguard with a broader set of responsibilities and a more clearly defined role in maritime security.

But the budget debate suggests that the more immediate question is whether the agency can maintain the capability it already has.

House deputy minority floor leader Antonio Tinio told This Week in Asia on Monday that he was unsure if any of the cuts would be restored.

As for the Senate, Ejercito promised on Sunday in an interview with radio station DZBB that he would restore some of the cuts by “realigning” funds from agencies with historically low utilisation rates of their annual budgets.

“Be reassured that we have been very consistent in supporting the coastguard,” he said. “We will find ways to ensure that we have the capability to respond. We may not be able to trade shots with China, but at least we should have a minimum credible defence posture.”

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore or bust: how Indonesian student’s crowdfunding plea shows degree of desirability
item.description:
For 28-year-old Indonesian professional Evelyn Clarissa Siregar, asking strangers to help fund her MBA in Singapore was a gamble: she knew the request was unconventional but hoped putting her dream out in public might open a door.

Instead, her appeal for more than S$100,000 (US$78,000) to fund her business programme at Singapore Management University (SMU) drew fierce online criticism, with some labelling her entitled and questioning her plans.

“I never expected the backlash to become this big,” Siregar told This Week in Asia, saying she felt “overwhelmed” by the response.
item.content:encoded:
For 28-year-old Indonesian professional Evelyn Clarissa Siregar, asking strangers to help fund her MBA in Singapore was a gamble: she knew the request was unconventional but hoped putting her dream out in public might open a door.

Instead, her appeal for more than S$100,000 (US$78,000) to fund her business programme at Singapore Management University (SMU) drew fierce online criticism, with some labelling her entitled and questioning her plans.

“I never expected the backlash to become this big,” Siregar told This Week in Asia, saying she felt “overwhelmed” by the response.

“Once I finally had the capacity to face everything again, I went back and read all [their] comments and responses. One by one. I cringed, feeling uncomfortable.”

But Siregar said the experience had not changed her desire to study in Singapore. The city state continues to attract Indonesians with its high-ranking universities, proximity and reputation – even though the cost can put a degree there beyond many students’ reach.

“Singapore is a small country, but it’s packed with experts in finance, business and science,” said Siregar, who works as a sales manager at an internet services provider in Jakarta. “Everything feels within reach. That’s what really attracts me to Singapore.”

On September 16, Siregar was accepted into SMU’s MBA programme, which will start in January and require S$82,480 in tuition. She secured a S$3,000 Asean student discount but that was “far from enough”, she said.

The price tag is particularly stark for an Indonesian student. SMU’s S$82,480 tuition works out to about 1.15 billion rupiah. By comparison, the School of Business and Management at Indonesia’s well-regarded Institut Teknologi Bandung lists total tuition of 99.15 million rupiah for its General Management MBA.

Siregar said she had applied for three scholarships but secured only one. She also tried to apply for a job in Singapore, but nothing panned out. “In my [MBA] application, I’ve stated that I wouldn’t rely on my parents financially and that I would rely heavily on scholarships and internships or part-time work,” she said.

Three days after receiving her acceptance, she published a pitch on Instagram asking internet users to fund her study and living expenses, which she estimated would cost “S$2,000-S$2,500 per month, for 10-15 months”. Siregar wrote that she would pay back her investors with her “skills and experiences”.

“I’ve always believed in negotiation. If someone says no, I don’t necessarily take it as the end,” she said.

Her pitch ultimately brought no sponsors, but it did bring a barrage of criticism, as commenters questioned her credentials and the feasibility of her plan.

“As someone who invests in a lot of business, you are all talk. There is no fixed guarantee if you can replace the capital I spent … you are just a kid with entitled behaviour. No numbers, no return on investment. We all have dreams; know the boundaries if you can’t afford it,” one social media user said.

“Why not come to Singapore, work for a few years, and earn enough to go for a master’s? Isn’t that probably a better approach? That’s what most locals here do instead of asking for a donation based on a pitch with zero return,” another said.

Sought-after destination

Singapore’s appeal to Siregar lies not just in its universities but in the access she believes studying there could provide. That aspiration is shared by other Indonesian students, although their routes can look very different.

Tri Maira Pangestuti, who graduated in August from a master’s programme in environmental management at the National University of Singapore (NUS), received an Indonesian government scholarship in 2022 as her mother is a farmer raising three children on her own in a village in Central Java.

She was also accepted into a master’s programme in Sydney, but chose NUS because “it was ranked the eighth best university in the world at that time”, she said.

Studying at NUS yielded professional benefits, from acquiring practical skills closely tied to industrial needs, such as conducting environmental risk assessments for international supply chains, to receiving strong backing from her academic advisers for her PhD applications, the 28-year-old said.

“I really want to be a professor at NUS. I’m currently applying for a PhD at Stanford University and the University of Helsinki in Finland. I don’t know which university will accept me, but I plan to return to Singapore as an assistant professor after receiving my PhD,” Tri said.

Tri, who uses a prosthetic as her left eye is blind, said she also appreciated how NUS accommodated her disability – for example, by giving her an additional 25 minutes during exams.

“In Indonesia, I attended public schools from kindergarten to undergraduate, never a school specifically for children with disabilities. In ninth grade, my gym teacher held back my report card because I couldn’t swim. The gym teacher didn’t provide any learning adjustments,” Tri said.

NUS ranks third as the foreign university destination for Indonesian students, Kompass newspaper reported in May 2024. As of 2022, there are 2,282 NUS alumni from Indonesia, 769 of whom graduated from the business studies programme.

Sulfikar Amir, associate professor at the School of Social Sciences at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, said many Indonesian students were drawn to the city state because of its reputation as an elite educational hub and the availability of scholarships from the government, universities and corporations.

“Singaporean universities offer world-class infrastructure and educational facilities, which are on a par with, and sometimes even better than, universities in the US, Britain and elsewhere in Europe,” Sulfikar said.

“There’s also added value … because Singapore’s culture is relatively similar to Indonesia. Students can still experience warmth, unlike in cold and individualistic Europe.”

For Siregar, the path towards a Singaporean degree remains uncertain. Though she has yet to receive any sponsors from her pitch, that had not stopped her from pursuing “other passions and stories”.

“I’ve put my dream out there, and if anyone wants to follow along, that’s great,” she said. “But I’m more than my MBA journey.”

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s Forest City wants a rebirth. Scams, crime stand in the way
item.description:
Behind the unmarked door of a shoplot along a quiet commercial stretch of Forest City in Malaysia’s Johor state, four customers sat tapping away, playing slot-style games on tablets.

A stern-looking man stood guard at the entrance, his eyes darting around.

The customers could place bets starting from around 20 ringgit (US$4.89). Instead of handing over cash, they paid for gambling credits using Malaysia’s Touch ’n Go e-wallet. They were then issued tablets from behind the counter with pre-installed slot games.
item.content:encoded:
Behind the unmarked door of a shoplot along a quiet commercial stretch of Forest City in Malaysia’s Johor state, four customers sat tapping away, playing slot-style games on tablets.

A stern-looking man stood guard at the entrance, his eyes darting around.

The customers could place bets starting from around 20 ringgit (US$4.89). Instead of handing over cash, they paid for gambling credits using Malaysia’s Touch ’n Go e-wallet. They were then issued tablets from behind the counter with pre-installed slot games.

“Most of our customers are foreigners. Many play for hours and usually top up their credits a few times,” said the woman manning the counter. Many of them are workers living in Forest City, she said.

The apparent gambling operation observed on a recent visit is among several questionable or controversial activities that have emerged at the sprawling development as it tries to leave its “ghost town” reputation behind.

A US$100 billion megaproject on the southwestern edge of Peninsular Malaysia, Forest City comprises high-rise flats, landed homes and villas interspersed with commercial shop lots.

In July, Johor police arrested 335 people in raids on alleged online scam operations there.

The police seized computers and mobile phones and said the syndicates were involved in schemes including fraudulent cryptocurrency investments and romance scams targeting victims overseas.

That same month, the authorities ordered Network School, a community catering to technology entrepreneurs and digital nomads, to cease operations after finding breaches of licensing conditions and the approved use of its premises.

Residents, property owners and experts said the episodes are a fresh setback for Forest City as it tries to rehabilitate its image and attract investment.

The development has been trying to reinvent itself as an investment destination, anchored by its status as a special financial zone (SFZ).

The SFZ is expected to surpass its 2 billion ringgit investment target this year after attracting more than 250 inquiries from prospective investors including financial institutions, family offices and business services firms.

Criminologist P Sundramoorthy said the scam operations and episodes like Network School have “reputational consequences” for the development.

“It can affect property values, business confidence, tourism, investment decisions and the willingness of people to live and work there,” added Sundramoorthy, who is with Universiti Sains Malaysia.

For some residents, the recent police raids have raised concerns about crime.

Muhammad Aidi Rashid, who rents a two-bedroom flat at Ataraxia Park on the southwestern part of the development, installed closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras outside his door and additional locks after hearing of alleged scam operations in neighbouring blocks.

“I worry for the safety of my wife because she is alone at home when I’m at work,” said Aidi, 33, a technician at nearby Tanjung Pelepas port.

Property agent Aqil Amran, who manages Forest City flats through local firm Ceiloz Realty, said his company has encountered suspected scam operations involving tenants even after the police crackdown.

In one case, a flat owner became suspicious after a tenant’s electricity bill exceeded 1,000 ringgit a month.

“When we went down to the unit to do checks, we saw many tech devices for [alleged] scam activity and we terminated the rental contract and chased the tenant out,” Aqil said, adding that the case was referred to the police.

Sundramoorthy said Forest City’s sizeable number of vacant residential and commercial properties could make it vulnerable to such operations. Based on figures provided by Country Garden in 2023, 9,000 people were living in the development across 28,000 residential units.

“It can provide opportunities for illicit operators to rent premises without immediately attracting attention,” Sundramoorthy said.

Forest City’s location about 10km (6 miles) from the Tuas Second Link and proximity to Singapore could also be attractive to transnational criminal networks, he added, given that the city state is a global air hub.

The July raids underscored the cross-border nature of such operations: police said 332 of the 335 people arrested were foreigners, most of them Chinese nationals, and their targets included people beyond Malaysia’s borders.

Not all of Forest City’s recent controversies have involved alleged criminal activity.

Network School was closed over licensing and premises-use breaches, but Johor-based property consultant Samuel Tan said the episode nevertheless “dealt a blow to Forest City’s public image”.

“In the short term, [both Network School and the scam raids] have naturally heightened buyer and tenant circumspection,” said Tan, CEO of Olive Tree Property Consultants.

“Retail investors and prospective occupiers are understandably cautious, leading to a temporary chilling effect on casual inquiries and rental momentum.”

Before the controversies, Forest City was already seeing weakening prices and thin transaction volumes.

According to property transaction service Datanah, Forest City’s median transaction price between June 2025 and June 2026 was 547 ringgit per sq ft, down 12 per cent from the preceding 12 months.

It recorded only 13 sales between June 2025 and June 2026 in a development with at least 28,000 residential units.

Its latest recorded transaction was on June 18, before the scam raids and Network School saga.

However, experts cautioned that transaction data can lag and there is not enough evidence to attribute the subsequent absence of recorded sales to the controversies.

Forest City’s property market has already struggled for years.

According to Tan, its residential and commercial properties have historically traded at a discount to the wider Johor Bahru market. A three-bedroom Forest City flat is currently valued at around 550,000 ringgit, compared with upwards of 1 million ringgit in Johor Bahru, according to Aqil.

“Because much of its organic residential demand was already subdued, the reputational hit has manifested more as headline noise than a catastrophic collapse in core asset values,” Tan said.

But expectations had been growing that the SFZ and wider Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) could improve Forest City’s fortunes this year, he added.

The development remains firmly a buyer’s market. “On sales especially, demand has been low because there are many owners looking to sell, but there are not many buyers,” Aqil said.

Commercial property owners are feeling another consequence of the recent controversies: greater scrutiny.

Singaporean Justin Ong, 59, who owns a Forest City shoplot for investment, said the management and local authorities have been asking businesses for permits, documentation and proper tenancy agreements following the Network School episode.

Ong is currently renting his shoplot out to a food stall operator on an informal basis and now needs to draw up legal paperwork for submission.

“It makes things cumbersome and businesses will be more wary [of moving operations to Forest City],” he said. “It also adds a layer of administrative work that was previously not required.”

Tan, however, said tighter checks could ultimately benefit Forest City.

“Legitimate financial institutions, family offices and corporate tenants require a well-regulated, clean jurisdiction,” he said.

“Enforcing strict permit protocols signals to the market that the authorities are serious about governance.”

CNA has asked master developer Country Garden about Forest City’s current occupancy rate and whether it has seen recent changes in residential or commercial demand.

CNA has also asked Country Garden and the Johor police about measures to detect and deter illegal activity, and the latter for statistics on crimes reported in Forest City.

Despite the recent bad press, some property owners remain optimistic.

Singaporean investor Tan Kin Lian, who owns two Forest City flats, said the recent episodes have had little impact on residents’ everyday lives.

“Even if these [operations] occupy some of the residential units, they don’t bother the other residents. Now that they are gone, I think life will continue as before,” he said.

He acknowledged that his Forest City properties have declined in value over the years, but believes their relatively low prices and the opportunities created by the SFZ and the JS-SEZ leave room for growth.

“The prices of property in Forest City as compared to that in Singapore are roughly eight times [less], so for Singaporeans, if you’re keen on purchasing a second home and don’t want to pay too much money … it’s an inexpensive option,” he said.

Country Garden has publicly backed the police crackdown and called for a permanent police presence in Forest City.

Munira Mustaffa, executive director of security consultancy Chasseur Group, said this could deter crime but would not address the underlying conditions that allow illicit operations to take root.

Residential areas in Forest City can be accessed by registered owners and tenants using access cards and there are security guards at every entrance. However, Munira noted that this protocol has not been sufficient in deterring scam operations.

The authorities and developers should also improve control of its access and surveillance, engage the community and find legitimate uses for vacant spaces, Munira said.

Sundramoorthy suggested a broader framework involving the police, immigration and customs authorities, the local council and Forest City’s management.

Property owners and agents could also flag warning signs such as unusually high electricity consumption, frequent short-term occupancy or excessive numbers of occupants, he said.

Amid the negative publicity, there have been some promising signs.

Besides the hundreds of investor inquiries about the SFZ through the Invest Malaysia Facilitation Centre Johor, Malaysian entrepreneur Jeff Yew in August reportedly proposed reviving the former Network School site as a technology campus with a “Malaysia first” approach.

“These are indeed substantive reasons for cautious optimism,” Tan said.

Shedding the “ghost town” label will ultimately require legitimate businesses, jobs and people willing to live and work in Forest City for the long term, he added.

For residents such as Aidi, a sense of security is the starting point.

“Hopefully if people feel safe, the right businesses will open and the community will be more vibrant,” he said.

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] China warns Japan over WWII history as business delegation visits Beijing
item.description:
China’s top diplomat Wang Yi and Vice-Premier He Lifeng met Japan’s former foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya in Beijing, marking the highest-ranking Chinese official reception for a Japanese visit in nearly a year.

Analysts, however, cautioned that the high-level reception should not be seen as an opening to a diplomatic thaw. Instead, they viewed the encounter as a calculated exercise by Beijing in selective engagement.

Iwaya arrived in the Chinese capital on Sunday at the head of a 50-member delegation of corporate executives, in a trip aimed at restoring stability to bilateral ties amid heightened friction.
item.content:encoded:
China’s top diplomat Wang Yi and Vice-Premier He Lifeng met Japan’s former foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya in Beijing, marking the highest-ranking Chinese official reception for a Japanese visit in nearly a year.

Analysts, however, cautioned that the high-level reception should not be seen as an opening to a diplomatic thaw. Instead, they viewed the encounter as a calculated exercise by Beijing in selective engagement.

Iwaya arrived in the Chinese capital on Sunday at the head of a 50-member delegation of corporate executives, in a trip aimed at restoring stability to bilateral ties amid heightened friction.

Meeting Iwaya on Monday, Wang warned that bilateral relations were facing a “severe situation” and had “yet to be normalised” ahead of next year’s 55th anniversary of diplomatic ties, according to a read-out from the Chinese foreign ministry.

“A country that challenges its post-war ‘peace constitution’ or attempts to rewrite the history of wartime aggression … cannot face the world, let alone open up a future,” Wang cautioned.

Wang also urged Tokyo to “correct the erroneous words and deeds” of its leadership regarding Taiwan as soon as possible.

Japan must learn from historical lessons on the 80th anniversary of the Tokyo Trials, established by the Allies to try Japanese war criminals after World War II, he added.

Wang is a member of the ruling Communist Party’s elite 24-man Politburo and director of the Central Foreign Affairs Commission office. Iwaya previously travelled to Beijing in December 2024, during his tenure as foreign minister in Shigeru Ishiba’s government.

On Tuesday, Iwaya also met Vice-Premier He at the Great Hall of the People, according to Kyodo News.

The Japanese mission’s arrival in Beijing closely followed last week’s summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump in Washington, where the two leaders hailed the two countries’ wartime alliance against Japan during World War II.

Tokyo has been watching the signs of a stabilising momentum between Beijing and Washington with unease, prompting a 20-minute telephone call on Saturday between Trump and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

Iwaya’s visit, as head of the Japan Association for the Promotion of International Trade, is part of an effort to help break a prolonged bilateral stalemate ignited by Takaichi’s remarks last year about Taiwan.

In November, Takaichi told the Japanese parliament that a Taiwan contingency could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” that could permit Japan to respond as part of collective self-defence.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

The political fallout from Takaichi’s remarks brought official ministerial exchanges between Beijing and Tokyo to an abrupt halt.

On Tuesday, the Chinese foreign ministry issued a scathing rebuke, accusing Tokyo of “abandoning” bilateral diplomatic agreements.

Asked about the “grave difficulties” in relations as the two sides mark 54 years of diplomatic engagement, ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said that Takaichi’s Taiwan remarks “openly challenge China’s national sovereignty and renege on both the original spirit of normalising diplomatic ties and Japan’s political commitments to China”.

Formal channels blocked

The depth of the chill was on display in July when Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi reported a brief interaction with Wang on the sidelines of Asean-related meetings in Manila. Beijing swiftly issued an outright denial, insisting no such contact took place.

With formal channels blocked, Japanese commercial and parliamentary groups have stepped in to keep communications open.

Xu Weijun, an associate research professor at the Institute of Public Policy at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou, said Wang’s reception reflected an upgrade in diplomatic protocol, and that Beijing was beginning to selectively raise its level of engagement with Japan.

China was drawing deliberate distinctions between the Takaichi administration’s security posture and the pragmatic interests of companies, friendship organisations, and moderate factions within the ruling party, he added.

“For Beijing, the primary function of this meeting is not a thaw, but an occasion to reiterate Beijing’s conditions for normalising China-Japan relations.”

Toru Horiuchi, a China-Japan relations expert at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, echoed this view, saying that Iwaya’s visit was a good opportunity for Wang to “reiterate the demand” that Takaichi retract her remarks on Taiwan “if she is serious about promoting better relations”.

The ongoing trade association mission, originally scheduled for June, was delayed following the death of its long-time president, former foreign minister Yohei Kono, who met Chinese Premier Li Qiang in Beijing during a similar trade delegation last year.

During Monday’s talks, Iwaya acknowledged that current ties were “worrying”. He pledged that the association would honour Kono’s legacy and work to steer relations back to the principles of the four foundational China-Japan political documents.

Zhang Yun, a professor of international relations at Nanjing University, said Wang’s remarks reflected a hope that Iwaya could carry forward Kono’s legacy, continue contributing to China-Japan ties, and encourage other friendly Japanese figures and groups to contribute to the advancement of bilateral ties.

He added that Japan’s current strategy – maintaining cordiality with the US while lacking communication with China – risked leaving it diplomatically compromised.

“Out of fear of being bypassed, Takaichi rushes to meet the US beforehand to talk up the China threat, and afterwards hopes to be better informed about what was discussed. This model is unsustainable.”

Rather than worrying about being bypassed, it would be better for Tokyo to contemplate how to actually improve relations with Beijing, Zhang said.

The Wang-Iwaya meeting builds on a succession of Japanese business and legislative delegations to Beijing.

Chinese foreign vice-minister Hua Chunying received an interim four-member mission of the Japanese trade association June, while Lu Kang, a deputy director of the ruling party’s international department, met a bipartisan group of young Japanese parliamentarians in late August.

In mid-September, another delegation of young lawmakers from the Japan-China Friendship Parliamentarians’ Union was received by assistant foreign minister Liu Bin.

Meanwhile, with Takaichi showing no signs of retracting her remarks, Horiuchi expressed doubts that the encounter would pave the way for a bilateral leaders’ meeting at the Apec summit in Shenzhen in November.

“Such a meeting without Japanese concession would be politically risky for Xi,” he observed.

In a recent nationwide survey by Japanese media outlet Asahi Shimbun, 57 per cent of respondents were of the view that Takaichi should make efforts to improve ties with China.

Among supporters of Takaichi’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party, 58 per cent said an improved relationship with China was necessary.

item.title: [SCMP] Bukhara Biennial spearheads cultural blossoming of the city as well as the wider Uzbekistan
item.description:
It might sound and look like an odd juxtaposition: chef-nun Jeong Kwan, of Netflix documentary series Chef’s Table fame, unearthing kimchi she has been fermenting for 10 weeks next to a new installation by British sculptor Antony Gormley.

Yet, set in Bukhara’s 16th century Khoja Kalon Mosque, the two made perfect sense as collaborative highlights of the closing ceremony of the inaugural Bukhara Biennial, which ran from September 5 to November 23 last year.

A contemporary art festival, the Bukhara Biennial was conceived by the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF) and forms part of a broader plan to revitalise Uzbekistan’s living heritage as well as establish a permanent cultural district in the historic city. Its first theme, “Recipes for Broken Hearts”, was inspired by Uzbekistan’s national dish, plov. A hearty meal of rice layered with meat, spices and vegetables, the ideas of healing and restoration imbued in plov were the conceptual crux of the gastronomy, art, craft, architecture, music and performance on display.
item.content:encoded:
It might sound and look like an odd juxtaposition: chef-nun Jeong Kwan, of Netflix documentary series Chef’s Table fame, unearthing kimchi she has been fermenting for 10 weeks next to a new installation by British sculptor Antony Gormley.

Yet, set in Bukhara’s 16th century Khoja Kalon Mosque, the two made perfect sense as collaborative highlights of the closing ceremony of the inaugural Bukhara Biennial, which ran from September 5 to November 23 last year.

A contemporary art festival, the Bukhara Biennial was conceived by the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF) and forms part of a broader plan to revitalise Uzbekistan’s living heritage as well as establish a permanent cultural district in the historic city. Its first theme, “Recipes for Broken Hearts”, was inspired by Uzbekistan’s national dish, plov. A hearty meal of rice layered with meat, spices and vegetables, the ideas of healing and restoration imbued in plov were the conceptual crux of the gastronomy, art, craft, architecture, music and performance on display.

Gormley’s Close (2025) – created from mud bricks with Uzbek artist Temur Jumaev – channelled the theme by exploring vulnerability, communal recovery and a reconnection to ancestral roots. Jeong Kwan’s kimchi was woven into a collaborative culinary performance with Indian artist Subodh Gupta. Blending Korean temple food with Bihari fare, the hybrid meal was served inside Gupta’s pavilion-like installation, Salt Carried With the Wind (2024-25), situated outside the Ayozjon Caravanserai, one of four in an interconnected complex, on a site once occupied by Bukhara’s spice market.

All through the event, the locations were significant, as the Bukhara Biennial was designed to house site-specific installations, soundscapes and performances not in purpose-built, white-cube galleries, but in restored or adapted caravanserais (merchant inns), madrasas (educational institutions), trading domes and mosques. While fellow Silk Road stopover Samarkand and the national capital, Tashkent, are undergoing their own cultural transformations, this preservation-first approach is what sets Bukhara apart.

Since its establishment in the 6th century BC as one of the main centres of the Persian Empire, Bukhara’s status grew as a spiritual nexus for Sufism and as an intellectual hub and home to scholars, poets and artisans. That Bukhara has lived many lives is evident from both its monumental buildings, spanning the 5th to 20th centuries, and the most intricately embroidered gold zardosi motifs and ikat prints on silks and various textiles found in the shops of the Old Town.

In the city’s Registan square, the curved, mounded walls of the Ark of Bukhara, a sizeable citadel, stand tall. Built in the 5th century, the compound housed rulers and their courts until 1920, when it was attacked by the Soviet Red Army, which deposed the emir of Bukhara and established Bolshevik rule. Next to the fortress stands the most prominent reminder of that later era: the steely, industrial Shukhov Tower, a water supply, forming a visual paradox that differentiates Bukhara from the more uniform Tashkent, where the Soviet influence is starkly evident in the brutalist buildings that dominate that city.

Across the street from the Ark of Bukhara, the early-18th century Bolo Hauz Mosque dazzles with its intricate, three-dimensional muqarnas decoration and vibrant mosaic tilework. Its linear lines present a striking contrast to the more rounded, ancient structures elsewhere in the Old Town, both charting the evolution of Islamic architecture. Just a short walk away stands the 10th century Ismail Samani Mausoleum, the soft, circular geometry and woven pattern capturing an aesthetic from when the region’s prominent Zoroastrian community was in the early stages of converting to Islam.

Revitalising these venerated sites, and others, was a crucial aspect of the agenda, as “the plan to reanimate restored and previously closed landmarks and open them up as living sites of making and dialogue was […] appreciated not only by the inhabitants of Bukhara, but also the tourists”, claims Gayane Umerova, chairwoman of the ACDF and the commissioner behind the inaugural Bukhara Biennial.

She enlisted Dubai- and Tokyo-based Lebanese architect Wael Al Awar and his studio, Waiwai, to execute this vision, to revive and make accessible to its inhabitants as much of Bukhara’s history as possible. In addition to repairing mosques, caravanserais and other structures, the most dramatic intervention the architect made was to pedestrianise large parts of the Old Town. “We created outdoor spaces, seating and platforms where the local community could gather recreationally, and use beyond the biennial,” says Al Awar.
